docs.text: Module 7, Part II: Finite And Infinite Rod Theory ¶ This is the second part of Module 7. Read Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations first, then use this derivation in Part III: Rod Instrument And Stationary Fin . This reference develops Lienhard and Lienhard Section 4.5, textbook pp. 163-173. It collects Eqs. (4.27)-(4.51) in one place so you can follow the logic from a physical fin to the finite-length and infinite-length rod models used in Module 7, Part III. Module 7 Priorities ¶ Module 7 has two priorities, in this order: Build the six-thermistor instrument. This is the primary objective of the module. Establish one TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors as a checked measurement system, then develop the Arduino acquisition and Python software needed to display and record all six temperatures together. The default is to use the raw readings when the six sensors agree within \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) in a common bath; apply calibration corrections only if that check fails. Understand heat transport in a long, thin cylinder. Use Fourier's law, conservation of energy, side cooling, and boundary conditions to develop and test the one-dimensional heat-transport model for the rod. Part II concentrates on the second priority. Its finite-rod and semi-infinite solutions are the predictions that the six-thermistor instrument will test in Part III. How to use your time. Parts I and II are primarily work to complete at home. You may use up to one hour of class time to begin this theory work; then finish it at home and bring specific questions to class. Preserve the remaining laboratory time for Part III, where you will build, check, and test the six-thermistor instrument and its software. Learning Objectives ¶ These are the Part II objectives supporting Module 7's second priority. By the end of Module 7, Part II, you should be able to: Use Fourier conduction, Newton cooling, and conservation of energy to derive the stationary one-dimensional heat equation and check every term's units. Apply the base-temperature and insulated-tip boundary conditions to obtain the finite-rod temperature profile. Interpret \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) and \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=hPL^2/(kA)\) as resistance ratios that compare radial conduction with surface convection and axial conduction with distributed side convection, respectively. Obtain the semi-infinite exponential profile as a limit of the finite-rod solution and quantify the resulting approximation error at the sensor positions. Recognize the range of applications of fins for heat transfer. Part II Vocabulary And Notation ¶ This table extends the foundational Module 7 vocabulary from Part I . Term Meaning Fin A solid that conducts heat along its length while exchanging heat with the surrounding fluid through its surface. Analysis base and tip The analysis base at \(x=0\) is the plane where the rod temperature is measured or prescribed; the tip at \(x=L\) is the far end of the analyzed section. For the course rod, the first thermistor hole is the analysis base. \(A\) , \(P\) , and \(PL\) \(A\) is the cross-sectional area normal to axial heat flow, \(P\) is the cross-sectional perimeter, and \(PL\) is the lateral surface area of a uniform rod, excluding its ends. Stationary or steady state A condition in which temperature no longer changes with time, although heat can continue to flow. Boundary condition A physical constraint imposed at a boundary, such as prescribed base temperature, zero tip heat flux, or convection from the tip. Adiabatic or insulated tip A tip through which no heat flows: \(dT/dx=0\) at \(x=L\) . Convecting tip A tip that transfers heat to the surroundings with coefficient \(h_L\) . Normalized excess temperature, \(\Theta\) \(\Theta=(T-T_\infty)/(T_0-T_\infty)\) ; it is 1 at the prescribed-temperature base and dimensionless. Dimensionless position, \(\xi=x/L\) Position scaled by the analyzed length from the first thermistor hole to the tip, placing the analysis base at \(\xi=0\) and the tip at \(\xi=1\) . Fin parameter, \(m=\sqrt{hP/(kA)}\) The inverse axial decay length, with units m \(^{-1}\) . The characteristic decay length is \(1/m\) . \(mL\) Rod length divided by decay length. It measures how strongly the finite tip can influence the temperature profile. Transverse Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}=h(A/P)/k\) The resistance ratio testing whether radial temperature variation across a section may be neglected. Parallel Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=hPL^2/(kA)=(mL)^2\) The course's descriptive name for the resistance ratio comparing axial conduction over the rod length with distributed side convection. Lienhard calls it a hybrid Biot number. Tip Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}=h_LL/k\) The dimensionless strength of convection from the tip relative to axial conduction. It drops out for an insulated tip. Finite and semi-infinite models The finite model retains the boundary at \(x=L\) ; the semi-infinite model neglects the far-end influence over the measured region. How To Use This Reference ¶ Read this page alongside Lienhard Section 4.5 for A4. Use the single Module 7 workload budget for all three parts; do not count this reading a second time. This page is not a separate submission and should not be copied into another report. Annotate the derivation with three questions in mind: Which term comes from Fourier conduction along the rod? Which term comes from Newton cooling through the rod's side? Which boundary condition distinguishes the finite insulated-tip solution from the semi-infinite solution? What A Fin Does ¶ A fin conducts heat along a solid while exchanging heat with the surrounding fluid through its surface. Increasing surface area can greatly increase heat transfer. Extended metal surfaces increase the area available for heat transfer. Here fins are used to cool a CPU in a computer. Lienhard and Lienhard, Fig. 4.7, textbook p. 165: a speculative biological example of cooling fins. Thermal fins appear in technologies ranging from air-cooled engines to semiconductor heat sinks. The same conduction problem appears in each case, and the fin loses heat to the surrounding air by natural or forced convection. Sidebar: Where Are Thermal Fins Used? The common design idea is to conduct heat from a source into an extended solid surface. What happens at that surface depends on the application. Application Heat reaches the extended surface by Heat leaves the surface by Electronic heat sink Conduction from a semiconductor package Natural or fan-driven convection Air-cooled engine Conduction through the cylinder and cylinder head Convection to air moving naturally, with the vehicle, or from a fan Both applications use Newton's law of cooling, \[ \dot Q_{\mathrm{conv}}=hA_s\left(T_s-T_\infty\right), \] where natural or forced airflow continually replaces warmed air near the fins and carries the transferred heat away. Geometry And The One-Dimensional Assumption ¶ Lienhard and Lienhard, Fig. 4.8, textbook p. 166: a fin of length \(L\) , cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , conductivity \(k\) , side coefficient \(h\) , and tip coefficient \(h_L\) . Course coordinate convention. In the textbook figure, the base is the physical end where the fin joins the warmer body. For the course rod, we choose the first thermistor hole as the analysis base and define it to be \(x=0\) . It is neither the physical end of the rod nor the thermistor embedded in the TEC. Its measured temperature supplies the boundary value \(T(0,t)\) , and \(L\) is the distance from this first hole to the rod tip. Choosing this interior reference plane is valid because the equations apply to the portion of rod from that plane to the tip. As derived in Part I , the transverse Biot number must be small to treat a cylinder as a one-dimensional object: \[ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} =\frac{h(A/P)}{k}\ll1. \tag{4.27} \] Transverse And Parallel Resistance Ratios ¶ Part I defines the Biot number as a ratio of thermal resistances. Applied across a rod section, \[ \boxed{ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} \sim \frac{R_{\mathrm{radial\ conduction}}} {R_{\mathrm{surface\ convection}}} =\frac{h(A/P)}{k} }. \] For a circular rod, \(A/P=R/2\) . Thus \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) means that only a small center-to-surface temperature difference is needed to supply the heat lost to the air, so each cross section is nearly isothermal. This is the same argument developed in Part I and is not a comparison with axial conduction. For the axial comparison, assume a uniform cylindrical rod of length \(L\) , constant cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , conductivity \(k\) , and side heat-transfer coefficient \(h\) . Axial conduction crosses the end-on area \(A\) , whereas side convection acts over the cylinder's entire lateral area \(PL\) (excluding the two ends). The characteristic heat-transfer rates are therefore \[ \dot Q_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}} \sim \frac{kA}{L}\Delta T_{\parallel}, \qquad \dot Q_{\mathrm{side\ convection}} \sim hPL\Delta T_{\mathrm{side}}. \] Here \(\Delta T_{\parallel}\) is a representative temperature change along the rod, while \(\Delta T_{\mathrm{side}}\) is a representative rod-to-room temperature difference. They are not generally the same actual temperature difference. To compare the capacities of the two transport mechanisms, use a common characteristic temperature scale \(\Delta T\) . Equivalently, \[ R_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}}\sim\frac{L}{kA}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{side\ convection}}\sim\frac{1}{hPL}. \] Their ratio defines the parallel Biot number: \[ \boxed{ \mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel} \equiv \frac{R_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}}} {R_{\mathrm{side\ convection}}} =\frac{hPL^2}{kA} =(mL)^2 }. \] We use the descriptive name \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\) in this course because the ratio compares axial conduction with distributed side convection. Lienhard describes the same quantity \((mL)^2\) as a hybrid Biot number . When \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\ll1\) , axial conduction carries heat along the rod readily compared with side convection. When \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\gg1\) , much of the heat is lost from the side before it reaches the far end, and the temperature decays strongly along the rod. The side loss is distributed continuously rather than occurring in one lump, so this resistance ratio is a scaling interpretation of the fin equation. The condition that justifies a one-dimensional fin model is \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) : it allows each cross section to be represented by one temperature \(T(x)\) . The value of \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=(mL)^2\) does not determine whether the model is one-dimensional. Instead, it determines how strongly the temperature decays along the rod. When \(mL\) is sufficiently large, the measured region may also be approximated as semi-infinite. Energy Balance And Differential Equation ¶ Steady-state assumption. Part I derived the time-dependent heat equation for conduction without side loss. Here we add distributed convective cooling from the side of the rod, but first consider only the stationary temperature profile. At steady state, the temperature at every position is constant in time: \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=0. \] Each differential slice therefore stores no net energy. Axial heat conducted into the slice minus axial heat conducted out must equal the heat lost by convection from its side. An energy balance on a slice of width \(\delta x\) with cross-sectional area \(A\) and side area \(P\delta x\) , as shown in Lienhard Figure 4.8 is \[ -kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x+\delta x} +kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_x +hP\delta x\,[T(x)-T_\infty]=0. \tag{4.28} \] As \(\delta x\rightarrow0\) , \[ \frac{ \left.dT/dx\right|_{x+\delta x} -\left.dT/dx\right|_x }{\delta x} \rightarrow \frac{d^2T}{dx^2} =\frac{d^2(T-T_\infty)}{dx^2}. \tag{4.29} \] Therefore, \[ \frac{d^2(T-T_\infty)}{dx^2} =\frac{hP}{kA}(T-T_\infty). \tag{4.30} \] Solving this second-order differential equation requires two boundary conditions. Three common types appear in heat-transfer problems: Dirichlet boundary condition. This condition specifies the temperature itself. At the base of the rod, \[ T(0)=T_0. \] Neumann boundary condition. This condition specifies the temperature derivative, or equivalently the conductive heat flux. An insulated tip has zero heat flux: \[ \left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x=L}=0. \] Robin boundary condition. This condition relates the temperature to its derivative. At a convecting tip, conductive heat flow to the tip equals heat loss from the tip by Newton's law of cooling: \[ -kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x=L} =h_LA\left[T(L)-T_\infty\right]. \] Thus, the base has a Dirichlet condition. For a convecting tip, the second condition is Robin: \[ (T-T_\infty)_{x=0}=T_0-T_\infty, \qquad -kA\left.\frac{d(T-T_\infty)}{dx}\right|_{x=L} =h_LA(T-T_\infty)_{x=L}. \tag{4.31a} \] For an insulated tip, the second condition is Neumann: \[ (T-T_\infty)_{x=0}=T_0-T_\infty, \qquad \left.\frac{d(T-T_\infty)}{dx}\right|_{x=L}=0. \tag{4.31b} \] Dimensional Analysis And Dimensionless Form ¶ The dimensional functional relation is \[ T-T_\infty =\operatorname{fn}(T_0-T_\infty,x,L,kA,hP,h_LA). \tag{4.32} \] Define \[ \Theta=\frac{T-T_\infty}{T_0-T_\infty}, \qquad \xi=\frac{x}{L}, \qquad m=\sqrt{\frac{hP}{kA}}, \qquad \mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}=\frac{h_LL}{k}. \] Then a convecting-tip fin has \[ \Theta=\operatorname{fn} \left(\xi,mL,\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}\right), \tag{4.33a} \] whereas an adiabatic-tip fin has \[ \Theta=\operatorname{fn}(\xi,mL). \tag{4.33b} \] Choosing A Dimensionless Position Coordinate ¶ The quantity \(m\) is not itself a dimensionless coordinate: it has units of inverse length. Both \[ \xi=\frac{x}{L} \qquad\text{and}\qquad X=mx=\frac{x}{1/m} \] are valid dimensionless coordinates, but they emphasize different length scales. The rod length \(L\) is the geometric scale, whereas \(1/m\) is the thermal decay length set by axial conduction and side cooling. For a finite rod, \(\xi=x/L\) is convenient because the base is always at \(\xi=0\) and the tip is always at \(\xi=1\) . The physics then appears in the separate dimensionless group \[ mL=\frac{L}{1/m}, \] which compares the rod length with the thermal decay length. We could instead use \(X=mx\) . Equation (4.34) would then become \[ \frac{d^2\Theta}{dX^2}=\Theta, \] but the tip would be located at \(X=mL\) rather than at a fixed coordinate. Nothing physical changes because \(X=(mL)\xi\) ; the two choices merely organize the same information differently. When the rod is effectively infinite and the tip no longer matters, \(mx\) becomes the natural coordinate and the solution is \(\Theta=e^{-mx}\) . Lienhard, p. 167, Eqs. (4.32)-(4.33b) uses \(\xi=x/L\) for the finite-fin dimensional analysis. On p. 173, Eq. (4.50) , the long-fin limit is written as \(e^{-mL\xi}=e^{-mx}\) , and the following paragraph interprets \((mL)^2\) as a hybrid Biot number comparing axial conduction resistance with the overall resistance to side convection. Why The Tip Biot Number Disappears For An Adiabatic Tip ¶ For a convecting tip, \(h_L\) enters through the tip boundary condition: \[ -\left.\frac{d\Theta}{d\xi}\right|_{\xi=1} =\underbrace{\frac{h_LL}{k}}_{\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}}\Theta(1). \] Thus \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}\) measures the strength of convection from the tip relative to axial conduction. For an adiabatic tip, the heat flux at the tip is zero: \[ \left.\frac{d\Theta}{d\xi}\right|_{\xi=1}=0. \] There is no tip heat-transfer coefficient \(h_L\) in this boundary condition. Consequently, \(h_L\) is absent from the dimensional functional relation and no independent tip Biot number can be formed. Equivalently, one may set \(h_L=0\) and obtain \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}=0\) , but saying that the parameter drops out of the problem better expresses the dimensional-analysis logic. The transverse Biot number does not disappear: it remains the separate test of whether each cross section can be assigned one temperature. Lienhard, p. 167, immediately following Eq. (4.33a) makes this variable-counting argument explicitly: removing \(h_L\) leaves one fewer variable but the same fundamental dimensions, so the corresponding dimensionless group \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}\) is removed, giving Eq. (4.33b). The differential equation becomes \[ \frac{d^2\Theta}{d\xi^2}=(mL)^2\Theta. \tag{4.34} \] Its general solution is \[ \Theta=C_1e^{mL\xi}+C_2e^{-mL\xi}. \tag{4.35} \] Sidebar: Finite Rod With An Insulated Tip The dimensionless boundary conditions are \[ \Theta(0)=1, \qquad \left.\frac{d\Theta}{d\xi}\right|_{\xi=1}=0. \tag{4.36} \] Substitution into the general solution gives \[ C_1+C_2=1, \qquad C_1e^{mL}-C_2e^{-mL}=0. \tag{4.37} \] The hyperbolic functions used to simplify the result are \[ \begin{aligned} \sinh z&=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{2},& \cosh z&=\frac{e^z+e^{-z}}{2},\\ \tanh z&=\frac{\sinh z}{\cosh z},& \coth z&=\frac{\cosh z}{\sinh z}. \end{aligned} \tag{4.38} \] Their needed derivatives are \[ \frac{d}{dz}\sinh z=\cosh z, \qquad \frac{d}{dz}\cosh z=\sinh z. \tag{4.39} \] The constants are \[ C_1=\frac{e^{-mL}}{2\cosh(mL)}, \qquad C_2=1-\frac{e^{-mL}}{2\cosh(mL)}. \tag{4.40} \] The finite insulated-tip temperature distribution is \[ \Theta(\xi) =\frac{\cosh[mL(1-\xi)]}{\cosh(mL)} =\frac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)}. \tag{4.41} \] The heat-transfer rate at the base is \[ \dot Q_0 =-kA\left.\frac{d(T-T_\infty)}{dx}\right|_{x=0}. \tag{4.42} \] Thus, \[ \frac{\dot Q_0L}{kA(T_0-T_\infty)} =mL\frac{\sinh(mL)}{\cosh(mL)} =mL\tanh(mL), \tag{4.43} \] or \[ \frac{\dot Q_0} {\sqrt{kAhP}\,(T_0-T_\infty)} =\tanh(mL). \tag{4.44} \] At the tip, \[ \Theta_{\mathrm{tip}}=\frac{1}{\cosh(mL)}. \tag{4.45} \] Sidebar: Exact Convecting-Tip Solution The dimensionless boundary conditions become \[ \Theta(0)=1, \qquad -\left.\frac{d\Theta}{d\xi}\right|_{\xi=1} =\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}\Theta(1). \tag{4.46} \] Substitution into the general solution gives \[ \begin{aligned} C_1+C_2&=1,\\ -mL(C_1e^{mL}-C_2e^{-mL}) &=\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}} (C_1e^{mL}+C_2e^{-mL}). \end{aligned} \tag{4.47} \] The exact temperature distribution is \[ \Theta(\xi) = \frac{ \cosh[mL(1-\xi)] +(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}/mL)\sinh[mL(1-\xi)] }{ \cosh(mL) +(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}/mL)\sinh(mL) }. \tag{4.48} \] The corresponding base heat rate is \[ \frac{\dot Q_0} {\sqrt{kAhP}\,(T_0-T_\infty)} = \frac{ (\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}/mL)+\tanh(mL) }{ 1+(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}/mL)\tanh(mL) }. \tag{4.49} \] Infinite-Rod Limit ¶ When \(mL\gg1\) , the finite solution approaches \[ \lim_{mL\rightarrow\infty}\Theta =e^{-mL\xi} =e^{-mx}. \tag{4.50} \] The base heat rate becomes \[ \dot Q_0=\sqrt{kAhP}\,(T_0-T_\infty). \tag{4.51} \] Equation (4.51) follows directly from the infinite-rod temperature profile. Because \[ \Theta =\frac{T(x)-T_\infty}{T_0-T_\infty} =e^{-mx}, \] the dimensional temperature profile is \[ T(x)-T_\infty=(T_0-T_\infty)e^{-mx}. \] Fourier's law gives the heat entering the rod at its base: \[ \dot Q_0 =-kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x=0}. \] Differentiating the temperature profile gives \[ \frac{dT}{dx} =-m(T_0-T_\infty)e^{-mx}. \] At the base, \(x=0\) and \(e^{-mx}=1\) , so \[ \dot Q_0=kAm(T_0-T_\infty). \] Finally, substituting \(m=\sqrt{hP/(kA)}\) gives \[ kAm =kA\sqrt{\frac{hP}{kA}} =\sqrt{kAhP}, \] which produces Eq. (4.51). Physically, this is the rate at which heat must enter the base to replace all the heat lost by convection from the surface of the semi-infinite fin. Lienhard recommends \(mL\gtrsim5\) when using the infinite-fin approximation for temperature and \(mL\gtrsim3\) when using it for the base heat rate. In Module 7, Part III, you will calculate the actual finite-versus-infinite error at every sensor rather than relying only on these general thresholds. What To Be Able To Explain ¶ Why does Eq. (4.27) concern the radius , whereas \(mL\) concerns the length ? Which term in Eq. (4.28) represents side heat loss? What physical assumption changes Eq. (4.31a) into Eq. (4.31b)? How does Eq. (4.41) retain information about the far end? Why is Eq. (4.50) an approximation rather than a new physical law? Starting from Eq. (4.28), derive Eq. (4.30) and check every term's units. Starting from the general solution, use the base and insulated-tip boundary conditions to obtain Eq. (4.41). Show mathematically how Eq. (4.41) approaches Eq. (4.50) when the far end becomes irrelevant. These are assessed in the A4 written derivation and may be sampled in the C5 oral check. Understanding the derivation matters more than reproducing a long sequence of algebra from memory.

docs.text: This is the second part of Module 7. Read Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations first, then use this derivation in Part III: Rod Instrument And Stationary Fin . This reference develops Lienhard and Lienhard Section 4.5, textbook pp. 163-173. It collects Eqs. (4.27)-(4.51) in one place so you can follow the logic from a physical fin to the finite-length and infinite-length rod models used in Module 7, Part III.
docs.title: Module 7, Part II: Finite And Infinite Rod Theory

docs.text: Module 7 has two priorities, in this order: Build the six-thermistor instrument. This is the primary objective of the module. Establish one TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors as a checked measurement system, then develop the Arduino acquisition and Python software needed to display and record all six temperatures together. The default is to use the raw readings when the six sensors agree within \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) in a common bath; apply calibration corrections only if that check fails. Understand heat transport in a long, thin cylinder. Use Fourier's law, conservation of energy, side cooling, and boundary conditions to develop and test the one-dimensional heat-transport model for the rod. Part II concentrates on the second priority. Its finite-rod and semi-infinite solutions are the predictions that the six-thermistor instrument will test in Part III. How to use your time. Parts I and II are primarily work to complete at home. You may use up to one hour of class time to begin this theory work; then finish it at home and bring specific questions to class. Preserve the remaining laboratory time for Part III, where you will build, check, and test the six-thermistor instrument and its software.

docs.text: These are the Part II objectives supporting Module 7's second priority. By the end of Module 7, Part II, you should be able to: Use Fourier conduction, Newton cooling, and conservation of energy to derive the stationary one-dimensional heat equation and check every term's units. Apply the base-temperature and insulated-tip boundary conditions to obtain the finite-rod temperature profile. Interpret \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) and \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=hPL^2/(kA)\) as resistance ratios that compare radial conduction with surface convection and axial conduction with distributed side convection, respectively. Obtain the semi-infinite exponential profile as a limit of the finite-rod solution and quantify the resulting approximation error at the sensor positions. Recognize the range of applications of fins for heat transfer.
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: This table extends the foundational Module 7 vocabulary from Part I . Term Meaning Fin A solid that conducts heat along its length while exchanging heat with the surrounding fluid through its surface. Analysis base and tip The analysis base at \(x=0\) is the plane where the rod temperature is measured or prescribed; the tip at \(x=L\) is the far end of the analyzed section. For the course rod, the first thermistor hole is the analysis base. \(A\) , \(P\) , and \(PL\) \(A\) is the cross-sectional area normal to axial heat flow, \(P\) is the cross-sectional perimeter, and \(PL\) is the lateral surface area of a uniform rod, excluding its ends. Stationary or steady state A condition in which temperature no longer changes with time, although heat can continue to flow. Boundary condition A physical constraint imposed at a boundary, such as prescribed base temperature, zero tip heat flux, or convection from the tip. Adiabatic or insulated tip A tip through which no heat flows: \(dT/dx=0\) at \(x=L\) . Convecting tip A tip that transfers heat to the surroundings with coefficient \(h_L\) . Normalized excess temperature, \(\Theta\) \(\Theta=(T-T_\infty)/(T_0-T_\infty)\) ; it is 1 at the prescribed-temperature base and dimensionless. Dimensionless position, \(\xi=x/L\) Position scaled by the analyzed length from the first thermistor hole to the tip, placing the analysis base at \(\xi=0\) and the tip at \(\xi=1\) . Fin parameter, \(m=\sqrt{hP/(kA)}\) The inverse axial decay length, with units m \(^{-1}\) . The characteristic decay length is \(1/m\) . \(mL\) Rod length divided by decay length. It measures how strongly the finite tip can influence the temperature profile. Transverse Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}=h(A/P)/k\) The resistance ratio testing whether radial temperature variation across a section may be neglected. Parallel Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=hPL^2/(kA)=(mL)^2\) The course's descriptive name for the resistance ratio comparing axial conduction over the rod length with distributed side convection. Lienhard calls it a hybrid Biot number. Tip Biot number, \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}=h_LL/k\) The dimensionless strength of convection from the tip relative to axial conduction. It drops out for an insulated tip. Finite and semi-infinite models The finite model retains the boundary at \(x=L\) ; the semi-infinite model neglects the far-end influence over the measured region.

docs.title: How To Use This Reference

docs.text: A fin conducts heat along a solid while exchanging heat with the surrounding fluid through its surface. Increasing surface area can greatly increase heat transfer. Extended metal surfaces increase the area available for heat transfer. Here fins are used to cool a CPU in a computer. Lienhard and Lienhard, Fig. 4.7, textbook p. 165: a speculative biological example of cooling fins. Thermal fins appear in technologies ranging from air-cooled engines to semiconductor heat sinks. The same conduction problem appears in each case, and the fin loses heat to the surrounding air by natural or forced convection. Sidebar: Where Are Thermal Fins Used? The common design idea is to conduct heat from a source into an extended solid surface. What happens at that surface depends on the application. Application Heat reaches the extended surface by Heat leaves the surface by Electronic heat sink Conduction from a semiconductor package Natural or fan-driven convection Air-cooled engine Conduction through the cylinder and cylinder head Convection to air moving naturally, with the vehicle, or from a fan Both applications use Newton's law of cooling, \[ \dot Q_{\mathrm{conv}}=hA_s\left(T_s-T_\infty\right), \] where natural or forced airflow continually replaces warmed air near the fins and carries the transferred heat away.
docs.title: What A Fin Does

docs.text: Lienhard and Lienhard, Fig. 4.8, textbook p. 166: a fin of length \(L\) , cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , conductivity \(k\) , side coefficient \(h\) , and tip coefficient \(h_L\) . Course coordinate convention. In the textbook figure, the base is the physical end where the fin joins the warmer body. For the course rod, we choose the first thermistor hole as the analysis base and define it to be \(x=0\) . It is neither the physical end of the rod nor the thermistor embedded in the TEC. Its measured temperature supplies the boundary value \(T(0,t)\) , and \(L\) is the distance from this first hole to the rod tip. Choosing this interior reference plane is valid because the equations apply to the portion of rod from that plane to the tip. As derived in Part I , the transverse Biot number must be small to treat a cylinder as a one-dimensional object: \[ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} =\frac{h(A/P)}{k}\ll1. \tag{4.27} \]
docs.title: Geometry And The One-Dimensional Assumption

docs.text: Part I defines the Biot number as a ratio of thermal resistances. Applied across a rod section, \[ \boxed{ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} \sim \frac{R_{\mathrm{radial\ conduction}}} {R_{\mathrm{surface\ convection}}} =\frac{h(A/P)}{k} }. \] For a circular rod, \(A/P=R/2\) . Thus \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) means that only a small center-to-surface temperature difference is needed to supply the heat lost to the air, so each cross section is nearly isothermal. This is the same argument developed in Part I and is not a comparison with axial conduction. For the axial comparison, assume a uniform cylindrical rod of length \(L\) , constant cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , conductivity \(k\) , and side heat-transfer coefficient \(h\) . Axial conduction crosses the end-on area \(A\) , whereas side convection acts over the cylinder's entire lateral area \(PL\) (excluding the two ends). The characteristic heat-transfer rates are therefore \[ \dot Q_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}} \sim \frac{kA}{L}\Delta T_{\parallel}, \qquad \dot Q_{\mathrm{side\ convection}} \sim hPL\Delta T_{\mathrm{side}}. \] Here \(\Delta T_{\parallel}\) is a representative temperature change along the rod, while \(\Delta T_{\mathrm{side}}\) is a representative rod-to-room temperature difference. They are not generally the same actual temperature difference. To compare the capacities of the two transport mechanisms, use a common characteristic temperature scale \(\Delta T\) . Equivalently, \[ R_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}}\sim\frac{L}{kA}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{side\ convection}}\sim\frac{1}{hPL}. \] Their ratio defines the parallel Biot number: \[ \boxed{ \mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel} \equiv \frac{R_{\mathrm{axial\ conduction}}} {R_{\mathrm{side\ convection}}} =\frac{hPL^2}{kA} =(mL)^2 }. \] We use the descriptive name \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\) in this course because the ratio compares axial conduction with distributed side convection. Lienhard describes the same quantity \((mL)^2\) as a hybrid Biot number . When \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\ll1\) , axial conduction carries heat along the rod readily compared with side convection. When \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}\gg1\) , much of the heat is lost from the side before it reaches the far end, and the temperature decays strongly along the rod. The side loss is distributed continuously rather than occurring in one lump, so this resistance ratio is a scaling interpretation of the fin equation. The condition that justifies a one-dimensional fin model is \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) : it allows each cross section to be represented by one temperature \(T(x)\) . The value of \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\parallel}=(mL)^2\) does not determine whether the model is one-dimensional. Instead, it determines how strongly the temperature decays along the rod. When \(mL\) is sufficiently large, the measured region may also be approximated as semi-infinite.
docs.title: Transverse And Parallel Resistance Ratios

docs.text: Steady-state assumption. Part I derived the time-dependent heat equation for conduction without side loss. Here we add distributed convective cooling from the side of the rod, but first consider only the stationary temperature profile. At steady state, the temperature at every position is constant in time: \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=0. \] Each differential slice therefore stores no net energy. Axial heat conducted into the slice minus axial heat conducted out must equal the heat lost by convection from its side. An energy balance on a slice of width \(\delta x\) with cross-sectional area \(A\) and side area \(P\delta x\) , as shown in Lienhard Figure 4.8 is \[ -kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x+\delta x} +kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_x +hP\delta x\,[T(x)-T_\infty]=0. \tag{4.28} \] As \(\delta x\rightarrow0\) , \[ \frac{ \left.dT/dx\right|_{x+\delta x} -\left.dT/dx\right|_x }{\delta x} \rightarrow \frac{d^2T}{dx^2} =\frac{d^2(T-T_\infty)}{dx^2}. \tag{4.29} \] Therefore, \[ \frac{d^2(T-T_\infty)}{dx^2} =\frac{hP}{kA}(T-T_\infty). \tag{4.30} \] Solving this second-order differential equation requires two boundary conditions. Three common types appear in heat-transfer problems: Dirichlet boundary condition. This condition specifies the temperature itself. At the base of the rod, \[ T(0)=T_0. \] Neumann boundary condition. This condition specifies the temperature derivative, or equivalently the conductive heat flux. An insulated tip has zero heat flux: \[ \left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x=L}=0. \] Robin boundary condition. This condition relates the temperature to its derivative. At a convecting tip, conductive heat flow to the tip equals heat loss from the tip by Newton's law of cooling: \[ -kA\left.\frac{dT}{dx}\right|_{x=L} =h_LA\left[T(L)-T_\infty\right]. \] Thus, the base has a Dirichlet condition. For a convecting tip, the second condition is Robin: \[ (T-T_\infty)_{x=0}=T_0-T_\infty, \qquad -kA\left.\frac{d(T-T_\infty)}{dx}\right|_{x=L} =h_LA(T-T_\infty)_{x=L}. \tag{4.31a} \] For an insulated tip, the second condition is Neumann: \[ (T-T_\infty)_{x=0}=T_0-T_\infty, \qquad \left.\frac{d(T-T_\infty)}{dx}\right|_{x=L}=0. \tag{4.31b} \]
docs.title: Energy Balance And Differential Equation

docs.text: The dimensional functional relation is \[ T-T_\infty =\operatorname{fn}(T_0-T_\infty,x,L,kA,hP,h_LA). \tag{4.32} \] Define \[ \Theta=\frac{T-T_\infty}{T_0-T_\infty}, \qquad \xi=\frac{x}{L}, \qquad m=\sqrt{\frac{hP}{kA}}, \qquad \mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}=\frac{h_LL}{k}. \] Then a convecting-tip fin has \[ \Theta=\operatorname{fn} \left(\xi,mL,\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{tip}}\right), \tag{4.33a} \] whereas an adiabatic-tip fin has \[ \Theta=\operatorname{fn}(\xi,mL). \tag{4.33b} \]
docs.title: Dimensional Analysis And Dimensionless Form

docs.text: The quantity \(m\) is not itself a dimensionless coordinate: it has units of inverse length. Both \[ \xi=\frac{x}{L} \qquad\text{and}\qquad X=mx=\frac{x}{1/m} \] are valid dimensionless coordinates, but they emphasize different length scales. The rod length \(L\) is the geometric scale, whereas \(1/m\) is the thermal decay length set by axial conduction and side cooling. For a finite rod, \(\xi=x/L\) is convenient because the base is always at \(\xi=0\) and the tip is always at \(\xi=1\) . The physics then appears in the separate dimensionless group \[ mL=\frac{L}{1/m}, \] which compares the rod length with the thermal decay length. We could instead use \(X=mx\) . Equation (4.34) would then become \[ \frac{d^2\Theta}{dX^2}=\Theta, \] but the tip would be located at \(X=mL\) rather than at a fixed coordinate. Nothing physical changes because \(X=(mL)\xi\) ; the two choices merely organize the same information differently. When the rod is effectively infinite and the tip no longer matters, \(mx\) becomes the natural coordinate and the solution is \(\Theta=e^{-mx}\) . Lienhard, p. 167, Eqs. (4.32)-(4.33b) uses \(\xi=x/L\) for the finite-fin dimensional analysis. On p. 173, Eq. (4.50) , the long-fin limit is written as \(e^{-mL\xi}=e^{-mx}\) , and the following paragraph interprets \((mL)^2\) as a hybrid Biot number comparing axial conduction resistance with the overall resistance to side convection.
docs.title: Choosing A Dimensionless Position Coordinate

docs.text: Module 1 Assignment: First Contact With The Instrument ¶ Introductory Material ¶ Purpose ¶ In Module 1 you will meet the temperature-control instrument that we will build toward during the semester. It uses an Arduino, a thermistor, a thermoelectric cooler, an H-bridge driver, a power supply, a heat exchanger, an oscilloscope, and laptop software. If you haven't already, read the course Overview . Module 1 occupies Sessions S2 and S3 . Use S2 to begin the Arduino, oscilloscope, and analog-input work, and S3 to complete the averaging and PWM work and save the evidence required for A1. Before class, your job is to arrive ready to connect to an Arduino, upload a simple program, and think clearly about safety. Vocabulary ¶ Arduino Uno : the microcontroller board that reads voltages and sends control signals. Serial Monitor : the Arduino IDE window that shows text sent from the Arduino to the laptop. Digital output : a pin that the Arduino can set near 0 V or 5 V. Oscilloscope : an instrument that displays voltage versus time. Thermistor : a resistor whose resistance changes with temperature. TEC/Peltier element : a bidirectional thermal actuator. It can heat one side and cool the other depending on current direction. H-bridge : an electronic circuit that lets the low-power Arduino control the amount and direction of current from a high-power supply through a load. PWM : pulse-width modulation, a way to control average power using fast on/off switching. Safety Boundary For Module 1 ¶ In Module 1, the Arduino is powered by USB. The TEC power supply stays off. You may inspect the TEC, H-bridge, heat exchanger, thermistor, and safety cutoff, but you will not power the TEC during Module 1. This is deliberate. The course begins by verifying the measurement and communication chain before applying actuator power. Pre-Class Assignment ¶ Before Class ¶ Complete these steps before Module 1. Install the Arduino IDE on the laptop you plan to use in lab, if possible. Read this assignment and write down any question that feels basic or confusing. Skim the vocabulary list below. If you cannot install software before class, come anyway. We will handle setup in lab. Pre-Class Questions ¶ Write short answers before class. These are not meant to be polished. What is the difference between a sensor and an actuator? Why should the TEC power supply remain off while we are only testing Arduino upload and serial communication? What do you expect an Arduino digital output to look like on an oscilloscope? If software says "toggle every 500 ms," what period and frequency would you expect to measure? Ask for help rather than silently exceeding it because of installation or access problems. In-Class Assignment ¶ What You Will Do ¶ You will: Upload Arduino sketches from the Arduino IDE. Open Serial Monitor and read "heartbeat" messages from the Arduino. Probe an Arduino digital PWM output with an oscilloscope to determine frequency and duty cycle. Read a potentiometer voltage with analogRead . Quantify potentiometer-signal noise and test how averaging changes it. Use an averaged analog reading to control LED brightness via the PWM output. Compare the measured signals to the code that generated them. Get Oriented ¶ Spend 5-10 minutes reading Arduino's introduction, What is Arduino? , and another 5-10 minutes reviewing Hardware for temperature control . The hardware page describes the course apparatus and links to details about its components; there are no exercises on that page. The Arduino IDE includes permanent example sketches that are worth learning because you can find them again after this course. Open them from: File -> Examples The official built-in examples provide another permanent reference. Part 1: Blink And Digital Output ¶ Do the official Arduino Blink tutorial using both the built-in LED and an external LED. The external LED must be current limited, so place a resistor between 200 \(\Omega\) and 4000 \(\Omega\) in series with the LED. Follow the schematic in the tutorial. Change the HIGH:LOW time ratio from 1:1 to 10:1 and then 1:10. Play with the on and off times. Part 2: AnalogReadSerial ¶ Do the official Arduino AnalogReadSerial tutorial . Use a 100 kΩ potentiometer as a voltage divider that supplies 0-5 V to the analog input. Connect one outer terminal to Arduino 5V , the other outer terminal to Arduino GND , and the center wiper to A0 . If you feel the need to bend the legs of the pot, something is wrong! View the readings with both Serial Monitor and Serial Plotter from the Arduino IDE Tools menu. Slow the interval between reports to a sensible rate. Rotate the potentiometer and confirm that the reported ADC number responds. Part 3 develops this observation into a quantitative measurement of ADC digitization and averaging. Read Analog, ADC, And PWM for explanations of how analog to digital conversion works. Part 3: Quantify The Power Of Averaging ¶ Continue using the 100 kΩ potentiometer as a voltage divider. 3A: Observe The Integer ADC Readings ¶ Starting from AnalogReadSerial , write a sketch that continuously reads A0 and prints the result as an integer . Display the same stream in both Serial Monitor and Serial Plotter. Use a single labeled quantity that Serial Plotter recognizes, such as ADC:512 Turn the potentiometer carefully to both ends of its range. Record the minimum and maximum ADC values that you can obtain. Then set the potentiometer close to the midpoint of the measured range, \[ n_{\mathrm{mid}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{min}}+n_{\mathrm{max}}}{2}, \] and leave it untouched for the remaining measurements. Hold the potentiometer fixed at approximately the midpoint and observe the output. Then choose at least one substantially different setting and repeat. Describe and explain what you see in both displays. In particular: Do the reported values vary even when you do not touch the potentiometer? Do the values change continuously, or do they occupy discrete integer levels? Why? What does Serial Monitor reveal that is difficult to see in Serial Plotter, and vice versa? Checkpoint : Call the instructor over at this point and show him what you see on the Serial Plotter. 3B: Convert ADC Number To Voltage ¶ Modify your code so that it converts each ADC number \(n\) to voltage and prints the voltage continuously: \[ V \approx V_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{n}{1023}. \] Use the measured reference voltage if you have measured it; otherwise use the nominal value \(V_{\mathrm{ref}}=5.00\ \mathrm{V}\) . The Arduino Uno has a 10-bit ADC, so it divides the input range into \(2^{10}=1024\) levels. Its nominal one-count voltage resolution is \[ \Delta V_{\mathrm{ADC}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{ref}}}{2^{10}}. \] Calculate this resolution in millivolts. For a 5.00 V reference it is about 4.88 mV. Explain why printing many decimal places does not, by itself, give the ADC finer physical resolution. 3C: Compare One Reading With A 1000-Reading Average ¶ Rewrite the voltage sketch so that it repeatedly produces: 100 sequential voltage values , each obtained from one reading of A0 . 100 sequential voltage values , each obtained by averaging 1000 readings of A0 . Return to step 1 and repeat forever. Keep the potentiometer fixed. Print only one plotted voltage quantity per line. In Serial Monitor, also identify the point number and whether it came from \(N=1\) or \(N=1000\) , without creating additional plotted curves. For example, the output may look like this: Ave1000_Point_1 Voltage_V:2.4561 Ave1000_Point_2 Voltage_V:2.4564 Ave1_Point_1 Voltage_V:2.4570 Serial Monitor displays each complete line. Serial Plotter treats each newline as a new plotted point and needs only one numeric quantity per line for this experiment. It ignores unrecognized text such as Ave1000_Point_1 , while the stable Voltage_V:number field supplies the one number to plot. Keep the field name Voltage_V the same for both averaging modes; using different numeric field names would make Serial Plotter create separate curves. Open Serial Plotter and wait until it contains both kinds of data. Stop the plotter when the transition between an unaveraged block and a 1000-reading average block is approximately halfway across the graph, as in the figure below. Your numerical values and detailed trace need not look identical to the example. Save this screenshot and the corresponding numerical output. Checkpoint : Call your instructor over to show him plots of the data for the averaged and non-averaged signal on the Serial Plotter. (a) For each 100-point block, calculate the mean voltage and sample standard deviation \(s\) . In this exercise, use \(s\) as an empirical estimate of the noise-limited voltage resolution of the reported value. Compare the measured ratio \(s_{1000}/s_1\) with the independent-noise prediction \[ s_{1000} \approx \frac{s_1}{\sqrt{1000}} \approx 0.0316s_1. \] (b) A second way to measure the effective resolution in millivolts for the unaveraged and averaged blocks is by looking at the smallest discrete voltage jump between two subsequent data points. Compare the unaveraged smallest discrete voltage jump between two subsequent data points with the ADC's fixed one-count digitization step \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) . Each individual conversion is still a 10-bit measurement, but averaging can produce a result with additional effective bits of precision when the input is stable and independent noise causes the readings to sample neighboring ADC codes. The improvement in precision is approximately \(\sqrt{N}\) . Therefore, the number of effective bits gained by averaging \(N\) independent measurements is \[ b_{\mathrm{gained}} = \log_2\!\left(\sqrt{N}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 N. \] Equivalently, averaging \(2^m\) independent measurements ideally provides \(m/2\) additional binary digits, or bits, of precision. Because \(1000\approx 2^{10}\) and \(\sqrt{1000}\approx 32=2^5\) , averaging 1000 readings can ideally add about five effective bits of precision to the estimated voltage. The \(1/\sqrt{N}\) improvement requires that the underlying voltage remains constant, the fluctuations have approximately zero mean and are sufficiently independent, and there is enough analog noise or dither for repeated conversions to sample neighboring ADC codes. If every reading returns the same ADC code, averaging cannot recover additional information. There are many likely departures from the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) prediction, including drift, correlated pickup, quantization, and variation of the Arduino reference voltage. Averaging improves precision under these conditions, but it does not automatically improve absolute accuracy or remove calibration errors. 3D: Measure The Time Cost Of Averaging ¶ Use micros() immediately before and after the loop that acquires 1000 readings. Record the elapsed time in microseconds, calculate the corresponding number of analogRead() conversions per second, and compare your result with the Arduino reference value of roughly \(100\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) per conversion. At that rate, 1000 readings alone should require roughly 0.10 s, before any additional calculation or Serial output time. Explain the tradeoff. Averaging over a finite interval acts as a low-pass filter: rapid fluctuations tend to cancel, but changes occurring during the averaging window are smoothed or delayed. Improved voltage precision therefore comes with reduced time resolution. Checkpoint : Call your instructor over and explain this to him. Part 4: LED Brightness From PWM Controlled By Averaged Analog Input ¶ First, understand a PWM signal by reading Basics of PWM . Return the potentiometer to the analog input. Modify your Arduino code to use the averaged potentiometer voltage to set the brightness of an LED with PWM. The signal chain is: pot voltage -> averaged ADC 10-bit number -> voltage -> map to PWM 8-bit number-> analogWrite -> oscilloscope -> LED brightness Start by printing the averaged voltage and PWM value to Serial Monitor so you can see what the code is doing. Then measure the PWM output pin with the oscilloscope while you turn the potentiometer. What is the period, amplitude and duty-cycle of the PWM as a function of voltage? The Analog, ADC, And PWM reference explains why PWM is a switching waveform rather than a continuously variable voltage. Finally, connect the PWM pin to an LED with an appropriate series resistor and confirm that the LED brightness follows the potentiometer. Record the PWM high and low voltages, period, frequency, and duty cycle at two substantially different potentiometer settings. Determine which quantities change and which remain approximately fixed. If you use Arduino Uno pin 9, compare the measured frequency with the expected value of approximately 490 Hz. Compare this with the roughly 50-60 Hz range above which ordinary flicker often appears steady to the eye. Explain why the LED looks continuously lit even though the oscilloscope resolves individual pulses. Checkpoint : Call your instructor over and show him the PWM traces as you vary the potentiometer. You should expect to revise your sketches after the first upload. Debugging board selection, port selection, baud rate, wiring, and timing is part of the lab. Each student must submit a text response to the Moodle C1 Team Checkoff activity by 5:00 PM on September 9 . The text may be identical for both members of a team because it documents shared repository evidence, but each student must make a separate Moodle submission. The text response must give both team members' names, the team repository URL, the full Git commit hash demonstrated during the checkoff, and the paths to the project README.md and principal Arduino sketch or sketches. Update the project README.md to identify the sketches and measurements that were tested. Make a meaningful commit and push it to GitHub. Everyone should be able to answer Questions 9 & 10. Be prepared to answer without asking an AI agent during the checkoff. Show where the Arduino sketch is stored. What did you change, and how can you tell the uploaded board is running that version? What is the difference between saving a file, committing it, and pushing it? Starting from the cited commit, use the repository history to locate and inspect the preceding committed version of one file. What protection does this history provide when a later edit goes wrong? A 10-bit ADC uses a 5.00 V reference. How many output codes are possible, what are the minimum and maximum codes, and what voltage is represented by one ADC count? Why can averaging independent readings improve voltage precision? Derive the number of effective bits gained from \(N\) readings, and estimate the gain for \(N=1000\) . State the assumptions required for this result. Approximately how fast can an Arduino Uno acquire standard analogRead() measurements, and how long should 1000 readings take? How would you measure the actual time with micros() ? Explain why averaging over this interval acts as a low-pass filter and identify the cost in time resolution. The official Arduino analogRead() reference gives the approximate conversion time. Point to the LED PWM waveform on the oscilloscope. Measure its period and calculate its frequency. What are its high and low voltages and duty cycle? Which of these quantities changes when you turn the potentiometer? If you used Arduino Uno pin 9, compare your measurement with the expected PWM frequency of approximately 490 Hz. Roughly how rapidly can the human eye follow an LED turning on and off before the flashes appear to merge into steady light? Compare the typical 50-60 Hz flicker-fusion range with your measured PWM frequency. Why does the LED appear steady even though the oscilloscope shows that it repeatedly switches on and off? Explain why the visual threshold is not one universal frequency but depends on brightness, contrast, and viewing conditions. In this module, the Arduino's principal way of sensing a continuously varying physical quantity is through an analog input. Concisely describe the Arduino Uno analog input, including what it measures, its voltage range, ADC resolution and code range, and approximate acquisition time. In this module, the Arduino's principal way of producing a continuously adjustable actuator command is through a PWM output. Concisely describe the Arduino Uno PWM output, including its voltage levels, command range, duty cycle and frequency, and why a power stage is required to run a motor. Explain why PWM is not a true analog voltage. Collect Your A1 Evidence During Class ¶ The post-class assignment is expected to take 90-120 minutes . To stay near the lower end of that range, collect and save all measurements, code, and images while you still have the Arduino and oscilloscope in front of you. Before leaving S3, complete this checklist. If an item cannot be completed, show the instructor what is missing before you leave. [ ] Save a labeled photograph or quick sketch of the apparatus. [ ] Save all Arduino code used to complete the activities and produce the submitted measurements. You may organize the work into as many or as few sketches as you find useful. [ ] Record the minimum, maximum, and selected midrange ADC values. [ ] Save a Serial Plotter screenshot with the transition between the 100-point \(N=1\) and \(N=1000\) voltage blocks near the center of the graph. [ ] Save a Serial Plotter screenshot with only the \(N=1000\) voltage block so you can estimate the miniumun discrete voltage jump. [ ] Record the measured time for 1000 analogRead() conversions and the corresponding conversion rate. [ ] Save an oscilloscope screenshot or clear hand sketch of the LED PWM waveform. [ ] Record the high and low voltages, period, frequency, and duty cycle for the three Blink timing ratios and for two LED-PWM settings. [ ] Fill in the averaging table below. [ ] Write two or three bullet points about what the oscilloscope revealed that the serial displays did not. [ ] Answer in writing questions 9 and 10 of C1. Potentiometer block Reported points Readings averaged per point \(N\) Mean voltage Sample standard deviation \(s\) \(s/s_1\) measured \(s/s_1\) predicted Unaveraged 100 1 mV 1.000 1.000 Long average 100 1000 mV 0.0316 This is the only required table. Report the oscilloscope measurements in a concise labeled list or in prose. Include units with every measured quantity. Calculate \[ f=\frac{1}{T}, \qquad D=100\%\frac{t_{\mathrm{HIGH}}}{T}. \] For Arduino PWM, the expected duty cycle is approximately \[ D_{\mathrm{expected}}=100\%\frac{\texttt{analogWrite value}}{255}. \] Post-Class Assignment ¶ A1: Module 1 Evidence Note ¶ Assessment code: A1 , graded team assignment, 5 points Due: Monday, September 14, at 5:00 PM Repository file: docs/module_notes/module_01_evidence.md Moodle submission: Each student uploads A1_Lastname_Lastname.pdf ; teammates may upload the same PDF Expected post-class time: 90-120 minutes , provided the in-class evidence checklist is complete A1 assesses the scientific and technical evidence from Module 1. It is separate from the C1 in-class assessment , which you will demonstrate during S4. You will complete the in-class C1 checkoff before submitting A1 . Use the questions and feedback from that checkoff to improve the clarity, organization, and technical accuracy of your written evidence note. Assemble And Submit The Note ¶ After class, complete these steps in order: Create or open docs/module_notes/module_01_evidence.md . At the top, give the assignment code, team members, date, and repository URL. Add the labeled apparatus photograph or sketch collected in class. Link to every Arduino file used to produce the submitted results. You may organize the work into one evolving sketch or several focused sketches; the choice is yours. Do not paste pages of Arduino code into the note. Document the ADC digitization results. Include the measured minimum, maximum, and midrange ADC values; the calculated one-count voltage resolution in millivolts; and an explanation of why the readings occupy discrete levels. Document the averaging results. Include the centered Serial Plotter screenshot comparing the 100-point \(N=1\) and \(N=1000\) blocks, the \(N=1000\) -only screenshot, the measured minimum discrete voltage jump, and the completed averaging table. Compare the measured voltage resolutions with the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) prediction. Report the measured time for 1000 conversions and explain why averaging improves precision while acting as a low-pass filter that reduces time resolution. Document the oscilloscope results. Include the LED-PWM oscilloscope image or hand sketch and report the requested Blink and PWM high and low voltages, period, frequency, and duty cycle with units. Then answer in three to five sentences: What did the oscilloscope show that the Serial Monitor and Serial Plotter did not? Distinguish a direct electrical measurement from values chosen and printed by software. Discuss the individual pulses and waveform timing; the serial displays show reported samples rather than the fast PWM waveform itself. Proofread the complete note. Check that every figure is legible and labeled, every measured quantity has units, and every code link opens the exact file used for the experiment. Teammates may upload the same PDF. Pushed Git checkpoint: Save the current files, create a Git commit with a meaningful message, and push that commit to GitHub. Record the repository URL and full commit hash so the submitted version can be located. This checkpoint, abbreviated GC , is not a separate assignment; it preserves the exact code, evidence, and notes supporting an A# or C# assessment. docs.text: In Module 1 you will meet the temperature-control instrument that we will build toward during the semester. It uses an Arduino, a thermistor, a thermoelectric cooler, an H-bridge driver, a power supply, a heat exchanger, an oscilloscope, and laptop software. Record the elapsed time in microseconds, calculate the corresponding number of analogRead() conversions per second, and compare your result with the Arduino reference value of roughly \(100\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) per conversion. At that rate, 1000 readings alone should require roughly 0.10 s, before any additional calculation or Serial output time. Explain the tradeoff. Averaging over a finite interval acts as a low-pass filter: rapid fluctuations tend to cancel, but changes occurring during the averaging window are smoothed or delayed. Improved voltage precision therefore comes with reduced time resolution. Checkpoint : Call your instructor over and explain this to him.
docs.title: 3D: Measure The Time Cost Of Averaging

docs.text: First, understand a PWM signal by reading Basics of PWM . Return the potentiometer to the analog input. Modify your Arduino code to use the averaged potentiometer voltage to set the brightness of an LED with PWM. The signal chain is: pot voltage -> averaged ADC 10-bit number -> voltage -> map to PWM 8-bit number-> analogWrite -> oscilloscope -> LED brightness Start by printing the averaged voltage and PWM value to Serial Monitor so you can see what the code is doing. Then measure the PWM output pin with the oscilloscope while you turn the potentiometer. What is the period, amplitude and duty-cycle of the PWM as a function of voltage? The Analog, ADC, And PWM reference explains why PWM is a switching waveform rather than a continuously variable voltage. Finally, connect the PWM pin to an LED with an appropriate series resistor and confirm that the LED brightness follows the potentiometer. Record the PWM high and low voltages, period, frequency, and duty cycle at two substantially different potentiometer settings. Determine which quantities change and which remain approximately fixed. If you use Arduino Uno pin 9, compare the measured frequency with the expected value of approximately 490 Hz. Compare this with the roughly 50-60 Hz range above which ordinary flicker often appears steady to the eye. Explain why the LED looks continuously lit even though the oscilloscope resolves individual pulses. Checkpoint : Call your instructor over and show him the PWM traces as you vary the potentiometer. You should expect to revise your sketches after the first upload. Debugging board selection, port selection, baud rate, wiring, and timing is part of the lab.

docs.text: Each student will answer one workflow question from Questions 1-3 and one measurement question from Questions 4-8. Everyone should be able to answer Questions 9 & 10. Be prepared to answer without asking an AI agent during the checkoff. Show where the Arduino sketch is stored. What did you change, and how can you tell the uploaded board is running that version? What is the difference between saving a file, committing it, and pushing it? Starting from the cited commit, use the repository history to locate and inspect the preceding committed version of one file. What protection does this history provide when a later edit goes wrong? A 10-bit ADC uses a 5.00 V reference. How many output codes are possible, what are the minimum and maximum codes, and what voltage is represented by one ADC count? Why can averaging independent readings improve voltage precision? Derive the number of effective bits gained from \(N\) readings, and estimate the gain for \(N=1000\) . State the assumptions required for this result. Approximately how fast can an Arduino Uno acquire standard analogRead() measurements, and how long should 1000 readings take? How would you measure the actual time with micros() ? Explain why averaging over this interval acts as a low-pass filter and identify the cost in time resolution. The official Arduino analogRead() reference gives the approximate conversion time. Point to the LED PWM waveform on the oscilloscope. Measure its period and calculate its frequency. What are its high and low voltages and duty cycle? Which of these quantities changes when you turn the potentiometer? If you used Arduino Uno pin 9, compare your measurement with the expected PWM frequency of approximately 490 Hz. Roughly how rapidly can the human eye follow an LED turning on and off before the flashes appear to merge into steady light? Compare the typical 50-60 Hz flicker-fusion range with your measured PWM frequency. Why does the LED appear steady even though the oscilloscope shows that it repeatedly switches on and off? Explain why the visual threshold is not one universal frequency but depends on brightness, contrast, and viewing conditions. In this module, the Arduino's principal way of sensing a continuously varying physical quantity is through an analog input. Concisely describe the Arduino Uno analog input, including what it measures, its voltage range, ADC resolution and code range, and approximate acquisition time. In this module, the Arduino's principal way of producing a continuously adjustable actuator command is through a PWM output. Concisely describe the Arduino Uno PWM output, including its voltage levels, command range, duty cycle and frequency, and why a power stage is required to run a motor. Explain why PWM is not a true analog voltage.

Before leaving S3, complete this checklist. If an item cannot be completed, show the instructor what is missing before you leave. [ ] Save a labeled photograph or quick sketch of the apparatus. [ ] Save all Arduino code used to complete the activities and produce the submitted measurements. You may organize the work into as many or as few sketches as you find useful. [ ] Record the minimum, maximum, and selected midrange ADC values. [ ] Save a Serial Plotter screenshot with the transition between the 100-point \(N=1\) and \(N=1000\) voltage blocks near the center of the graph. [ ] Save a Serial Plotter screenshot with only the \(N=1000\) voltage block so you can estimate the miniumun discrete voltage jump. [ ] Record the measured time for 1000 analogRead() conversions and the corresponding conversion rate. [ ] Save an oscilloscope screenshot or clear hand sketch of the LED PWM waveform. [ ] Record the high and low voltages, period, frequency, and duty cycle for the three Blink timing ratios and for two LED-PWM settings. [ ] Fill in the averaging table below. [ ] Write two or three bullet points about what the oscilloscope revealed that the serial displays did not. [ ] Answer in writing questions 9 and 10 of C1. Potentiometer block Reported points Readings averaged per point \(N\) Mean voltage Sample standard deviation \(s\) \(s/s_1\) measured \(s/s_1\) predicted Unaveraged 100 1 mV 1.000 1.000 Long average 100 1000 mV 0.0316 This is the only required table. Report the oscilloscope measurements in a concise labeled list or in prose. Include units with every measured quantity. Calculate \[ f=\frac{1}{T}, \qquad D=100\%\frac{t_{\mathrm{HIGH}}}{T}. \] For Arduino PWM, the expected duty cycle is approximately \[ D_{\mathrm{expected}}=100\%\frac{\texttt{analogWrite value}}{255}. \]
