Part 5: Explain The One-Lump P Transient And Its Limit ¶ Now analyze the same dimensional one-lump model used throughout this module. The solution explains why its P-controlled response cannot oscillate. If the real apparatus oscillates, the difference identifies physics missing from the model. Substituting the P-control law into the energy balance gives \[ C\frac{dT}{dt} =P_uK_pT_{\mathrm{set}}+HT_{\mathrm{amb}} -(H+P_uK_p)T. \] Setting \(dT/dt=0\) gives the closed-loop steady-state temperature, \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{HT_{\mathrm{amb}}+P_uK_pT_{\mathrm{set}}} {H+P_uK_p}. \] Now define the displacement from steady state, \[ \theta(t)=T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Substitution reduces the entire closed-loop P model to \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Compare this directly with the open-loop displacement equation from Part 2, \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-H\theta. \] For the displacement dynamics, closing the P-control loop therefore makes the simple replacement \[ \boxed{H\longrightarrow H+P_uK_p}. \] The additional term \(P_uK_p\) acts like an additional restoring conductance: for the same displacement from steady state, feedback produces a larger rate of return. This replacement applies to the homogeneous transient equation; the steady-state temperature must still be calculated from the closed-loop forcing terms above. Separate variables and integrate: \[ \frac{d\theta}{\theta} =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\,dt, \] \[ \ln\!\left(\frac{\theta(t)}{\theta(0)}\right) =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t. \] Therefore the displacement is \[ \boxed{ \theta(t)=\theta(0) \exp\!\left(-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t\right) }. \] Now return from the displacement \(\theta\) to the measured temperature using \(T=T_{\mathrm{ss}}+\theta\) . Since \(\theta(0)=T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) , the temperature is \[ \boxed{ T(t)=T_{\mathrm{ss}} +\left[T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\right] \exp\!\left(-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t\right) }. \] Equivalently, \[ T(t)=T_{\mathrm{ss}} +\left[T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\right]e^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{cl}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{C}{H+P_uK_p}. \] Using \(\tau=C/H\) and the dimensionless loop gain \(L=\chi K_p\) , \[ \boxed{ \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{\tau}{1+\chi K_p}=\frac{\tau}{1+L}. } \] Increasing gain has two effects Increasing \(K_p\) does two things at the same time: It decreases droop. \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{1+\chi K_p}. \] It speeds up the response by decreasing the closed-loop time constant. \[ \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{\tau}{1+\chi K_p}. \] Thus, in this unsaturated one-lump model, both droop and response time are reduced by the same factor, \(1+\chi K_p\) . Larger gain moves the temperature closer to the setpoint and makes it approach its steady value more quickly. To find the eigenvalue directly, try an exponential mode, \[ \theta(t)=\theta_0e^{\lambda t}, \qquad \frac{d\theta}{dt}=\lambda\theta. \] Substitute this trial solution into the homogeneous P equation: \[ C\lambda\theta=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Cancel the nonzero factor \(\theta\) . There is only one eigenvalue, \[ \lambda=-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}, \] and it is real and negative for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. The exponential is always positive, so \(T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) retains its initial sign while shrinking toward zero. The response therefore cannot cross the steady state, overshoot, or oscillate. Increasing \(K_p\) decreases both droop and \(\tau_{\mathrm{cl}}\) ; it does not create the additional dynamical state or time delay needed for oscillation. Thus the ideal one-lump P model is stable and non-oscillatory for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. A measured overshoot, sustained oscillation, or growing oscillation is behavior this model cannot produce and therefore falsifies it as a model of the transient response. This first-order example is the simplest version of both mathematical views. Its state-space matrix has only one entry, so it has one real eigenvalue. The equivalent scalar equation is only first order, so its characteristic equation has the same single real root. There is no pair of complex eigenvalues and therefore no oscillatory exponential mode. Return to the high-gain trace saved in Module 5. Mark the late-time value \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) and the first overshoot. If the measured temperature crosses \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) , its behavior is incompatible with this one-lump solution. State the contradiction directly: the model predicts a monotonic exponential, whereas the apparatus shows an underdamped transient. This is evidence that the model is inadequate, not that the exponential solution is wrong. The one-lump model is missing thermal lag between where the TEC applies heat and where the thermistor measures temperature. The simplest extension is to represent these locations as two coupled thermal masses. This two-lump model is introduced below and developed systematically in Part II. Why a Thermal Control System Can Oscillate Without Mechanical Inertia Begin with the familiar mass and spring. A damped mechanical oscillator obeys \[ m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0. \] Its two state variables are position \(x\) and velocity \(\dot x\) . Ignoring damping for the moment, the spring force is zero when the mass passes through \(x=0\) , but the velocity is largest there. Kinetic energy carries the mass past equilibrium. This is mechanical inertia: zero restoring force does not imply zero velocity. A one-lump thermal model cannot coast. Its P-controlled displacement obeys \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Temperature is its only state variable. If the net heat flow becomes zero, then \(dT/dt=0\) immediately. The temperature cannot coast through equilibrium, so the model produces one monotonic exponential and cannot overshoot. The apparatus contains a hidden thermal state. The simplest improvement is a two-lump thermal model . One lump represents the region near the TEC, where heat is applied. The other represents the block and thermistor, where temperature is measured. Each lump stores thermal energy, and heat takes time to move between them. With P control, \(u=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_m)\) , where \(T_m\) is the measured temperature. Suppose \(T_m\) reaches the setpoint and the controller reduces its command. The TEC-side region can still be hotter than the measured block, so stored energy continues flowing toward the thermistor and \(T_m\) continues rising. The temperature overshoots not because it has mechanical momentum, but because the measured temperature does not reveal all the thermal energy already stored elsewhere in the apparatus. The qualitative correspondence is Mass-spring oscillator Thermal control system measured position \(x\) measured temperature \(T_m\) hidden velocity \(\dot x\) hidden TEC-side temperature \(T\) kinetic energy carries the mass past equilibrium stored heat continues flowing after \(T_m\) reaches the setpoint mechanical inertia supplies the second state thermal storage and transport supply the second state The phase-lag interpretation. The thermistor reports the effect of a TEC command only after heat has propagated to the measured block. The controller therefore acts partly on old information. As gain increases, this lag can make the correction arrive too late, after which the controller overcorrects in the opposite direction. This qualitative model explains why the real apparatus can overshoot even though the one-lump model cannot. Module 6, Part II introduces the coupled two-lump equations, shows why they form a second-order system, and explores their behavior quantitatively. Thus the nearly model-independent steady-state energy balance can succeed even when the one-lump transient model fails. Part II develops and tests the two-lump explanation quantitatively. Part 6: Add Integral Action In Simulation ¶ Keep the same dimensional one-lump energy balance. PI control changes only the command supplied to the TEC. Define the temperature error and its accumulated value as \[ e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T, \qquad q(t)=q(0)+\int_0^t e(t')\,dt'. \] The PI command is \[ u=K_p e+K_iq, \] so the physical model remains \[ \boxed{ C\frac{dT}{dt} =P_u\left[K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T)+K_iq\right] -H(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}), \qquad \frac{dq}{dt}=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T. } \] The simulation first updates the integral state, \[ q_{n+1}=q_n+(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_n)\Delta t, \] then calculates and clamps the command using the accepted value of \(q_{n+1}\) , \[ u_n=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_n)+K_iq_{n+1}, \] and finally advances the temperature: \[ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{\tau} \left(T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u_n-T_n\right). \] Select pi in the simulation and begin with a stable \(K_p\) . Use Zero integral to clear the controller memory before a comparison. Watch the displayed values of \(e\) , \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and the applied command while the temperature approaches the setpoint. Why does the temperature initially move away from the setpoint? The steady integral contribution replaces the nonzero proportional error that was required to provide the steady command under P-only control. Why Integral Windup Occurs The PI controller first calculates a requested command , \[ u_{\mathrm{req}}=K_pe+K_iq, \qquad q_{n+1}=q_n+e_n\Delta t. \] The actuator can apply only a limited command, so the program clamps that request: \[ u_{\mathrm{applied}} =\operatorname{clamp}(u_{\mathrm{req}},-u_{\max},u_{\max}). \] Suppose a large positive error requests more than \(u_{\max}\) . The applied PWM cannot increase further, but ordinary integration keeps adding the positive error to \(q\) . The extra integral contribution has no immediate effect on the TEC because the actuator is already saturated. It is stored in the controller instead. When the temperature later approaches the setpoint, the error and proportional contribution become small, but the accumulated integral contribution can remain large. The controller therefore continues driving the TEC through the setpoint. It may take a long time for error of the opposite sign to unwind the stored integral, producing excessive overshoot and slow recovery. The anti-windup rule used here is conditional integration : if the command is saturated and the current error would push it farther into saturation, hold \(q\) fixed; otherwise, update \(q\) , including when the error helps bring the command out of saturation. The PWM clamp, anti-windup rule, and Zero integral control have different jobs. The clamp protects the actuator, anti-windup controls the growth of the controller's memory during normal operation, and Zero integral deliberately clears that memory before a new comparison. Why PI Can Be Underdamped ¶ PI control adds the accumulated error as a second state variable. The one-lump P model has only one state and therefore produces one monotonic exponential; the one-lump PI model has two coupled states and can overshoot or oscillate. For an unsaturated PI controller at steady state, the integral state must stop changing. Because \(dq/dt=e\) , \[ \frac{dq}{dt}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_{\mathrm{ss}}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{\mathrm{ss}}=T_{\mathrm{set}}. \] The steady-state heat balance is therefore \[ 0=P_u u_{\mathrm{ss}} -H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}), \] which requires \[ u_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})}{P_u}. \] At zero error the proportional contribution is zero, so the integral contribution supplies the entire steady command: \[ u_{\mathrm{ss}}=K_iq_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Combining these results gives \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}}=T_{\mathrm{set}}, \qquad q_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})}{P_uK_i}. \] This result assumes stable control, a reachable setpoint, no sustained actuator saturation, and continued integral action. Two routes to the same PI time dependence The one-lump PI model will now be analyzed in two parallel ways. Coupled-state or matrix route: keep \((\theta,z)\) as two state variables, write \(\dot{\mathbf{x}}=A\mathbf{x}\) , and find the allowed exponential modes from \(\det(\lambda I-A)=0\) . Higher-order ODE route: eliminate \(z\) and obtain one second-order equation for \(\theta\) . Substituting \(\theta\propto e^{\lambda t}\) gives its characteristic polynomial. The determinant and the characteristic polynomial are the same quadratic. The two routes therefore predict the same \(\lambda_\pm\) , the same decay rates, and the same oscillation frequency. They are two descriptions of one physical dynamics, not two different models. From Two First-Order Equations To One Second-Order Equation ¶ The one-lump thermal plant has one state, its temperature \(T\) . PI control adds the accumulated error \(q\) as a second state. The closed-loop model therefore has two coupled first-order differential equations even though it contains only one thermal lump. Those two first-order equations can be combined into one second-order differential equation for temperature. Define the temperature and integral-state displacements from steady state, \[ \theta=T-T_{\mathrm{set}}, \qquad z=q-q_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Because \(e=-\theta\) , the two coupled first-order equations are \[ \frac{d\theta}{dt} =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\theta +\frac{P_uK_i}{C}z, \qquad \frac{dz}{dt}=-\theta. \] In matrix form, \[ \frac{d}{dt} \begin{pmatrix}\theta\\z\end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{ \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{H+P_uK_p}{C} & \dfrac{P_uK_i}{C}\\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} }_{A} \begin{pmatrix}\theta\\z\end{pmatrix}. \] To eliminate \(z\) , first multiply the temperature equation by \(C\) , \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt} =-(H+P_uK_p)\theta+P_uK_i z. \] Differentiate this equation with respect to time: \[ C\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} =-(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta}{dt} +P_uK_i\frac{dz}{dt}. \] The second first-order equation says \(dz/dt=-\theta\) . Substituting it removes the integral-state variable and gives \[ \boxed{ C\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} +(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta}{dt} +P_uK_i\theta=0 }. \] Thus the two coupled first-order equations for \((\theta,z)\) are equivalent to one second-order differential equation for \(\theta\) . The integral controller's memory supplies the additional dynamical state that makes overshoot and oscillation possible in the one-lump PI model. Eigenvalues And The Time Response ¶ Try an exponential solution, \(\theta(t)=\theta_0e^{\lambda t}\) . Substitution into the second-order differential equation gives \[ C\lambda^2+(H+P_uK_p)\lambda+P_uK_i=0. \] The eigenvalues \(\lambda_+\) and \(\lambda_-\) are the two roots of this quadratic equation. Applying the quadratic formula gives \[ \boxed{ \lambda_\pm =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C} \pm \sqrt{ \left(\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}\right)^2 -\frac{P_uK_i}{C} } }. \] The matrix route gives exactly the same equation: \[ \det(\lambda I-A) =\lambda^2 +\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\lambda +\frac{P_uK_i}{C}=0. \] Thus the roots of the scalar second-order equation are the eigenvalues of the coupled first-order matrix. In either language, each root supplies a time factor \(e^{\lambda t}\) . Define the envelope relaxation rate and natural angular frequency, \[ \gamma=\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}, \qquad \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{P_uK_i}{C}}. \] Then \[ \lambda_\pm=-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-\omega_n^2}. \] For positive \(C\) , \(H\) , \(P_u\) , \(K_p\) , and \(K_i\) , the real parts of both eigenvalues are always negative. Thus this ideal, unsaturated one-lump PI model is always stable : every transient eventually decays toward steady state. Stability does not require a monotonic response, however. If \(\omega_n>\gamma\) , the square root is imaginary, and \[ \lambda_\pm=-\gamma\pm i\omega_d, \qquad \boxed{\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_n^2-\gamma^2}}. \] The temperature displacement is then a decaying oscillation, \[ \boxed{ \theta(t)=e^{-\gamma t} \left[A\cos(\omega_dt)+B\sin(\omega_dt)\right] }. \] The negative real part, \(-\gamma\) , makes the oscillation envelope decay; the imaginary part, \(\omega_d\) , sets the oscillation period \(T_{\mathrm{osc}}=2\pi/\omega_d\) . The response is therefore stable but underdamped. How diagonalization solves the matrix ODE Write the state vector and its equation as \[ \mathbf{x}(t)= \begin{pmatrix}\theta(t)\\z(t)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}. \] Look for one exponential mode, \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{v}e^{\lambda t}, \] where the constant vector \(\mathbf{v}\) gives the relative amounts of temperature displacement and integral-state displacement in that mode. Substitution and cancellation of the nonzero exponential give \[ (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0. \] We want a nonzero eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) . If \(A-\lambda I\) were invertible, multiplying by its inverse would force \(\mathbf{v}=0\) . A nonzero solution is therefore possible only when the matrix is singular: \[ \boxed{\det(A-\lambda I)=0}. \] This determinant equation finds the allowed eigenvalues. For each eigenvalue, solving \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0\) gives its eigenvector. If the two eigenvectors are independent, put them in the columns of \[ V=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}_+&\mathbf{v}_-\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda= \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_+&0\\0&\lambda_-\end{pmatrix}. \] The eigenvalue equations together say \(AV=V\Lambda\) . Change coordinates by writing \(\mathbf{x}=V\mathbf{y}\) . Because \(V\) is constant, \[ V\frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt} =AV\mathbf{y} =V\Lambda\mathbf{y}, \] so multiplication by \(V^{-1}\) gives \[ \frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt}=\Lambda\mathbf{y}. \] Because \(\Lambda\) is diagonal, the coupled system has become two independent scalar equations, \[ \frac{dy_+}{dt}=\lambda_+y_+, \qquad \frac{dy_-}{dt}=\lambda_-y_-. \] Their solutions are \(y_\pm(t)=y_\pm(0)e^{\lambda_\pm t}\) . Transforming back gives \[ \boxed{ \mathbf{x}(t) =V \begin{pmatrix} e^{\lambda_+t}&0\\0&e^{\lambda_-t} \end{pmatrix} V^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0) =e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0) }. \] Thus diagonalization expresses the matrix exponential as two ordinary exponential modes whose eigenvalues are the quadratic roots derived above. Complex-conjugate eigenvalues combine to produce a real decaying oscillation. At critical damping, a repeated eigenvalue may provide only one eigenvector; the matrix exponential still exists, and the solution can contain a term proportional to \(t e^{\lambda t}\) . Compare this equation with the standard second-order form \[ \lambda^2+2\zeta\omega_n\lambda+\omega_n^2=0. \] The natural angular frequency and damping ratio are therefore \[ \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{P_uK_i}{C}}, \qquad \boxed{ \zeta=\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2\sqrt{CP_uK_i}} }. \] The dimensionless damping ratio \(\zeta\) identifies the transition: \(\zeta>1\) : overdamped, with two real negative roots; \(\zeta=1\) : critically damped; and \(\zeta<1\) : underdamped, with a complex-conjugate pair and a decaying oscillation. As the eigenvalues show above, all three responses are stable for positive parameters. In particular, underdamped means that the oscillations decay; it does not mean unstable. Constant-amplitude oscillations that last forever would be marginally stable, and growing oscillations would be unstable. Neither is predicted by this unsaturated one-lump PI model with positive parameters. For the underdamped one-lump PI model, the temperature approaches steady state as a decaying sinusoid, \[ \boxed{ T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}} =A e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\cos(\omega_d t-\phi) }, \qquad \omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}. \] The exponential envelope has decay time \[ \tau_{\mathrm{decay}}=\frac{1}{\gamma}, \qquad \boxed{ \gamma=\zeta\omega_n =\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C} }. \] Thus \(\gamma\) is the relaxation rate : increasing \(\gamma\) makes the oscillation envelope decay more rapidly. The damped oscillation frequency and period are \[ \boxed{ \omega_d =\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2} =\sqrt{ \frac{P_uK_i}{C} -\left(\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}\right)^2 } }, \qquad T_{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_d}. \] The dimensionless quality factor is \[ \boxed{ Q=\frac{\omega_n}{2\gamma} =\frac{1}{2\zeta} =\frac{\sqrt{CP_uK_i}}{H+P_uK_p} }. \] The quality factor is related to, but is not equal to, the number of oscillation periods in one decay time. For an underdamped response, \[ \boxed{ \frac{\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}}{T_{\mathrm{osc}}} =\frac{\omega_d}{2\pi\gamma} =\frac{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}{2\pi\zeta} =\frac{Q}{\pi}\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4Q^2}} }. \] When damping is weak, \(\zeta\ll1\) , this becomes \(\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}/T_{\mathrm{osc}}\approx Q/\pi\) , or \(Q\approx\pi\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}/T_{\mathrm{osc}}\) . Thus \(Q<1/2\) is overdamped, \(Q=1/2\) is critically damped, and \(Q>1/2\) is underdamped. Larger \(Q\) means that the oscillation loses a smaller fraction of its amplitude per cycle. Within this ideal unsaturated one-lump PI model, increasing \(K_i\) decreases \(\zeta\) and makes oscillation more likely, while increasing \(K_p\) increases \(\zeta\) . The simulation displays this one-lump PI damping ratio . It is not the damping ratio of the full two-lump model developed in Part II. This result is included for interpretation, not as a required A3 derivation. Use the simulation to observe how \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) change the response. Part 7: Implement PI Control And Collect The Experimental Goldilocks Plots ¶ Use your working Module 5 P controller as the starting point. Do not replace the Arduino's independent temperature shutdown or the existing signed-PWM clamp. Implement the integral state and the conditional-integration rule introduced above : \[ q_{n+1}=q_n+e_n\Delta t, \qquad u_n=K_pe_n+K_iq_{n+1}. \] Calculate \(\Delta t\) from the actual elapsed time between accepted temperature measurements. Display and save \(e\) , \(u_P=K_pe\) , \(u_I=K_iq\) , the requested command, and the applied command. Provide a control that sets \(q=0\) before a new comparison. Use conditional integration for anti-windup: if the requested command is already beyond the PWM limit and the current error would drive it farther into saturation, do not update \(q\) on that step. The output clamp and independent Arduino safety shutdown remain active even when anti-windup is working. Before applying actuator power, complete the required safety checkoff: show the instructor the lines that calculate \(e\) , \(q\) , \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and the clamped command. Then begin the Goldilocks study. The first successful P and PI validation traces may count among the eight retained runs when they use the matched conditions specified below: Use the same safe setpoints and a stable \(K_p\) from Module 5. Set \(K_i=0\) , zero the integral state, and record a P-only response. Retain it as a Goldilocks run if it meets the protocol below. Set PWM to zero before changing controller mode or resetting the integral. Choose a small positive \(K_i\) after exploring it in the simulation. Zero the integral state, enable PI, and record the response from comparable initial conditions. Retain it as a Goldilocks run if it meets the protocol below. Confirm that \(u_I\) grows while a persistent error remains and that the steady error becomes smaller than in the P-only run. Stop and set PWM to zero if the temperature moves in the wrong direction, the display freezes, saturation persists unexpectedly, or oscillations grow. Do not collect extra traces solely to validate the controller. If a validation run does not meet the matched Goldilocks conditions, use it only for debugging and do not include it in A3. Complete the eight-run study below before beginning Part II. Experimental Goldilocks Study ¶ Use one apparatus, one PWM limit, and the same two temperature setpoints for all eight retained runs. Each run must contain an upward setpoint step and a downward setpoint step so that heating and cooling are compared under matched conditions. Begin each step from a settled or clearly documented initial temperature. Run Controller Gain choice Purpose 1 P Small \(K_p\) Monotonic; relatively slow response or large droop 2 P Critical \(K_p\) Near the observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot 3 P Underdamped \(K_p\) Overshoot or ringing with a clearly decaying envelope 4 P Oscillatory \(K_p\) Sustained oscillation with approximately constant late-time amplitude 5 PI Small: fixed PI \(K_p\) ; small \(K_i\) Slow integral correction; strongly damped 6 PI Critical: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; larger \(K_i\) Near the observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot 7 PI Underdamped: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; larger \(K_i\) Overshoot or ringing with a clearly decaying envelope 8 PI Oscillatory: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; largest \(K_i\) Sustained oscillation with approximately constant late-time amplitude For P runs, set \(K_i=0\) . Increase \(K_p\) in controlled steps to locate the four distinct P conditions. Here critical is an experimental, operational boundary: the response is close to the transition between monotonic and overshooting behavior. Underdamped means the oscillation envelope decays; oscillatory means that several late-time cycles retain approximately constant amplitude. For Run 4, begin above the Run 3 gain and continue increasing \(K_p\) while keeping every other condition fixed. Reset between runs and preserve the first clear sustained-oscillation trace. If the oscillation grows or reaches a temperature or PWM limit, stop and retain the preceding trace. This fourth P trace is a deliberate model test. The one-lump P model predicts a monotonic exponential for every positive \(K_p\) . Part II will show that the linear two-lump P model can predict underdamped ringing, but its oscillations must decay. Sustained experimental P-control oscillation is therefore inconsistent with the transient predictions of both models. Hint for PI control: the integral term contributes part of the output \(u\) , so begin by exploring \(K_p\) values near but slightly below the Run 2 value. Choose one PI value of \(K_p\) , hold it fixed for Runs 5–8, and change only \(K_i\) to locate the four PI conditions. Use the same operational meanings of critical , underdamped , and oscillatory given above. Reset the integral state before every run. Here critical PI response means the experimentally observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot. It is not the same as \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) in Part II, which denotes the boundary between stable and unstable two-lump PI control. At \(K_i=K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , the ideal two-lump model is marginally stable and predicts sustained oscillation. Preserve time series for measured temperature, setpoint, signed applied PWM, \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and error. Record the actual gains, initial temperatures, PWM limit, sample interval, and anti-windup setting. The Arduino temperature shutdown and PWM clamp remain active for every run. Make and label the eight experimental Goldilocks plots during this lesson. Part II asks you to make the eight corresponding simulation plots and compare them under matched conditions. Preserve Your Evidence ¶ Before closing the simulation or dismantling the apparatus, save the settings, data, plots, and calculations needed for A3. Commit the simulation and your Markdown record so the analysis is reproducible. git status git add README.md docs data python/Lab_6_7_modeling_tec.py git commit -m "Analyze open-loop P and PI temperature control" git push A3: Feedback Data And Lumped-Model Memo ¶ Due: Wednesday, October 21, at 6:00 PM Type: team, 10 points Moodle file: A3_Lastname_Lastname.pdf Moodle submission: Each student uploads the team PDF separately; teammates may upload the same PDF Repository file: docs/assessments/a3_feedback_model.md Analysis and submission target: about 2 hours after the in-class analysis is complete How A3 Is Divided Between Parts I And II ¶ Complete after A3 questions Work completed in that part Part I Questions 1, 2, and 4 Derive the one-lump predictions; present the eight experimental Goldilocks plots and step-response metrics; analyze PI steady state, windup, and anti-windup. Part II Questions 3 and 5 Hold the physical model parameters fixed, vary only the controller gains, produce the eight two-lump Goldilocks plots, compare simulation with experiment, and assess the model limits. Question 2 contains the experimental reference measurements. Question 3 uses Part II to make and interpret the corresponding simulations. Do not try to complete Questions 3 or 5 before completing Part II. The final A3 assembly consists of selecting the already completed comparison plots and table, writing the short interpretation, checking paths, committing, pushing, and submitting the PDF. The one-lump derivation is part of this paper, not a separate graded document. Use the eight experimental Goldilocks plots produced in Part 7 and the eight corresponding simulation plots produced in Part II. No additional runs are required for A3. A3 Questions ¶ Answer the following questions concisely. Support each answer with equations, measured values, or plots where requested. 1. One-Lump Model And P-Control Predictions ¶ Starting from the dimensional one-lump energy balance, show that \(\tau=C/H\) and \(\chi=P_u/H\) , then write the model using your measured \(\tau\) and \(\chi\) . Derive the P-control droop, \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{1+\chi K_p}, \] and the closed-loop time constant, \[ \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{\tau}{1+\chi K_p}. \] Explain why increasing \(K_p\) both decreases droop and speeds up the response. Identify the dimensionless loop gain. Compare one representative open-loop or P-control prediction with measurement and state what agrees. 2. Experimental Goldilocks Plots And Step-Response Metrics ¶ Part 1: Experimental Goldilocks plots. Present eight experimental plots: four P responses and four PI responses at small, critical, underdamped, and oscillatory gain settings. Note that in the figure below, the oscillatory examples are not shown. However, I want you to show them. Within the P series vary \(K_p\) with \(K_i=0\) . Within the PI series hold one \(K_p\) fixed and vary \(K_i\) . For each plot, show the process output (measured temperature) and process input (signed applied PWM). The four curves in the reference figure below correspond to this part: the input \(u\) and output \(y\) for P control, and the input \(u\) and output \(y\) for PI control. Reference responses for (a) proportional control and (b) PI control. In this course, the input \(u\) is the signed PWM command applied to the TEC, and the output \(y\) is the measured temperature. Part 2: Step-response metrics. Analyze the largest-gain P and PI cases quantitatively. For both upward and downward steps, report rise time, percent overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, and oscillation period when applicable. Define the thresholds used for rise and settling times. These measured quantities provide the experimental reference for the guided simulation exercise on increasing and suppressing oscillation . In that exercise, you will vary model parameters and determine which changes increase or suppress the same response features measured here. Step-response attributes: rise time, percent overshoot, settling time, and steady-state error. 3. Simulation Goldilocks Plots And Experiment-Theory Comparison ¶ To be answered after completing Part II. Present eight two-lump simulation plots corresponding qualitatively to the eight experimental plots in Question 2. Every simulation must use the same physical parameters \(\chi_c\) , \(\chi_h\) , \(\tau\) , \(G\) , \(C_T/C\) , TEC voltage, TEC resistance, setpoints, starting conditions, and PWM limit because all eight experiments use the same apparatus. Change only controller mode, \(K_p\) , and \(K_i\) as required by the guided eight-run protocol in Part II . The simulated gain values need not equal the experimental gain values: keep the plant fixed and vary only \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) to test whether the model can reproduce the same sequence of behaviors. Label each P plot with the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) and each PI plot with the displayed \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) . Use these stability measures to explain rise time, overshoot, settling, and oscillation decay. For the shared physical parameter set, also calculate \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) and identify which of the four two-lump P gains lie below, near, or above it. Also run the one-lump P model at four increasing values of \(K_p\) and show the four responses together in one comparison figure. Classify each response as stable non-oscillatory, stable underdamped, marginally stable, or unstable, and state whether the selected model permits that behavior. Identify one important agreement and one important disagreement between simulation and experiment. 4. PI Steady State, Assumptions, And Windup ¶ Part 1: Ideal PI steady state. Assume ideal PI behavior and \(T_{\mathrm{set}}=55\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . What is the steady-state temperature \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) ? Use \(u=u_P+u_I=K_pe+K_iq\) and \(dq/dt=e\) to justify your answer and explain how integral action removes droop. Part 2: Conditions for the ideal result. What assumptions must hold for the result in Part 1 to be reached? Address closed-loop stability, the available PWM range, actuator saturation, continued integral action, and temperature measurement. Explain integral windup, describe your anti-windup rule, and state what happens when the integral state is reset after PI control has reached steady state. 5. Model Limits And Gain Selection ¶ To be answered after completing Part II. Explain mathematically why the one-lump P-control model cannot overshoot. Use the two-lump equations and your sixteen Goldilocks plots to explain how internal thermal lag produces behavior absent from the one-lump model. Compare the experimental oscillatory P run with the highest-gain response from each simulation. Do either the one-lump or two-lump P simulations produce sustained oscillations? Since the experiment does, investigate the origin of the discrepancy: what checks would distinguish a measurement or data-recording artifact from physical dynamics omitted by the models? State which explanation is better supported by your evidence. Explain why the one-lump model is falsified by overshoot and why the linear two-lump P model is falsified when the measured oscillations do not decay. State which steady-state predictions remain useful. Use \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) , \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) , and \(\rho_I\) to justify your final \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) , then name one physical effect that a better model should include. Offer arguments why inclusion of the physical effect you identify would improve the model. What To Submit ¶ Submit one PDF containing concise responses to all five questions, the eight experimental and eight two-lump simulation Goldilocks plots, the four-gain one-lump comparison figure, the guided comparison answers, and links to the underlying data, analysis code, and GitHub modeling checkpoint. Integrate the Module 5 interpretation questions into A3 Questions 1 and 5, and integrate the windup thought experiment into Question 4 rather than repeating either set separately. A3 Rubric ¶ Criterion Points One-lump energy balance, measured parameters, P-control droop, response speed, and dimensionless gain are correct 2 Eight experimental Goldilocks plots use matched conditions, with small, critical, underdamped, and oscillatory runs for both P and PI control; the oscillatory runs are quantified in both directions 2 Both models are tested with four increasing P gains; eight two-lump simulation Goldilocks plots vary only controller gains while using one common set of physical parameters and are compared with experiment 2 Integral action, reset, windup, and anti-windup are explained using the controller equations 2 The two-lump explanation, quantitative stability criteria, model comparison, and final gain choice are justified 2 Oral Review Questions: PI Control ¶ Use this PI-control question to check your understanding and prepare A3: Why can integral action remove droop, and what is integral windup? How did changing \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) affect rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, and saturation in the physical apparatus? Also prepare the Module 5 P-control questions and Module 7 modeling questions . The A3 deadline and rubric are above.

docs.title: Module 6, Part I: P/PI Control And Lumped Modeling

docs.text: Module 5 showed that proportional feedback reduces steady-state error but can overshoot, ring, and oscillate. Module 6 develops the theory needed to distinguish what a one-lump model explains from behavior that requires additional thermal dynamics. The goal is to connect thermal physics, feedback equations, and the data you measured from the TEC. A central theme is stability : whether a disturbed response returns to its steady state, continues oscillating, or grows away from it. You will first identify these behaviors qualitatively in data and simulation, then connect them to quantitative model predictions. A second theme is that the same time dependence can be understood in two parallel ways. We can keep the coupled first-order equations, write them as a matrix equation, and obtain exponential modes from the matrix eigenvalues. Or we can eliminate the additional state variables, obtain one higher-order differential equation, and find the same exponential modes from its characteristic polynomial. Module 6 develops both descriptions side by side. You will begin with algebra, then simulate the one-lump model in time, then extend the model just enough to understand why integral control is useful and why real feedback loops can oscillate.
docs.title: Purpose

docs.text: By the end of Module 6, Part I, you should be able to: derive and interpret the one-lump energy balance, open-loop susceptibility, thermal time constant, and P-control droop; calculate how \(K_p\) changes one-lump P-control droop and response time, and explain why this first-order model is stable and cannot overshoot; use the one-lump PI damping ratio to predict qualitatively how \(K_p\) , \(K_i\) , and \(C\) affect oscillation and settling; distinguish rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, and stable, marginal, or growing oscillations in simulation and measurement; connect model predictions to measured susceptibility, time constant, droop, and transient response, and identify where the one-lump model fails; assess and falsify transient models by comparing their predicted decay with sustained high-gain P-control oscillations in the physical apparatus; hold the apparatus fixed while varying \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) , and use the resulting small, critical, underdamped, and oscillatory responses to separate controller effects from physical-plant effects; explain qualitatively how internal thermal storage and transport create phase lag and motivate a two-lump model; implement PI control on the physical TEC, including integral reset and anti-windup; generate eight experimental Goldilocks plots: four P-control and four PI-control responses at small, critical, underdamped, and oscillatory gains; then use them to choose gains that balance speed, steady-state accuracy, overshoot, settling, and stability. The Goldilocks plots are the principal way you achieve these objectives. They are assessed through the physical eight-run study, the eight corresponding simulation plots in Part II, and A3 Questions 1–5. In each study, the physical apparatus or model parameters remain fixed while only the controller gains are varied. The parallel matrix/eigenvalue and higher-order differential-equation descriptions are included for mathematical culture and interpretation. They support the stability discussion but are not a separate A3 derivation.
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: Read selectively: Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook . Section 1.3: read for energy-balance language and units. Chapter 4, especially Section 4.5: read for transient response and thermal time constants. Review your Module 4 and Module 5 data. Optional after class: Bechhoefer, Feedback for Physicists , pp. 795-797 , on feedback and stability. Do not try to learn all of transient heat transfer at once. For this module, you need the idea that a physical object has heat capacity, exchanges heat with its environment, and responds over a time scale.
docs.title: Reading

docs.text: Thermal capacitance (thermal mass): energy required to raise the lump's temperature by one degree. In this module, thermal mass is an informal synonym for thermal capacitance. Thermal resistance: opposition to passive heat flow between the lump and its surroundings. Heat-loss conductance: the inverse of thermal resistance; passive heat transfer per degree of temperature difference. Time constant: characteristic decay time. A first-order system has one time constant; a higher-order system can have more than one decay time. Command: the controller output \(u\) , expressed here as a signed PWM value. For example, a command of \(+25\) PWM means set \(u=+25\) PWM. Open-loop temperature susceptibility: steady-state temperature change per applied PWM command, with direction held fixed. P control: command proportional to the current temperature error. PI control: command equal to the sum of a proportional term and a term proportional to accumulated temperature error. Windup: continued growth of the integral term while the actuator is saturated. Anti-windup: a software rule that prevents or reverses inappropriate growth of the integral term while the actuator is saturated. Droop: nonzero steady-state temperature error in P-only control. Stable: after a disturbance, the response returns to its steady state. Underdamped: a stable response that crosses its steady state and oscillates with decreasing amplitude. Marginally stable: an idealized response whose oscillations persist at constant amplitude rather than decaying. Unstable: a response that moves farther from steady state; in an oscillatory instability, successive oscillations grow.

docs.text: The dimensional one-lump model is \[ C\frac{dT}{dt}=P_u u-H(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] This is the one-lump heat balance written in terms of the lump's temperature. It follows from the more general First Law in rate form. The change of energy in time is equal to the rate of heat into the lump minus the rate of heat out: \[ \frac{dU}{dt}=\dot Q_{\mathrm{in}}-\dot Q_{\mathrm{out}}. \] If the lump has constant thermal capacitance \(C\) , then \(dU=C\,dT\) , so \[ \frac{dU}{dt}=C\frac{dT}{dt}. \] Each of the three terms in the one-lump model therefore has units of power: 1. Energy storage \[ C\frac{dT}{dt}. \] The thermal capacitance \(C=mc_p\) has units J/K, and \(dT/dt\) has units K/s or °C/s. Their product has units J/s = W. A positive value means the lump is warming; a negative value means it is cooling. 2. TEC heating or cooling \[ P_u u. \] The signed PWM command \(u\) is positive for heating and negative for cooling. The effective TEC coefficient \(P_u\) has units W/PWM, so \(P_u u\) has units W. This term treats the rapidly switched PWM drive as an average thermal power. 3. Heat transfer to the surroundings \[ -H(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] The total heat-loss conductance \(H\) has units W/K, while \(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) is a temperature difference in K or °C. Their product has units W. If \(T>T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) , this term is negative and the lump loses heat. If \(T<T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) , the term is positive: the room transfers heat into the colder lump. The algebraic droop model below is the steady-state limit of this energy balance, where \(dT/dt=0\) .
docs.title: Part 1: Algebraic Droop Model

docs.text: The measured Module 4 open-loop relationship is \[ T=T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u, \] where \(\chi=dT/du\) is the open-loop susceptibility with respect to signed PWM. With the signed convention, \(\chi\) is positive: positive \(u\) heats and raises \(T\) , while negative \(u\) cools and lowers \(T\) . P-only feedback supplies \[ u=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T). \] Substitute the controller law into the measured open-loop relationship: \[ T=T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T). \] At steady state, collect the terms containing \(T\) : \[ (1+\chi K_p)T =T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi K_pT_{\mathrm{set}}. \] Subtract this result from \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) to obtain the droop: \[ \boxed{ T_{\mathrm{set}}-T= \frac{T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{1+\chi K_p}. } \] The product \(L=\chi K_p\) is dimensionless. It is the loop gain for this steady-state model. Part 2 derives \(\chi=P_u/H\) from the dimensional model. Using one of your Module 5 runs, use \(\chi\) , \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) , \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) , and \(K_p\) in the boxed equation to calculate the predicted settled temperature and droop. Compare the prediction with the measured Module 5 droop, then state one physical reason they may differ.
docs.title: Guided Derivation And Numerical Check

docs.text: Continue with the dimensional one-lump energy balance from Part 1: \[ C\frac{dT}{dt}=P_u u-H(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] This remains the physical foundation for the rest of Module 6. Divide by \(C\) : \[ \frac{dT}{dt} =\frac{P_u}{C}u-\frac{H}{C}(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] At steady state, \(dT/dt=0\) , so \[ T=T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\frac{P_u}{H}u. \] Comparison with the Module 4 measurement \(T=T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u\) identifies \[ \boxed{\chi=\frac{P_u}{H}}. \] For constant \(u\) , define the steady-state temperature \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}} =T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\frac{P_u}{H}u =T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u. \] Now define the displacement from that steady state: \[ \theta(t)=T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Because \(u\) and \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) are constant, substitution into the one-lump energy balance gives \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-H\theta, \] or \[ \frac{d\theta}{dt}=-\frac{H}{C}\theta. \] Its solution is \[ \theta(t)=\theta(0)e^{-(H/C)t} =\theta(0)e^{-t/\tau}. \] Comparison of the exponents identifies the open-loop thermal time constant: \[ \boxed{\tau=\frac{C}{H}}. \] The units confirm that this ratio is a time: \[ [\tau]=\frac{\mathrm{J/K}}{\mathrm{W/K}} =\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{J/s}}=\mathrm{s}. \] Sidebar: Dimensionless form The ratios \(\tau=C/H\) and \(\chi=P_u/H\) are the measured combinations that govern the one-lump model. Define \[ \hat t=\frac{t}{\tau}, \qquad \hat T=\frac{T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{\chi u_0}, \qquad \hat u=\frac{u}{u_0}. \] The open-loop model becomes \[ \frac{d\hat T}{d\hat t}=\hat u-\hat T. \] This shows that \(\tau\) supplies the time scale and \(\chi u_0\) supplies the temperature scale. For P control, the dimensionless loop gain is \(L=\chi K_p\) . See Stone, Sections 1.5.1-1.5.2 and Lienhard, Section 5.2 for fuller treatments. The two measured quantities are the thermal time constant and the open-loop susceptibility: \[ \boxed{\tau=\frac{C}{H}}, \qquad \boxed{\chi=\frac{P_u}{H}}. \] These two measured quantities determine the two parameter ratios that govern the dynamics: \[ \boxed{\frac{H}{C}=\frac{1}{\tau}}, \qquad \boxed{\frac{P_u}{C} =\frac{P_u/H}{C/H} =\frac{\chi}{\tau}}. \] Module 4 provides the heating and cooling susceptibilities, and a temperature step from Module 4 or Module 5 provides \(\tau\) . Use the susceptibility for the corresponding direction. Therefore, once \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) and the command \(u\) are specified, the model has no free parameters . Its transient temperature prediction can be compared directly with the measurement rather than fitted to it. The same dimensional energy balance can therefore be written entirely in terms of \(\chi\) and \(\tau\) : \[ \boxed{ \frac{dT}{dt} =\frac{T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u-T}{\tau}. } \] This is not a different model. It is the one-lump energy balance expressed in a form that can be simulated using your measured susceptibility and time constant. The quantity \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u\) is the steady temperature toward which the model moves for a constant command \(u\) ; \(\tau\) determines how quickly it moves there.
docs.title: Part 2: Express The One-Lump Model Using Measured Parameters

docs.text: Use a temperature step from Module 4 or Module 5. Use a trace in which every temperature value was calculated by averaging exactly 1,000 raw thermistor-voltage measurements, as required in Modules 2 through 5. One practical method: Identify the initial temperature, \(T_{\mathrm{initial}}\) . Identify the approximate final temperature, \(T_{\mathrm{final}}\) . Calculate 63 percent of the total change using \(T_{63}=T_{\mathrm{initial}} +0.63\left(T_{\mathrm{final}}-T_{\mathrm{initial}}\right)\) . Estimate \(\tau\) as the elapsed time when the temperature first reaches \(T_{63}\) . Record how uncertain your estimate is. The trace may not be a perfect exponential. In the dimensional model, this measurement determines the ratio \(C/H\) ; it does not separately determine \(C\) and \(H\) .

docs.text: Download the prepared Module 6/7 TEC simulation . Save it in your project repository as python/Lab_6_7_modeling_tec.py , then run it from the repository root: python python/Lab_6_7_modeling_tec.py For Module 6, select one_lump as the physical model. The program performs an Euler integration of the dimensional energy balance: \[ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{C} \left[P_u u_n-H(T_n-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\right]. \] Because your experiment measures \(\chi=P_u/H\) and \(\tau=C/H\) , the equivalent measured-parameter update is \[ \boxed{ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{\tau} \left(T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u_n-T_n\right). } \] Select measured under Physical parameters . Enter your measured \(\chi_c\) , \(\chi_h\) , and \(\tau\) , the on-state voltage measured across the TEC, and the TEC module resistance from the datasheet. Before running, use the steady-state equation to predict the final temperature for one heating command and one cooling command.

Before each run, predict the steady-state droop from the Part 1 result and the closed-loop time constant from the Part 5 result . docs.title: Continue With P Control

docs.text: Now analyze the same dimensional one-lump model used throughout this module. The solution explains why its P-controlled response cannot oscillate. If the real apparatus oscillates, the difference identifies physics missing from the model. Substituting the P-control law into the energy balance gives \[ C\frac{dT}{dt} =P_uK_pT_{\mathrm{set}}+HT_{\mathrm{amb}} -(H+P_uK_p)T. \] Setting \(dT/dt=0\) gives the closed-loop steady-state temperature, \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{HT_{\mathrm{amb}}+P_uK_pT_{\mathrm{set}}} {H+P_uK_p}. \] Now define the displacement from steady state, \[ \theta(t)=T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Substitution reduces the entire closed-loop P model to \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Compare this directly with the open-loop displacement equation from Part 2, \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-H\theta. \] For the displacement dynamics, closing the P-control loop therefore makes the simple replacement \[ \boxed{H\longrightarrow H+P_uK_p}. \] The additional term \(P_uK_p\) acts like an additional restoring conductance: for the same displacement from steady state, feedback produces a larger rate of return. This replacement applies to the homogeneous transient equation; the steady-state temperature must still be calculated from the closed-loop forcing terms above. Separate variables and integrate: \[ \frac{d\theta}{\theta} =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\,dt, \] \[ \ln\!\left(\frac{\theta(t)}{\theta(0)}\right) =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t. \] Therefore the displacement is \[ \boxed{ \theta(t)=\theta(0) \exp\!\left(-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t\right) }. \] Now return from the displacement \(\theta\) to the measured temperature using \(T=T_{\mathrm{ss}}+\theta\) . Since \(\theta(0)=T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) , the temperature is \[ \boxed{ T(t)=T_{\mathrm{ss}} +\left[T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\right] \exp\!\left(-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}t\right) }. \] Equivalently, \[ T(t)=T_{\mathrm{ss}} +\left[T(0)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\right]e^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{cl}}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{C}{H+P_uK_p}. \] Using \(\tau=C/H\) and the dimensionless loop gain \(L=\chi K_p\) , \[ \boxed{ \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{\tau}{1+\chi K_p}=\frac{\tau}{1+L}. } \] Increasing gain has two effects Increasing \(K_p\) does two things at the same time: It decreases droop. \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{1+\chi K_p}. \] It speeds up the response by decreasing the closed-loop time constant. \[ \tau_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{\tau}{1+\chi K_p}. \] Thus, in this unsaturated one-lump model, both droop and response time are reduced by the same factor, \(1+\chi K_p\) . Larger gain moves the temperature closer to the setpoint and makes it approach its steady value more quickly. To find the eigenvalue directly, try an exponential mode, \[ \theta(t)=\theta_0e^{\lambda t}, \qquad \frac{d\theta}{dt}=\lambda\theta. \] Substitute this trial solution into the homogeneous P equation: \[ C\lambda\theta=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Cancel the nonzero factor \(\theta\) . There is only one eigenvalue, \[ \lambda=-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}, \] and it is real and negative for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. The exponential is always positive, so \(T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) retains its initial sign while shrinking toward zero. The response therefore cannot cross the steady state, overshoot, or oscillate. Increasing \(K_p\) decreases both droop and \(\tau_{\mathrm{cl}}\) ; it does not create the additional dynamical state or time delay needed for oscillation. Thus the ideal one-lump P model is stable and non-oscillatory for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. A measured overshoot, sustained oscillation, or growing oscillation is behavior this model cannot produce and therefore falsifies it as a model of the transient response. This first-order example is the simplest version of both mathematical views. Its state-space matrix has only one entry, so it has one real eigenvalue. The equivalent scalar equation is only first order, so its characteristic equation has the same single real root. There is no pair of complex eigenvalues and therefore no oscillatory exponential mode. Return to the high-gain trace saved in Module 5. Mark the late-time value \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) and the first overshoot. If the measured temperature crosses \(T_{\mathrm{ss}}\) , its behavior is incompatible with this one-lump solution. State the contradiction directly: the model predicts a monotonic exponential, whereas the apparatus shows an underdamped transient. This is evidence that the model is inadequate, not that the exponential solution is wrong. The one-lump model is missing thermal lag between where the TEC applies heat and where the thermistor measures temperature. The simplest extension is to represent these locations as two coupled thermal masses. This two-lump model is introduced below and developed systematically in Part II. Why a Thermal Control System Can Oscillate Without Mechanical Inertia Begin with the familiar mass and spring. A damped mechanical oscillator obeys \[ m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0. \] Its two state variables are position \(x\) and velocity \(\dot x\) . Ignoring damping for the moment, the spring force is zero when the mass passes through \(x=0\) , but the velocity is largest there. Kinetic energy carries the mass past equilibrium. This is mechanical inertia: zero restoring force does not imply zero velocity. A one-lump thermal model cannot coast. Its P-controlled displacement obeys \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-(H+P_uK_p)\theta. \] Temperature is its only state variable. If the net heat flow becomes zero, then \(dT/dt=0\) immediately. The temperature cannot coast through equilibrium, so the model produces one monotonic exponential and cannot overshoot. The apparatus contains a hidden thermal state. The simplest improvement is a two-lump thermal model . One lump represents the region near the TEC, where heat is applied. The other represents the block and thermistor, where temperature is measured. Each lump stores thermal energy, and heat takes time to move between them. With P control, \(u=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_m)\) , where \(T_m\) is the measured temperature. Suppose \(T_m\) reaches the setpoint and the controller reduces its command. The TEC-side region can still be hotter than the measured block, so stored energy continues flowing toward the thermistor and \(T_m\) continues rising. The temperature overshoots not because it has mechanical momentum, but because the measured temperature does not reveal all the thermal energy already stored elsewhere in the apparatus. The qualitative correspondence is Mass-spring oscillator Thermal control system measured position \(x\) measured temperature \(T_m\) hidden velocity \(\dot x\) hidden TEC-side temperature \(T\) kinetic energy carries the mass past equilibrium stored heat continues flowing after \(T_m\) reaches the setpoint mechanical inertia supplies the second state thermal storage and transport supply the second state The phase-lag interpretation. The thermistor reports the effect of a TEC command only after heat has propagated to the measured block. The controller therefore acts partly on old information. As gain increases, this lag can make the correction arrive too late, after which the controller overcorrects in the opposite direction. This qualitative model explains why the real apparatus can overshoot even though the one-lump model cannot. Module 6, Part II introduces the coupled two-lump equations, shows why they form a second-order system, and explores their behavior quantitatively. Thus the nearly model-independent steady-state energy balance can succeed even when the one-lump transient model fails. Part II develops and tests the two-lump explanation quantitatively.
docs.title: Part 5: Explain The One-Lump P Transient And Its Limit

docs.text: Keep the same dimensional one-lump energy balance. PI control changes only the command supplied to the TEC. Define the temperature error and its accumulated value as \[ e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T, \qquad q(t)=q(0)+\int_0^t e(t')\,dt'. \] The PI command is \[ u=K_p e+K_iq, \] so the physical model remains \[ \boxed{ C\frac{dT}{dt} =P_u\left[K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T)+K_iq\right] -H(T-T_{\mathrm{amb}}), \qquad \frac{dq}{dt}=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T. } \] The simulation first updates the integral state, \[ q_{n+1}=q_n+(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_n)\Delta t, \] then calculates and clamps the command using the accepted value of \(q_{n+1}\) , \[ u_n=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_n)+K_iq_{n+1}, \] and finally advances the temperature: \[ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{\tau} \left(T_{\mathrm{amb}}+\chi u_n-T_n\right). \] Select pi in the simulation and begin with a stable \(K_p\) . Use Zero integral to clear the controller memory before a comparison. Watch the displayed values of \(e\) , \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and the applied command while the temperature approaches the setpoint.
docs.title: Part 6: Add Integral Action In Simulation

docs.text: Begin from the P-control case after it has developed visible droop. Select pi , press Zero integral , and resume. Watch \(e\) , \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and the applied command \(u\) while the temperature approaches the setpoint. Answer: While \(e>0\) , why does \(u_I\) continue to grow? As \(T\) reaches the setpoint, why does \(u_P\) approach zero? Why can \(u_I\) remain nonzero when \(e=0\) ? After steady state, press Zero integral again. Why does the temperature initially move away from the setpoint? The steady integral contribution replaces the nonzero proportional error that was required to provide the steady command under P-only control. Why Integral Windup Occurs The PI controller first calculates a requested command , \[ u_{\mathrm{req}}=K_pe+K_iq, \qquad q_{n+1}=q_n+e_n\Delta t. \] The actuator can apply only a limited command, so the program clamps that request: \[ u_{\mathrm{applied}} =\operatorname{clamp}(u_{\mathrm{req}},-u_{\max},u_{\max}). \] Suppose a large positive error requests more than \(u_{\max}\) . The applied PWM cannot increase further, but ordinary integration keeps adding the positive error to \(q\) . The extra integral contribution has no immediate effect on the TEC because the actuator is already saturated. It is stored in the controller instead. When the temperature later approaches the setpoint, the error and proportional contribution become small, but the accumulated integral contribution can remain large. The controller therefore continues driving the TEC through the setpoint. It may take a long time for error of the opposite sign to unwind the stored integral, producing excessive overshoot and slow recovery. The anti-windup rule used here is conditional integration : if the command is saturated and the current error would push it farther into saturation, hold \(q\) fixed; otherwise, update \(q\) , including when the error helps bring the command out of saturation. The PWM clamp, anti-windup rule, and Zero integral control have different jobs. The clamp protects the actuator, anti-windup controls the growth of the controller's memory during normal operation, and Zero integral deliberately clears that memory before a new comparison.
docs.title: Guided Simulation Exercise: Watch The Integral Contribution

docs.text: PI control adds the accumulated error as a second state variable. The one-lump P model has only one state and therefore produces one monotonic exponential; the one-lump PI model has two coupled states and can overshoot or oscillate. For an unsaturated PI controller at steady state, the integral state must stop changing. Because \(dq/dt=e\) , \[ \frac{dq}{dt}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_{\mathrm{ss}}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{\mathrm{ss}}=T_{\mathrm{set}}. \] The steady-state heat balance is therefore \[ 0=P_u u_{\mathrm{ss}} -H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}}), \] which requires \[ u_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})}{P_u}. \] At zero error the proportional contribution is zero, so the integral contribution supplies the entire steady command: \[ u_{\mathrm{ss}}=K_iq_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Combining these results gives \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}}=T_{\mathrm{set}}, \qquad q_{\mathrm{ss}} =\frac{H(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})}{P_uK_i}. \] This result assumes stable control, a reachable setpoint, no sustained actuator saturation, and continued integral action. Two routes to the same PI time dependence The one-lump PI model will now be analyzed in two parallel ways. Coupled-state or matrix route: keep \((\theta,z)\) as two state variables, write \(\dot{\mathbf{x}}=A\mathbf{x}\) , and find the allowed exponential modes from \(\det(\lambda I-A)=0\) . Higher-order ODE route: eliminate \(z\) and obtain one second-order equation for \(\theta\) . Substituting \(\theta\propto e^{\lambda t}\) gives its characteristic polynomial. The determinant and the characteristic polynomial are the same quadratic. The two routes therefore predict the same \(\lambda_\pm\) , the same decay rates, and the same oscillation frequency. They are two descriptions of one physical dynamics, not two different models.
docs.title: Why PI Can Be Underdamped

docs.text: The one-lump thermal plant has one state, its temperature \(T\) . PI control adds the accumulated error \(q\) as a second state. The closed-loop model therefore has two coupled first-order differential equations even though it contains only one thermal lump. Those two first-order equations can be combined into one second-order differential equation for temperature. Define the temperature and integral-state displacements from steady state, \[ \theta=T-T_{\mathrm{set}}, \qquad z=q-q_{\mathrm{ss}}. \] Because \(e=-\theta\) , the two coupled first-order equations are \[ \frac{d\theta}{dt} =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\theta +\frac{P_uK_i}{C}z, \qquad \frac{dz}{dt}=-\theta. \] In matrix form, \[ \frac{d}{dt} \begin{pmatrix}\theta\\z\end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{ \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{H+P_uK_p}{C} & \dfrac{P_uK_i}{C}\\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} }_{A} \begin{pmatrix}\theta\\z\end{pmatrix}. \] To eliminate \(z\) , first multiply the temperature equation by \(C\) , \[ C\frac{d\theta}{dt} =-(H+P_uK_p)\theta+P_uK_i z. \] Differentiate this equation with respect to time: \[ C\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} =-(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta}{dt} +P_uK_i\frac{dz}{dt}. \] The second first-order equation says \(dz/dt=-\theta\) . Substituting it removes the integral-state variable and gives \[ \boxed{ C\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} +(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta}{dt} +P_uK_i\theta=0 }. \] Thus the two coupled first-order equations for \((\theta,z)\) are equivalent to one second-order differential equation for \(\theta\) . The integral controller's memory supplies the additional dynamical state that makes overshoot and oscillation possible in the one-lump PI model.
docs.title: From Two First-Order Equations To One Second-Order Equation

docs.text: Try an exponential solution, \(\theta(t)=\theta_0e^{\lambda t}\) . Substitution into the second-order differential equation gives \[ C\lambda^2+(H+P_uK_p)\lambda+P_uK_i=0. \] The eigenvalues \(\lambda_+\) and \(\lambda_-\) are the two roots of this quadratic equation. Applying the quadratic formula gives \[ \boxed{ \lambda_\pm =-\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C} \pm \sqrt{ \left(\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}\right)^2 -\frac{P_uK_i}{C} } }. \] The matrix route gives exactly the same equation: \[ \det(\lambda I-A) =\lambda^2 +\frac{H+P_uK_p}{C}\lambda +\frac{P_uK_i}{C}=0. \] Thus the roots of the scalar second-order equation are the eigenvalues of the coupled first-order matrix. In either language, each root supplies a time factor \(e^{\lambda t}\) . Define the envelope relaxation rate and natural angular frequency, \[ \gamma=\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}, \qquad \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{P_uK_i}{C}}. \] Then \[ \lambda_\pm=-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-\omega_n^2}. \] For positive \(C\) , \(H\) , \(P_u\) , \(K_p\) , and \(K_i\) , the real parts of both eigenvalues are always negative. Thus this ideal, unsaturated one-lump PI model is always stable : every transient eventually decays toward steady state. Stability does not require a monotonic response, however. If \(\omega_n>\gamma\) , the square root is imaginary, and \[ \lambda_\pm=-\gamma\pm i\omega_d, \qquad \boxed{\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_n^2-\gamma^2}}. \] The temperature displacement is then a decaying oscillation, \[ \boxed{ \theta(t)=e^{-\gamma t} \left[A\cos(\omega_dt)+B\sin(\omega_dt)\right] }. \] The negative real part, \(-\gamma\) , makes the oscillation envelope decay; the imaginary part, \(\omega_d\) , sets the oscillation period \(T_{\mathrm{osc}}=2\pi/\omega_d\) . The response is therefore stable but underdamped. How diagonalization solves the matrix ODE Write the state vector and its equation as \[ \mathbf{x}(t)= \begin{pmatrix}\theta(t)\\z(t)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}. \] Look for one exponential mode, \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{v}e^{\lambda t}, \] where the constant vector \(\mathbf{v}\) gives the relative amounts of temperature displacement and integral-state displacement in that mode. Substitution and cancellation of the nonzero exponential give \[ (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0. \] We want a nonzero eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) . If \(A-\lambda I\) were invertible, multiplying by its inverse would force \(\mathbf{v}=0\) . A nonzero solution is therefore possible only when the matrix is singular: \[ \boxed{\det(A-\lambda I)=0}. \] This determinant equation finds the allowed eigenvalues. For each eigenvalue, solving \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0\) gives its eigenvector. If the two eigenvectors are independent, put them in the columns of \[ V=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}_+&\mathbf{v}_-\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda= \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_+&0\\0&\lambda_-\end{pmatrix}. \] The eigenvalue equations together say \(AV=V\Lambda\) . Change coordinates by writing \(\mathbf{x}=V\mathbf{y}\) . Because \(V\) is constant, \[ V\frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt} =AV\mathbf{y} =V\Lambda\mathbf{y}, \] so multiplication by \(V^{-1}\) gives \[ \frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt}=\Lambda\mathbf{y}. \] Because \(\Lambda\) is diagonal, the coupled system has become two independent scalar equations, \[ \frac{dy_+}{dt}=\lambda_+y_+, \qquad \frac{dy_-}{dt}=\lambda_-y_-. \] Their solutions are \(y_\pm(t)=y_\pm(0)e^{\lambda_\pm t}\) . Transforming back gives \[ \boxed{ \mathbf{x}(t) =V \begin{pmatrix} e^{\lambda_+t}&0\\0&e^{\lambda_-t} \end{pmatrix} V^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0) =e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0) }. \] Thus diagonalization expresses the matrix exponential as two ordinary exponential modes whose eigenvalues are the quadratic roots derived above. Complex-conjugate eigenvalues combine to produce a real decaying oscillation. At critical damping, a repeated eigenvalue may provide only one eigenvector; the matrix exponential still exists, and the solution can contain a term proportional to \(t e^{\lambda t}\) . Compare this equation with the standard second-order form \[ \lambda^2+2\zeta\omega_n\lambda+\omega_n^2=0. \] The natural angular frequency and damping ratio are therefore \[ \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{P_uK_i}{C}}, \qquad \boxed{ \zeta=\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2\sqrt{CP_uK_i}} }. \] The dimensionless damping ratio \(\zeta\) identifies the transition: \(\zeta>1\) : overdamped, with two real negative roots; \(\zeta=1\) : critically damped; and \(\zeta<1\) : underdamped, with a complex-conjugate pair and a decaying oscillation. As the eigenvalues show above, all three responses are stable for positive parameters. In particular, underdamped means that the oscillations decay; it does not mean unstable. Constant-amplitude oscillations that last forever would be marginally stable, and growing oscillations would be unstable. Neither is predicted by this unsaturated one-lump PI model with positive parameters. For the underdamped one-lump PI model, the temperature approaches steady state as a decaying sinusoid, \[ \boxed{ T(t)-T_{\mathrm{ss}} =A e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\cos(\omega_d t-\phi) }, \qquad \omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}. \] The exponential envelope has decay time \[ \tau_{\mathrm{decay}}=\frac{1}{\gamma}, \qquad \boxed{ \gamma=\zeta\omega_n =\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C} }. \] Thus \(\gamma\) is the relaxation rate : increasing \(\gamma\) makes the oscillation envelope decay more rapidly. The damped oscillation frequency and period are \[ \boxed{ \omega_d =\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2} =\sqrt{ \frac{P_uK_i}{C} -\left(\frac{H+P_uK_p}{2C}\right)^2 } }, \qquad T_{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_d}. \] The dimensionless quality factor is \[ \boxed{ Q=\frac{\omega_n}{2\gamma} =\frac{1}{2\zeta} =\frac{\sqrt{CP_uK_i}}{H+P_uK_p} }. \] The quality factor is related to, but is not equal to, the number of oscillation periods in one decay time. For an underdamped response, \[ \boxed{ \frac{\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}}{T_{\mathrm{osc}}} =\frac{\omega_d}{2\pi\gamma} =\frac{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}{2\pi\zeta} =\frac{Q}{\pi}\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4Q^2}} }. \] When damping is weak, \(\zeta\ll1\) , this becomes \(\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}/T_{\mathrm{osc}}\approx Q/\pi\) , or \(Q\approx\pi\tau_{\mathrm{decay}}/T_{\mathrm{osc}}\) . Thus \(Q<1/2\) is overdamped, \(Q=1/2\) is critically damped, and \(Q>1/2\) is underdamped. Larger \(Q\) means that the oscillation loses a smaller fraction of its amplitude per cycle. Within this ideal unsaturated one-lump PI model, increasing \(K_i\) decreases \(\zeta\) and makes oscillation more likely, while increasing \(K_p\) increases \(\zeta\) . The simulation displays this one-lump PI damping ratio . It is not the damping ratio of the full two-lump model developed in Part II. This result is included for interpretation, not as a required A3 derivation. Use the simulation to observe how \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) change the response.

docs.text: Use your working Module 5 P controller as the starting point. Do not replace the Arduino's independent temperature shutdown or the existing signed-PWM clamp. Display and save \(e\) , \(u_P=K_pe\) , \(u_I=K_iq\) , the requested command, and the applied command. Provide a control that sets \(q=0\) before a new comparison. Use conditional integration for anti-windup: if the requested command is already beyond the PWM limit and the current error would drive it farther into saturation, do not update \(q\) on that step. The output clamp and independent Arduino safety shutdown remain active even when anti-windup is working. Before applying actuator power, complete the required safety checkoff: show the instructor the lines that calculate \(e\) , \(q\) , \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and the clamped command. Then begin the Goldilocks study. The first successful P and PI validation traces may count among the eight retained runs when they use the matched conditions specified below: Use the same safe setpoints and a stable \(K_p\) from Module 5. Set \(K_i=0\) , zero the integral state, and record a P-only response. Retain it as a Goldilocks run if it meets the protocol below. Set PWM to zero before changing controller mode or resetting the integral. Choose a small positive \(K_i\) after exploring it in the simulation. Zero the integral state, enable PI, and record the response from comparable initial conditions. Retain it as a Goldilocks run if it meets the protocol below. Confirm that \(u_I\) grows while a persistent error remains and that the steady error becomes smaller than in the P-only run. Stop and set PWM to zero if the temperature moves in the wrong direction, the display freezes, saturation persists unexpectedly, or oscillations grow. docs.text: Use one apparatus, one PWM limit, and the same two temperature setpoints for all eight retained runs. Each run must contain an upward setpoint step and a downward setpoint step so that heating and cooling are compared under matched conditions. Begin each step from a settled or clearly documented initial temperature. Run Controller Gain choice Purpose 1 P Small \(K_p\) Monotonic; relatively slow response or large droop 2 P Critical \(K_p\) Near the observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot 3 P Underdamped \(K_p\) Overshoot or ringing with a clearly decaying envelope 4 P Oscillatory \(K_p\) Sustained oscillation with approximately constant late-time amplitude 5 PI Small: fixed PI \(K_p\) ; small \(K_i\) Slow integral correction; strongly damped 6 PI Critical: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; larger \(K_i\) Near the observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot 7 PI Underdamped: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; larger \(K_i\) Overshoot or ringing with a clearly decaying envelope 8 PI Oscillatory: Run 5 \(K_p\) ; largest \(K_i\) Sustained oscillation with approximately constant late-time amplitude For P runs, set \(K_i=0\) . Increase \(K_p\) in controlled steps to locate the four distinct P conditions. Here critical is an experimental, operational boundary: the response is close to the transition between monotonic and overshooting behavior. Underdamped means the oscillation envelope decays; oscillatory means that several late-time cycles retain approximately constant amplitude. For Run 4, begin above the Run 3 gain and continue increasing \(K_p\) while keeping every other condition fixed. Reset between runs and preserve the first clear sustained-oscillation trace. If the oscillation grows or reaches a temperature or PWM limit, stop and retain the preceding trace. This fourth P trace is a deliberate model test. The one-lump P model predicts a monotonic exponential for every positive \(K_p\) . Part II will show that the linear two-lump P model can predict underdamped ringing, but its oscillations must decay. Sustained experimental P-control oscillation is therefore inconsistent with the transient predictions of both models. Hint for PI control: the integral term contributes part of the output \(u\) , so begin by exploring \(K_p\) values near but slightly below the Run 2 value. Choose one PI value of \(K_p\) , hold it fixed for Runs 5–8, and change only \(K_i\) to locate the four PI conditions. Use the same operational meanings of critical , underdamped , and oscillatory given above. Reset the integral state before every run. Here critical PI response means the experimentally observed transition from monotonic response to overshoot. It is not the same as \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) in Part II, which denotes the boundary between stable and unstable two-lump PI control. At \(K_i=K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , the ideal two-lump model is marginally stable and predicts sustained oscillation. Preserve time series for measured temperature, setpoint, signed applied PWM, \(u_P\) , \(u_I\) , and error. Record the actual gains, initial temperatures, PWM limit, sample interval, and anti-windup setting. The Arduino temperature shutdown and PWM clamp remain active for every run. Make and label the eight experimental Goldilocks plots during this lesson. Part II asks you to make the eight corresponding simulation plots and compare them under matched conditions.
