docs.text: Module 6, Part II: TEC Process Model And The Simulation ¶ This is the second part of Module 6. Complete Part I: P/PI Control And Lumped Modeling first. Both parts use the same prepared simulation : Part I emphasizes the one-lump model, while Part II compares the one- and two-lump models. Introductory Material ¶ Purpose ¶ This part follows the first Module 6 modeling work and the initial physical PI implementation. Before beginning Part II, complete the physical \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) study and generate the eight experimental plots required by Module 6, Part I, A3 Question 2 . Part II connects three things: the physical TEC/block/thermistor system, the feedback-control equations, a Python simulation GUI that lets you change model parameters and watch the predicted temperature response. This module is not about perfect quantitative prediction. It is about learning how a simple model can qualitatively and quantitatively explain droop, overshoot, lag, damping, and the transition from stable to unstable control. Throughout Part II, use two parallel mathematical descriptions of the same dynamics. The coupled first-order energy balances form a state-space matrix whose eigenvalues determine the exponential modes. Eliminating the hidden states produces one higher-order differential equation whose characteristic polynomial has the same roots. Moving between these descriptions is a central reason for studying the two-lump model. How A3 Is Divided Between Parts I And II ¶ Complete after A3 questions Work completed in that part Part I Questions 1, 2, and 4 Derive the one-lump predictions; present the eight experimental Goldilocks plots and step-response metrics; analyze PI steady state, windup, and anti-windup. Part II (this page) Questions 3 and 5 Produce the eight two-lump simulation Goldilocks plots; compare simulation with experiment; explain the model limits and justify the selected gains. Part II does not replace or repeat the experimental analysis in Question 2. It supplies the simulation and model interpretation required for Question 3 and Question 5 . Learning Objectives ¶ By the end of Module 6, Part II, you should be able to: write and interpret the coupled energy balances for the TEC-side and measured-block thermal masses; show how two coupled first-order temperature equations produce one second-order equation for the measured temperature; use the two-lump model to explain how thermal storage and transport produce phase lag, overshoot, and behavior absent from the one-lump P model; calculate \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) and \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) and use them to classify two-lump P responses as over-, critically, or underdamped; calculate \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to predict stable, marginal, or unstable two-lump PI behavior; predict and verify how \(K_p\) , \(K_i\) , \(G\) , total capacitance, and capacitance division affect response speed, damping, and stability; hold all physical model parameters fixed while varying only \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) , so changes caused by controller tuning can be distinguished from changes to the modeled apparatus; characterize matched physical P and PI responses using rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, and oscillation period; generate eight simulation Goldilocks plots using one shared set of physical parameters and compare them with the eight experimental Goldilocks plots; test whether one- and two-lump P models can reproduce small, critical, underdamped, and sustained-oscillation behavior, and use a failure to reproduce sustained oscillation as evidence that a model is incomplete; and select and justify \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) by balancing rapid approach to the setpoint against overshoot, settling time, actuator limits, and stability while connecting theory, simulation, and measurement. The eight measured and eight simulated Goldilocks plots are the principal way you achieve these objectives. They are assessed together with the two-lump derivation in A3 Questions 3 and 5. The parallel matrix/eigenvalue and higher-order differential-equation routes are included for mathematical culture and interpretation. Follow how they produce the same characteristic polynomial, but do not prepare a separate A3 derivation of the matrix formalism. Class Theme ¶ Use Models To Explain Measurements In control theory, the process is the physical cause-and-effect system that turns the controller output into a measured response. Here, the PWM command changes the heat transported by the TEC; thermal capacitances store energy; thermal conductances move heat through the aluminum block and to the room; and the thermistor measures the resulting temperature. This chain from PWM command to measured temperature is the process we are modeling. At A Glance ¶ Before class, spend your time in this order: 25-30 min : Read the selected sections of Lienhard and prepare Problem 1.8 as a one-lump review. 15-20 min : Open the Python GUI and confirm that it runs. 20 min : Annotate the two-lump equations and organize your completed physical P/PI plots from Part I. During class on October 19, the approximate schedule for one 170-minute meeting is: 0-15 min : Inspect the completed P/PI plots and state what the one-lump model explains and fails to explain. 15-35 min : Review the one-lump energy balance with Lienhard Problem 1.8. 35-75 min : Develop the coupled two-lump balances and reduce them to a second-order equation for the measured temperature. 75-120 min : Compare one- and two-lump responses and connect thermal lag to the experimental plots. 120-155 min : Vary one parameter at a time and interpret the results using the equations. 155-170 min : Wrap up: what the model explains, what it leaves out, and why the long-rod experiment will require a spatial model. Required work takes priority over the optional parameter sweeps. Complete the two-lump derivation, one guided P transition, one guided PI stability transition, the one-time model calibration, and the eight retained Goldilocks plots before attempting optional extensions. Outside-Class Workload Budget ¶ Session Work Planned time S14 Read the selected Lienhard material and prepare Problem 1.8 30 minutes S14 Open the simulation, annotate the two-lump equations, and organize the completed P/PI plots 40 minutes S14 Total associated with S14 1 hour 10 minutes S15 Finish plot captions, comparison answers, and A3 evidence begun in class 120 minutes S15 Commit, push, and assemble the A3 submission 45 minutes S15 Total associated with S15 2 hours 45 minutes The Chapter 1 time is for reading with equations and physical interpretation, not for a quick skim. The optional extension is not part of the four-hour budget and should be attempted only after required work is complete. When To Do The Work ¶ Stage Required work Before class Complete the four preparation items under Before Class : selected reading and Problem 1.8, GUI check, annotated equations, and five two-lump theory responses. Bring the eight experimental plots from Part I. During class Develop the two-lump model, complete the required P and PI stability demonstrations, calibrate \(G\) and \(C_T/C\) once, lock the physical parameters, and begin the eight retained simulation plots. Before leaving class Save the shared model settings, every completed run, captions in progress, and links to the experimental data. After class Finish any remaining retained plots, answer the four comparison prompts, complete A3 Questions 3 and 5, and assemble, commit, push, and submit A3. Problem 1.8, the five theory prompts, guided predictions, and oral-review questions are formative preparation rather than separate submissions. A3 is the graded assessment; the eight simulation plots and comparison answers feed directly into A3 Questions 3 and 5. Vocabulary ¶ Process : the physical system being controlled. Here, the process is the TEC/block/thermistor thermal system. State variable : a number that describes the current state of the model, such as temperature. Heat : energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Heat is not the same thing as temperature; temperature tells how hot something is, while heat is energy moving into or out of the system. Lumped model : a model that treats an extended object as if the entire object were at the same temperature. The lump can be viewed as a point object of finite thermal mass. See the one-lump/two-lump figure . Thermal lag : delay between changing the actuator and observing the measured temperature response. Saturation : the actuator command reaches its limit, such as PWM 255. This could be a physical or software imposed limit. Stable : the response returns to steady state after a disturbance. Underdamped : a stable response with oscillations that decrease in amplitude. Marginally stable : an idealized response with constant-amplitude oscillations that continue forever. Unstable : a response that moves farther from steady state; oscillations grow rather than decay when the instability is oscillatory. The Python GUI separates the physical model from the controller. Select either a one-lump or two-lump process, then select open-loop, P, or PI control. Course-specific lumped-model diagram. The one-lump model assigns one temperature to the TEC, block, and thermistor assembly. It retains heat storage and heat loss to the room, but it cannot represent an internal temperature difference or delay. The two-lump model separates the TEC-side temperature \(T\) from the measured temperature \(T_m\) . Heat first crosses the internal conductance \(G\) and then leaves the measured lump through the room conductance \(H\) . Because the controller responds to \(T_m\) , this extra thermal store and transport step introduce lag that can produce overshoot and underdamped behavior. One-Lump Physical Model ¶ Part I developed the one-lump energy balance and its measured-parameter form . Carry those results forward rather than deriving them again. For comparison with the two-lump model, the one-lump capacitance is the sum \[ C=C_T+C_m, \] and the simulation continues to use \(P_{u,h}\) for heating and \(P_{u,c}\) for cooling, with \[ r=\frac{P_{u,h}}{P_{u,c}}=\frac{\chi_h}{\chi_c}. \] Two-Lump Physical Model ¶ The two-lump model separates the TEC-side temperature \(T\) from the measured temperature \(T_m\) : \[ C_T\frac{dT}{dt}=P_u(u)u-G(T-T_m), \] \[ C_m\frac{dT_m}{dt}=G(T-T_m)-H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] Here \(C_T\) and \(C_m\) are thermal capacitances. The conductance \(G\) couples the two lumps through the passive heat flow \(G(T-T_m)\) . The same heat that leaves the TEC-side lump enters the measured lump, so this term appears with opposite signs in the two equations. We simplify the apparatus by giving the TEC-side lump no separate path to the room; all heat loss to the room is represented by \(H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\) in the measured-lump equation. The controller responds to \(T_m\) , but \(T\) and \(T_m\) do not change at the same time. Which temperature changes first if someone opens a window and \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) suddenly decreases? Which changes first if \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) changes? This lag can produce overshoot or oscillation. Two routes through the two-lump model We will preserve both descriptions used in Part I. Matrix route: retain the TEC-side and measured-block temperatures as separate state variables. The eigenvalues of their coupled first-order matrix give the exponential time factors. Higher-order ODE route: eliminate the hidden TEC-side temperature. The measured temperature then obeys one second-order equation under P control. Its characteristic roots are the same eigenvalues. The matrix emphasizes interacting physical states. The higher-order equation emphasizes the measured output and makes damping formulas easier to recognize. From Two First-Order Equations To One Second-Order Equation ¶ Consider one heating or cooling direction so that \(P_u\) is constant, assume the PWM is not saturated, and use P control: \[ u=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_m). \] Let \(\theta_T\) and \(\theta_m\) be deviations of \(T\) and \(T_m\) from their steady-state values. The constant steady-state terms cancel, leaving \[ C_T\dot\theta_T=-G\theta_T+(G-P_uK_p)\theta_m, \] \[ C_m\dot\theta_m=G\theta_T-(G+H)\theta_m. \] Matrix Route: Two-Lump P Eigenvalues Keep both temperature displacements in the state vector, \[ \mathbf{x}= \begin{pmatrix}\theta_T\\\theta_m\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \dot{\mathbf{x}}=A_P\mathbf{x}, \] with \[ A_P= \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{G}{C_T} & \dfrac{G-P_uK_p}{C_T}\\[6pt] \dfrac{G}{C_m} & -\dfrac{G+H}{C_m} \end{pmatrix}. \] An exponential state mode has the form \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{v}e^{st}\) . A nonzero eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) exists only when \[ \det(sI-A_P)=0. \] Evaluating the determinant gives \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m s^2+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s+ G(H+P_uK_p)=0 }. \] This is precisely the characteristic polynomial obtained below by eliminating \(\theta_T\) . Real negative eigenvalues give sums of decaying exponentials. A complex-conjugate pair gives a real decaying oscillation: the real part sets the decay rate and the imaginary part sets the oscillation frequency. The second equation gives the hidden TEC-side temperature in terms of the measured temperature and its rate of change: \[ G\theta_T=C_m\dot\theta_m+(G+H)\theta_m. \] Differentiate the second equation, use the first equation to replace \(\dot\theta_T\) , and then use the expression above to replace \(\theta_T\) . The result is one second-order differential equation for the measured temperature: \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m\ddot\theta_m+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]\dot\theta_m+ G(H+P_uK_p)\theta_m=0. } \] Thus two coupled first-order equations for two stored-energy states are equivalent to one second-order equation for \(T_m\) . Substituting \(\theta_m\propto e^{st}\) gives \[ C_TC_m s^2+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s+ G(H+P_uK_p)=0. \] Divide by \(C_TC_m\) and compare with the standard second-order form \[ s^2+2\zeta\omega_n s+\omega_n^2=0. \] The two-lump P-control natural frequency and damping ratio are \[ \boxed{ \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{G(H+P_uK_p)}{C_TC_m}} }, \] \[ \boxed{ \zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}} =\frac{C_T(G+H)+C_mG} {2\sqrt{C_TC_mG(H+P_uK_p)}} }. \] This expression predicts the transition: \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}>1\) gives an overdamped response; \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}=1\) gives critical damping; and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}<1\) gives an underdamped response with overshoot or ringing. Because all coefficients in this second-order P-control equation are positive, the two-lump P model is stable for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. Its underdamped oscillations decay. Sustained oscillations that last forever or oscillations that grow are not predictions of this linear two-lump P model; observing either would falsify at least one of its assumptions or reveal omitted effects such as delay, saturation, or additional thermal states. For fixed physical parameters, increasing \(K_p\) increases the denominator and therefore decreases \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Sufficiently large P gain can move the two-lump model from overdamped to underdamped behavior. The critical gain is found by setting \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}=1\) : \[ \boxed{ K_{p,\mathrm{crit}} =\frac{1}{P_u} \left[ \frac{\left(C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right)^2} {4C_TC_mG}-H \right] }. \] The dependence on \(G\) is not monotonic. Very large \(G\) forces \(T\approx T_m\) and recovers one-lump behavior. Very small \(G\) nearly disconnects the measured mass from the TEC, producing a very slow response. For fixed \(C_T\) , \(C_m\) , and \(H\) , the damping ratio is smallest at \[ G=\frac{C_TH}{C_T+C_m}. \] Likewise, at fixed total capacitance \(C=C_T+C_m\) , putting almost all the capacitance in either lump suppresses the second-order behavior. The damping ratio is smallest when \[ \frac{C_T}{C}=\frac{G}{H+2G}, \] which is close to one-half when \(G\gg H\) . Thus a noticeable internal lag and two appreciable thermal stores promote ringing; neither phrase alone means that making \(G\) arbitrarily small always creates more oscillation. Complex eigenvalues produce an underdamped transient even though the apparatus contains no mechanical momentum. Thermal storage in two locations and delayed transport between them supply the two dynamical states. Stability Of Two-Lump PI Control ¶ PI control adds the integral state \[ q=\int e\,dt,\qquad \dot q=-\theta_m, \] and the command perturbation is \[ u=-K_p\theta_m+K_iq. \] Two-Lump PI: Three First-Order Equations Or One Third-Order Equation Let \(z=q-q_{\mathrm{ss}}\) and retain the three states \(\mathbf{x}=(\theta_T,\theta_m,z)^T\) . Their matrix equation is \[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}=A_{PI}\mathbf{x}, \qquad A_{PI}= \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{G}{C_T} & \dfrac{G-P_uK_p}{C_T} & \dfrac{P_uK_i}{C_T}\\[6pt] \dfrac{G}{C_m} & -\dfrac{G+H}{C_m} & 0\\[6pt] 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \] The matrix route uses \(\det(sI-A_{PI})=0\) to find three eigenvalues and three exponential factors \(e^{s_jt}\) . Alternatively, eliminate \(\theta_T\) and \(z\) . The measured-temperature displacement then obeys \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m\frac{d^3\theta_m}{dt^3} +\left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]\frac{d^2\theta_m}{dt^2} +G(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta_m}{dt} +GP_uK_i\theta_m=0 }. \] Substituting \(\theta_m\propto e^{st}\) gives the same cubic as the matrix determinant. The two descriptions therefore agree mode by mode. A real eigenvalue contributes a purely growing or decaying exponential; a complex-conjugate pair contributes an oscillation whose envelope grows or decays according to the sign of the pair's real part. Substitution into the two-lump equations gives the characteristic equation \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m s^3+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s^2+ G(H+P_uK_p)s+ GP_uK_i=0. } \] This equation is third order, so the complete response does not have one second-order damping ratio \(\zeta\) . It commonly has one real eigenvalue and a complex-conjugate pair; that pair produces the observed ringing. Write the cubic as \(a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0\) . All four coefficients above are positive. The Routh-Hurwitz stability condition therefore reduces to \[ a_2a_1>a_3a_0. \] The significance of the Routh-Hurwitz criterion is that it determines stability from the polynomial coefficients without explicitly calculating all three eigenvalues. For the convention used here, each free mode varies as \(e^{st}\) , so asymptotic stability requires every eigenvalue \(s\) to have a negative real part , not to be positive. The Routh-Hurwitz conditions are necessary and sufficient for that result. Solving the equality for the integral gain gives the stability boundary \[ \boxed{ K_{i,\mathrm{crit}} =\frac{\left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right](H+P_uK_p)} {C_TC_mP_u}. } \] A useful dimensionless measure of integral aggressiveness is \[ \boxed{\rho_I=\frac{K_i}{K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}}.} \] As \(\rho_I\) approaches 1 from below, the oscillatory pair becomes less damped. At \(\rho_I=1\) , the normalized polynomial factors as \((s+a)(s^2+b)\) : one eigenvalue remains negative while the other two are purely imaginary. The linear model then predicts sustained oscillation. For \(\rho_I>1\) , it predicts growing oscillation and instability. The qualitative classification is therefore: \(0<\rho_I<1\) : stable ; any oscillations decay; \(\rho_I=1\) : marginally stable ; ideal constant-amplitude oscillations persist forever; and \(\rho_I>1\) : unstable ; oscillations grow. This distinction is useful for model falsification. A stable underdamped trace may overshoot many times, but its envelope must shrink. A trace with constant amplitude lies on the predicted stability boundary, while a growing envelope lies beyond it. If the measured classification disagrees with the model's classification for the measured parameters, the model or one of its assumed parameter values is inadequate. The prediction of exponential growth applies only while the controller and plant remain linear. The apparatus cannot apply an arbitrarily large command: the H-bridge limits the signed command to \(-255\leq u\leq+255\) PWM. Once the requested command reaches either limit, the applied command is clipped and the linear characteristic equation no longer describes the complete response. Instead of growing forever, the simulated or physical temperature may approach a bounded nonlinear oscillation. This does not make the underlying linear model stable; it shows that actuator saturation has limited the instability. These results give practical rules of thumb: Change Expected effect Interpretation Increase \(K_i\) Increases \(\rho_I\) and promotes oscillation Integral action removes droop, but too much increases settling time or causes instability. Increase \(K_p\) at fixed \(K_i\) Raises \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) P action can improve the PI stability margin, although excessive \(K_p\) can already excite two-lump P overshoot. Decrease \(G\) over the apparatus-relevant range Increases internal lag and usually reduces PI stability margin The integral continues accumulating while \(T_m\) responds slowly. Extremely small or large \(G\) requires direct evaluation rather than this slogan. Make both \(C_T\) and \(C_m\) appreciable Strengthens two-state behavior Concentrating nearly all capacitance in one lump moves the system toward one-lump behavior. Increase total \(C\) without retuning gains Slows the plant and generally makes the same \(K_i\) more aggressive More error can accumulate before the measured temperature responds. Increase \(P_u\) Makes each PWM unit more effective The same numerical \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) produce stronger physical feedback. Saturate PWM with anti-windup off Produces integral windup The resulting overshoot is nonlinear controller memory, not solely the linear two-lump instability. The objective is not the shortest rise time at any cost. A large gain may reach the setpoint quickly on the first crossing but then overshoot and take longer to settle. A useful tuning procedure is: choose \(K_p\) for a fast P response without unacceptable overshoot; choose a slightly smaller \(K_p\) when adding integral action; increase \(K_i\) from zero until droop is removed on the desired timescale; stop increasing \(K_i\) when extra oscillation makes the settling time worse; verify both heating and cooling steps without sustained saturation. At steady state, both temperature derivatives are zero, so \[ P_u u=G(T-T_m)=H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] The internal conductance \(G\) sets the temperature difference between the two lumps, but it cancels from the overall balance \(P_u u=H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\) . This is the quantitative reason the one-lump model can predict the final measured temperature and P-control droop even when it fails to predict the high-gain transient. Controller Choices ¶ The measured temperature is \(T\) for the one-lump model and \(T_m\) for the two-lump model. Define \[ e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{meas}}. \] The three controller choices are \[ u=u_{\mathrm{user}}\quad\text{(open loop)}, \] \[ u=K_pe\quad\text{(P control)}, \] \[ u=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dt=u_P+u_I\quad\text{(PI control)}. \] The signed command is clamped to the PWM limit. If the anti-windup option is enabled, the program prevents the integral state from continuing to grow when the actuator is saturated in the same direction as the error. What The Algorithm Does At Each Time Step ¶ The simulation described in How To Run The Python GUI performs the numerical work, but you should understand its sequence: Read the model's measured temperature, \(T_n\) or \(T_{m,n}\) . Calculate the error \(e_n\) . For PI control, propose the integral update \(q_{n+1}=q_n+e_n\Delta t\) . Accept it unless anti-windup prevents the update; otherwise use \(q_{n+1}=q_n\) . Calculate the requested command for the selected controller: \(u_n=u_{\mathrm{user}}\) for open-loop control, \(u_n=K_pe_n\) for P control, or \(u_n=K_pe_n+K_iq_{n+1}\) for PI control. Clamp \(u_n\) to the signed PWM limit. Select \(P_{u,h}\) or \(P_{u,c}\) from the sign of the applied command. Evaluate the heat-balance derivatives and advance \(T\) and, for the two-lump model, \(T_m\) by one Euler step. For example, the first two-lump Euler updates are \[ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{C_T} \left[P_u(u_n)u_n-G(T_n-T_{m,n})\right], \] \[ T_{m,n+1}=T_{m,n}+\frac{\Delta t}{C_m} \left[G(T_n-T_{m,n})-H(T_{m,n}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\right]. \] You are not required to write this code. Looking Ahead: From Lumps To A Temperature Field The two-lump model is a crude spatial approximation. It replaces an extended apparatus with two internally uniform regions connected by a thermal conductance. It distinguishes a region near the TEC from a region near the thermistor, but it contains no continuous distance, temperature gradient, or spatial coordinate. The long-rod experiment cannot be described by a single temperature. It needs a temperature field that depends on longitudinal position and time: \[ T = T(x,t) \] For the rod we will move toward equations of the form \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} \] with an additional term that represents heat loss from the sides to the room: \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} - \beta\left(T - T_{\mathrm{room}}\right) \] In these equations, alpha is the thermal diffusivity in m²/s and beta is a side-loss rate constant in 1/s. You do not need to solve these equations or submit written answers about them in Module 6. They are included to show where the lumped-model sequence leads. Their purpose is to teach how the physical parameters set the stability margin and how the controller gains trade rapid approach against overshoot and settling time. Make The Eight Two-Lump Goldilocks Plots ¶ This exercise tests whether the model can reproduce the eight experimental Goldilocks conditions without asking you to search the entire parameter space. The apparatus did not change between runs, so all eight simulations must use one shared set of physical parameters . Only the controller gains \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) change. The simulated gains need not equal the experimental gains: the comparison asks whether tuning the controller alone can reproduce the same qualitative sequence while the physical model remains fixed. Use the two-lump PI stability criterion to predict and interpret the PI runs in terms of \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) . Step 1: Enter the measured quantities. Select two_lump and enter your measured \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) , \(\chi_c\) , \(\chi_h\) , and \(\tau\) . Use the same setpoints, initial temperatures, PWM limit, TEC voltage, and TEC resistance as the eight experiments. Begin with \(G=2\ \mathrm{W/K}\) and \(C_T/C=0.35\) . These are starting estimates for the unresolved internal structure, not additional measurements. Step 2: Calibrate the shared internal parameters once, then lock them. This is a one-time model-calibration step, not part of the controller-gain sweep. Select P control, set \(K_i=0\) , and enter the \(K_p\) from the experimental underdamped P run (Run 3) , whose oscillations decay. Do not use the sustained-oscillation Run 4, because the linear two-lump P model cannot reproduce that behavior. Compare the simulated and measured overshoot and oscillation decay. Read the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . A value above 1 predicts a monotonic response; a value below 1 predicts overshoot or ringing. Change only \(G\) and watch the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Move \(G\) in the direction that makes the simulated damping more like the underdamped experimental trace. If changing \(G\) is insufficient, restore the best \(G\) and vary \(C_T/C\) . Again, use the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) to choose the direction rather than guessing. Stop when the underdamped P simulation reproduces the qualitative behavior: monotonic, one overshoot, or repeated decaying oscillations. Exact fitting is not required. Record this one choice of \(G\) and \(C_T/C\) , then do not change either value again during any of the eight Goldilocks simulations. Step 3: Sweep \(K_p\) , then make the four P plots. Lock every physical parameter, keep \(K_i=0\) , and move only the \(K_p\) slider. Begin at low \(K_p\) and increase it until the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) passes from above 1 to below 1. Observe the corresponding transition from monotonic response to overshoot or ringing. This sweep is for understanding; it need not be saved. Now choose four increasing simulation values of \(K_p\) corresponding to the experimental labels small , critical , underdamped , and oscillatory . These gain values need not equal the experimental values. Use \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\approx1\) to locate the critical case and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}<1\) to locate an underdamped case. For the fourth case, continue increasing \(K_p\) and test whether the ideal two-lump P model ever produces sustained oscillations. It should not: its ringing must decay for every positive set of physical parameters. Preserve the highest-gain decaying response as the model's attempted oscillatory case. This failure to reproduce the sustained experimental trace is evidence against the model, not a reason to change the physical parameters. Plot only \(T_m\) if the TEC-side temperature obscures the measured response. Each retained plot caption must give \(K_p\) and the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Also run the one-lump P model at four increasing \(K_p\) values. Its four responses should remain monotonic, showing that it cannot reproduce either underdamped or sustained oscillation. Step 4: Sweep \(K_i\) , then make the four PI plots. First use a parameter set chosen to make the stability transition easy to see. Select direct constants , two_lump , and PI control, then enter: \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}=T_0=29\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{set}}=30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , preserving a small \(1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) step that avoids saturation; \(C=100\ \mathrm{J/K}\) and \(C_T/C=0.50\) , so the two thermal stores are equal and neither state disappears into a one-lump approximation; \(G=2.0\ \mathrm{W/K}\) , which is small enough to create visible internal lag without nearly disconnecting the measured mass; \(H=1.14\ \mathrm{W/K}\) , \(P_{u,c}=0.26\ \mathrm{W/PWM}\) , and \(r=2.0\) ; \(K_p=10\ \mathrm{PWM}/^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , which is large enough to respond but not so large that P action dominates the stability demonstration; PWM limit \(255\) and \(\Delta t=0.05\ \mathrm{s}\) . The equal capacitance split makes both dynamical states important. The appreciable total capacitance stores enough thermal energy to create a visible transient, the modest \(G\) creates phase lag, and the \(1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) step avoids saturation. With these values, the display should give approximately \[ K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\approx 1.25\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s}). \] Fix every setting except \(K_i\) . Try \(K_i=0.10\) , \(0.60\) , \(1.10\) , \(1.25\) , and \(1.40\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s})\) . The corresponding \(\rho_I\) values are approximately \(0.08\) , \(0.48\) , \(0.88\) , \(1.00\) , and \(1.12\) . Move the slider between these checkpoints and observe the continuous transition. The displayed \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) remains fixed because the plant and \(K_p\) are fixed, while \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) increases. For two-lump PI control, the simulation automatically extends the \(K_i\) slider beyond the calculated \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , even when a large \(K_p\) makes that boundary greater than 5. Observe the response in four regions: \(\rho_I\ll1\) : the system is stable and oscillations decay; \(\rho_I\) just below 1: the system is stable and underdamped, but oscillations decay slowly and settling takes a long time; \(\rho_I=1\) : the ideal model is marginally stable and oscillations persist forever at constant amplitude; and \(\rho_I>1\) : oscillations grow and the linear model is unstable. This is a simulation, so you may briefly cross the instability boundary. Pause and reset once the growing oscillation is clear. Keep anti-windup on and use a small enough setpoint step that the PWM does not saturate; otherwise you are testing windup and saturation rather than the linear stability criterion. Optional extension: observe growth followed by actuator saturation. After the required plots are complete, deliberately leave the linear regime. Keep the Step 4 physical parameters, \(K_p=10\) , the \(30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) setpoint, the \(\pm255\) PWM limit, and anti-windup on. Set \(K_i=3.0\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s})\) , select mass temperature only , use a rolling window of at least \(600\) s, and reset the simulation. Run for about \(700\) simulated seconds. You should see several growing temperature oscillations before the requested command reaches the PWM limit. The applied PWM then clips at \(+255\) or \(-255\) , and the temperature oscillation approaches a bounded amplitude rather than continuing to grow exponentially. Compare the command and temperature plots. Identify (1) the early interval in which the oscillation envelope grows, (2) the first time the applied PWM reaches a limit, and (3) the later bounded oscillation. Explain why the first interval is evidence of linear instability, while the later behavior is controlled by the nonlinear actuator limit. This is an exploration; do not add another plot to A3. After locating the transition, restore the one shared physical parameter set from Steps 1-3. Choose one PI value of \(K_p\) , hold it fixed, and vary only \(K_i\) to make small , critical , underdamped , and oscillatory PI responses. The simulated \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) values need not equal the experimental values. For each one: read the displayed \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) ; predict whether the oscillation should decay rapidly, decay slowly, or grow; reset the integral, keep anti-windup on, and run the simulation; and put \(K_p\) , \(K_i\) , \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , and \(\rho_I\) in the plot caption. The retained PI runs should progress from lower to higher \(\rho_I\) while all physical parameters and the chosen PI value of \(K_p\) remain fixed. Use the simulation response to locate the operational transition from monotonic to overshooting behavior for the critical case, a decaying oscillation for the underdamped case, and \(\rho_I\approx1\) for the sustained, marginally stable oscillatory case. Do not confuse the critical Goldilocks response with \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) . The Goldilocks label marks the damping transition from monotonic response to overshoot. In contrast, \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) is the stability boundary: at that larger value, the ideal two-lump PI model is marginally stable and sustains oscillation. Step 5: Preserve the eight plots. Use the same time range, temperature range, and labeling scheme as the eight experimental plots. Every plot must show the setpoint, measured mass temperature, and signed applied PWM. Before the plots, state the one shared physical parameter set in a sentence. Do not make a parameter table. After the plots, answer these four comparison prompts: Which P and PI simulation best reproduce the corresponding experimental rise time, overshoot, and settling behavior? How do decreasing \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) and the location of each gain relative to \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) organize the four P responses? How does increasing \(\rho_I\) organize the four PI responses? State one important agreement and one important disagreement between the eight simulations and eight experiments, then justify the P and PI gains that give the best compromise between speed and settling. In doing so, classify each response as stable non-oscillatory, stable underdamped, marginally stable, or unstable, and identify any observed behavior that falsifies the selected model. Optional windup demonstration: after preserving the eight plots, turn anti-windup off, reduce \(G\) , choose PI control, and apply a setpoint step large enough to saturate the PWM command. The measured temperature responds slowly, so the persistent error continues increasing the integral contribution even while the applied command is clamped. This extra overshoot is caused by stored controller error, not solely by the two-lump damping ratio. Turn anti-windup back on and press Zero integral before continuing. Use the sixteen Goldilocks plots, their captions, and the four comparison answers directly in A3 Questions 3 and 5. Explain why one-lump P control cannot oscillate and identify the heat flow that makes \(T_m\) lag behind \(T\) . Do not write a separate Part II report. Post-Class Assignment ¶ Preserve The A3 Evidence ¶ Before leaving S15, save the shared model settings, every completed simulation run, captions in progress, the exact run command, and links to the experimental data. After class, finish any remaining retained plots and the four comparison answers, then preserve the prepared simulation and completed A3 working materials in your repository. This is preparation for A3, not a separate submission. Oral Review Questions: Process Modeling ¶ Use this modeling question bank to check your understanding and prepare A3: Which physical lag in the apparatus can produce overshoot or oscillation as gain increases? Identify one model parameter, give its units, and explain its physical effect on the simulated response. Also prepare the Module 5 P-control questions and Module 6 PI-control question . Instructor Notes ¶ This module is a consolidation point after manual control and P/PI control. Keep the emphasis on physical interpretation, not formal control theory. Students should leave understanding why delay plus gain causes trouble. The long-rod model should be introduced as a preview, not fully derived here unless the class is ready.

docs.text: This is the second part of Module 6. Complete Part I: P/PI Control And Lumped Modeling first. Both parts use the same prepared simulation : Part I emphasizes the one-lump model, while Part II compares the one- and two-lump models.
docs.title: Module 6, Part II: TEC Process Model And The Simulation

docs.text: This part follows the first Module 6 modeling work and the initial physical PI implementation. Before beginning Part II, complete the physical \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) study and generate the eight experimental plots required by Module 6, Part I, A3 Question 2 . Part II connects three things: the physical TEC/block/thermistor system, the feedback-control equations, a Python simulation GUI that lets you change model parameters and watch the predicted temperature response. This module is not about perfect quantitative prediction. It is about learning how a simple model can qualitatively and quantitatively explain droop, overshoot, lag, damping, and the transition from stable to unstable control. Throughout Part II, use two parallel mathematical descriptions of the same dynamics. The coupled first-order energy balances form a state-space matrix whose eigenvalues determine the exponential modes. Eliminating the hidden states produces one higher-order differential equation whose characteristic polynomial has the same roots. Moving between these descriptions is a central reason for studying the two-lump model.

docs.text: By the end of Module 6, Part II, you should be able to: write and interpret the coupled energy balances for the TEC-side and measured-block thermal masses; show how two coupled first-order temperature equations produce one second-order equation for the measured temperature; use the two-lump model to explain how thermal storage and transport produce phase lag, overshoot, and behavior absent from the one-lump P model; calculate \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) and \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) and use them to classify two-lump P responses as over-, critically, or underdamped; calculate \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to predict stable, marginal, or unstable two-lump PI behavior; predict and verify how \(K_p\) , \(K_i\) , \(G\) , total capacitance, and capacitance division affect response speed, damping, and stability; hold all physical model parameters fixed while varying only \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) , so changes caused by controller tuning can be distinguished from changes to the modeled apparatus; characterize matched physical P and PI responses using rise time, overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, and oscillation period; generate eight simulation Goldilocks plots using one shared set of physical parameters and compare them with the eight experimental Goldilocks plots; test whether one- and two-lump P models can reproduce small, critical, underdamped, and sustained-oscillation behavior, and use a failure to reproduce sustained oscillation as evidence that a model is incomplete; and select and justify \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) by balancing rapid approach to the setpoint against overshoot, settling time, actuator limits, and stability while connecting theory, simulation, and measurement. The eight measured and eight simulated Goldilocks plots are the principal way you achieve these objectives. They are assessed together with the two-lump derivation in A3 Questions 3 and 5. The parallel matrix/eigenvalue and higher-order differential-equation routes are included for mathematical culture and interpretation. Follow how they produce the same characteristic polynomial, but do not prepare a separate A3 derivation of the matrix formalism.
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: Use Models To Explain Measurements In control theory, the process is the physical cause-and-effect system that turns the controller output into a measured response. Here, the PWM command changes the heat transported by the TEC; thermal capacitances store energy; thermal conductances move heat through the aluminum block and to the room; and the thermistor measures the resulting temperature. This chain from PWM command to measured temperature is the process we are modeling.

During class on October 19, the approximate schedule for one 170-minute meeting is: 0-15 min : Inspect the completed P/PI plots and state what the one-lump model explains and fails to explain. 15-35 min : Review the one-lump energy balance with Lienhard Problem 1.8. 35-75 min : Develop the coupled two-lump balances and reduce them to a second-order equation for the measured temperature. 75-120 min : Compare one- and two-lump responses and connect thermal lag to the experimental plots. 120-155 min : Vary one parameter at a time and interpret the results using the equations. 155-170 min : Wrap up: what the model explains, what it leaves out, and why the long-rod experiment will require a spatial model. docs.title: When To Do The Work

docs.text: Process : the physical system being controlled. Here, the process is the TEC/block/thermistor thermal system. State variable : a number that describes the current state of the model, such as temperature. Heat : energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Heat is not the same thing as temperature; temperature tells how hot something is, while heat is energy moving into or out of the system. Lumped model : a model that treats an extended object as if the entire object were at the same temperature. The lump can be viewed as a point object of finite thermal mass. See the one-lump/two-lump figure . Thermal lag : delay between changing the actuator and observing the measured temperature response. Saturation : the actuator command reaches its limit, such as PWM 255. This could be a physical or software imposed limit. Stable : the response returns to steady state after a disturbance. Underdamped : a stable response with oscillations that decrease in amplitude. Marginally stable : an idealized response with constant-amplitude oscillations that continue forever. Unstable : a response that moves farther from steady state; oscillations grow rather than decay when the instability is oscillatory.

docs.title: Symbol Glossary

docs.text: The Python GUI separates the physical model from the controller. Select either a one-lump or two-lump process, then select open-loop, P, or PI control. Course-specific lumped-model diagram. The one-lump model assigns one temperature to the TEC, block, and thermistor assembly. It retains heat storage and heat loss to the room, but it cannot represent an internal temperature difference or delay. The two-lump model separates the TEC-side temperature \(T\) from the measured temperature \(T_m\) . Heat first crosses the internal conductance \(G\) and then leaves the measured lump through the room conductance \(H\) . Because the controller responds to \(T_m\) , this extra thermal store and transport step introduce lag that can produce overshoot and underdamped behavior.
docs.title: Model Equations And Numerical Algorithm

docs.text: Part I developed the one-lump energy balance and its measured-parameter form . Carry those results forward rather than deriving them again. For comparison with the two-lump model, the one-lump capacitance is the sum \[ C=C_T+C_m, \] and the simulation continues to use \(P_{u,h}\) for heating and \(P_{u,c}\) for cooling, with \[ r=\frac{P_{u,h}}{P_{u,c}}=\frac{\chi_h}{\chi_c}. \]
docs.title: One-Lump Physical Model

docs.text: The two-lump model separates the TEC-side temperature \(T\) from the measured temperature \(T_m\) : \[ C_T\frac{dT}{dt}=P_u(u)u-G(T-T_m), \] \[ C_m\frac{dT_m}{dt}=G(T-T_m)-H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] Here \(C_T\) and \(C_m\) are thermal capacitances. The conductance \(G\) couples the two lumps through the passive heat flow \(G(T-T_m)\) . The same heat that leaves the TEC-side lump enters the measured lump, so this term appears with opposite signs in the two equations. We simplify the apparatus by giving the TEC-side lump no separate path to the room; all heat loss to the room is represented by \(H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\) in the measured-lump equation. The controller responds to \(T_m\) , but \(T\) and \(T_m\) do not change at the same time. Which temperature changes first if someone opens a window and \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) suddenly decreases? Which changes first if \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) changes? This lag can produce overshoot or oscillation. Two routes through the two-lump model We will preserve both descriptions used in Part I. Matrix route: retain the TEC-side and measured-block temperatures as separate state variables. The eigenvalues of their coupled first-order matrix give the exponential time factors. Higher-order ODE route: eliminate the hidden TEC-side temperature. The measured temperature then obeys one second-order equation under P control. Its characteristic roots are the same eigenvalues. The matrix emphasizes interacting physical states. The higher-order equation emphasizes the measured output and makes damping formulas easier to recognize.
docs.title: Two-Lump Physical Model

docs.text: Consider one heating or cooling direction so that \(P_u\) is constant, assume the PWM is not saturated, and use P control: \[ u=K_p(T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_m). \] Let \(\theta_T\) and \(\theta_m\) be deviations of \(T\) and \(T_m\) from their steady-state values. The constant steady-state terms cancel, leaving \[ C_T\dot\theta_T=-G\theta_T+(G-P_uK_p)\theta_m, \] \[ C_m\dot\theta_m=G\theta_T-(G+H)\theta_m. \] Matrix Route: Two-Lump P Eigenvalues Keep both temperature displacements in the state vector, \[ \mathbf{x}= \begin{pmatrix}\theta_T\\\theta_m\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \dot{\mathbf{x}}=A_P\mathbf{x}, \] with \[ A_P= \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{G}{C_T} & \dfrac{G-P_uK_p}{C_T}\\[6pt] \dfrac{G}{C_m} & -\dfrac{G+H}{C_m} \end{pmatrix}. \] An exponential state mode has the form \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{v}e^{st}\) . A nonzero eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) exists only when \[ \det(sI-A_P)=0. \] Evaluating the determinant gives \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m s^2+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s+ G(H+P_uK_p)=0 }. \] This is precisely the characteristic polynomial obtained below by eliminating \(\theta_T\) . Real negative eigenvalues give sums of decaying exponentials. A complex-conjugate pair gives a real decaying oscillation: the real part sets the decay rate and the imaginary part sets the oscillation frequency. The second equation gives the hidden TEC-side temperature in terms of the measured temperature and its rate of change: \[ G\theta_T=C_m\dot\theta_m+(G+H)\theta_m. \] Differentiate the second equation, use the first equation to replace \(\dot\theta_T\) , and then use the expression above to replace \(\theta_T\) . The result is one second-order differential equation for the measured temperature: \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m\ddot\theta_m+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]\dot\theta_m+ G(H+P_uK_p)\theta_m=0. } \] Thus two coupled first-order equations for two stored-energy states are equivalent to one second-order equation for \(T_m\) . Substituting \(\theta_m\propto e^{st}\) gives \[ C_TC_m s^2+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s+ G(H+P_uK_p)=0. \] Divide by \(C_TC_m\) and compare with the standard second-order form \[ s^2+2\zeta\omega_n s+\omega_n^2=0. \] The two-lump P-control natural frequency and damping ratio are \[ \boxed{ \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{G(H+P_uK_p)}{C_TC_m}} }, \] \[ \boxed{ \zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}} =\frac{C_T(G+H)+C_mG} {2\sqrt{C_TC_mG(H+P_uK_p)}} }. \] This expression predicts the transition: \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}>1\) gives an overdamped response; \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}=1\) gives critical damping; and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}<1\) gives an underdamped response with overshoot or ringing. Because all coefficients in this second-order P-control equation are positive, the two-lump P model is stable for positive physical parameters and negative feedback. Its underdamped oscillations decay. Sustained oscillations that last forever or oscillations that grow are not predictions of this linear two-lump P model; observing either would falsify at least one of its assumptions or reveal omitted effects such as delay, saturation, or additional thermal states. For fixed physical parameters, increasing \(K_p\) increases the denominator and therefore decreases \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Sufficiently large P gain can move the two-lump model from overdamped to underdamped behavior. The critical gain is found by setting \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}=1\) : \[ \boxed{ K_{p,\mathrm{crit}} =\frac{1}{P_u} \left[ \frac{\left(C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right)^2} {4C_TC_mG}-H \right] }. \] The dependence on \(G\) is not monotonic. Very large \(G\) forces \(T\approx T_m\) and recovers one-lump behavior. Very small \(G\) nearly disconnects the measured mass from the TEC, producing a very slow response. For fixed \(C_T\) , \(C_m\) , and \(H\) , the damping ratio is smallest at \[ G=\frac{C_TH}{C_T+C_m}. \] Likewise, at fixed total capacitance \(C=C_T+C_m\) , putting almost all the capacitance in either lump suppresses the second-order behavior. The damping ratio is smallest when \[ \frac{C_T}{C}=\frac{G}{H+2G}, \] which is close to one-half when \(G\gg H\) . Thus a noticeable internal lag and two appreciable thermal stores promote ringing; neither phrase alone means that making \(G\) arbitrarily small always creates more oscillation. Complex eigenvalues produce an underdamped transient even though the apparatus contains no mechanical momentum. Thermal storage in two locations and delayed transport between them supply the two dynamical states.
docs.title: From Two First-Order Equations To One Second-Order Equation

docs.text: PI control adds the integral state \[ q=\int e\,dt,\qquad \dot q=-\theta_m, \] and the command perturbation is \[ u=-K_p\theta_m+K_iq. \] Two-Lump PI: Three First-Order Equations Or One Third-Order Equation Let \(z=q-q_{\mathrm{ss}}\) and retain the three states \(\mathbf{x}=(\theta_T,\theta_m,z)^T\) . Their matrix equation is \[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}=A_{PI}\mathbf{x}, \qquad A_{PI}= \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{G}{C_T} & \dfrac{G-P_uK_p}{C_T} & \dfrac{P_uK_i}{C_T}\\[6pt] \dfrac{G}{C_m} & -\dfrac{G+H}{C_m} & 0\\[6pt] 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \] The matrix route uses \(\det(sI-A_{PI})=0\) to find three eigenvalues and three exponential factors \(e^{s_jt}\) . Alternatively, eliminate \(\theta_T\) and \(z\) . The measured-temperature displacement then obeys \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m\frac{d^3\theta_m}{dt^3} +\left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]\frac{d^2\theta_m}{dt^2} +G(H+P_uK_p)\frac{d\theta_m}{dt} +GP_uK_i\theta_m=0 }. \] Substituting \(\theta_m\propto e^{st}\) gives the same cubic as the matrix determinant. The two descriptions therefore agree mode by mode. A real eigenvalue contributes a purely growing or decaying exponential; a complex-conjugate pair contributes an oscillation whose envelope grows or decays according to the sign of the pair's real part. Substitution into the two-lump equations gives the characteristic equation \[ \boxed{ C_TC_m s^3+ \left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right]s^2+ G(H+P_uK_p)s+ GP_uK_i=0. } \] This equation is third order, so the complete response does not have one second-order damping ratio \(\zeta\) . It commonly has one real eigenvalue and a complex-conjugate pair; that pair produces the observed ringing. Write the cubic as \(a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0\) . All four coefficients above are positive. The Routh-Hurwitz stability condition therefore reduces to \[ a_2a_1>a_3a_0. \] The significance of the Routh-Hurwitz criterion is that it determines stability from the polynomial coefficients without explicitly calculating all three eigenvalues. For the convention used here, each free mode varies as \(e^{st}\) , so asymptotic stability requires every eigenvalue \(s\) to have a negative real part , not to be positive. The Routh-Hurwitz conditions are necessary and sufficient for that result. Solving the equality for the integral gain gives the stability boundary \[ \boxed{ K_{i,\mathrm{crit}} =\frac{\left[C_T(G+H)+C_mG\right](H+P_uK_p)} {C_TC_mP_u}. } \] A useful dimensionless measure of integral aggressiveness is \[ \boxed{\rho_I=\frac{K_i}{K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}}.} \] As \(\rho_I\) approaches 1 from below, the oscillatory pair becomes less damped. At \(\rho_I=1\) , the normalized polynomial factors as \((s+a)(s^2+b)\) : one eigenvalue remains negative while the other two are purely imaginary. The linear model then predicts sustained oscillation. For \(\rho_I>1\) , it predicts growing oscillation and instability. The qualitative classification is therefore: \(0<\rho_I<1\) : stable ; any oscillations decay; \(\rho_I=1\) : marginally stable ; ideal constant-amplitude oscillations persist forever; and \(\rho_I>1\) : unstable ; oscillations grow. This distinction is useful for model falsification. A stable underdamped trace may overshoot many times, but its envelope must shrink. A trace with constant amplitude lies on the predicted stability boundary, while a growing envelope lies beyond it. If the measured classification disagrees with the model's classification for the measured parameters, the model or one of its assumed parameter values is inadequate. The prediction of exponential growth applies only while the controller and plant remain linear. The apparatus cannot apply an arbitrarily large command: the H-bridge limits the signed command to \(-255\leq u\leq+255\) PWM. Once the requested command reaches either limit, the applied command is clipped and the linear characteristic equation no longer describes the complete response. Instead of growing forever, the simulated or physical temperature may approach a bounded nonlinear oscillation. This does not make the underlying linear model stable; it shows that actuator saturation has limited the instability. These results give practical rules of thumb: Change Expected effect Interpretation Increase \(K_i\) Increases \(\rho_I\) and promotes oscillation Integral action removes droop, but too much increases settling time or causes instability. Increase \(K_p\) at fixed \(K_i\) Raises \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) P action can improve the PI stability margin, although excessive \(K_p\) can already excite two-lump P overshoot. Decrease \(G\) over the apparatus-relevant range Increases internal lag and usually reduces PI stability margin The integral continues accumulating while \(T_m\) responds slowly. Extremely small or large \(G\) requires direct evaluation rather than this slogan. Make both \(C_T\) and \(C_m\) appreciable Strengthens two-state behavior Concentrating nearly all capacitance in one lump moves the system toward one-lump behavior. Increase total \(C\) without retuning gains Slows the plant and generally makes the same \(K_i\) more aggressive More error can accumulate before the measured temperature responds. Increase \(P_u\) Makes each PWM unit more effective The same numerical \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) produce stronger physical feedback. Saturate PWM with anti-windup off Produces integral windup The resulting overshoot is nonlinear controller memory, not solely the linear two-lump instability. The objective is not the shortest rise time at any cost. A large gain may reach the setpoint quickly on the first crossing but then overshoot and take longer to settle. A useful tuning procedure is: choose \(K_p\) for a fast P response without unacceptable overshoot; choose a slightly smaller \(K_p\) when adding integral action; increase \(K_i\) from zero until droop is removed on the desired timescale; stop increasing \(K_i\) when extra oscillation makes the settling time worse; verify both heating and cooling steps without sustained saturation. At steady state, both temperature derivatives are zero, so \[ P_u u=G(T-T_m)=H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \] The internal conductance \(G\) sets the temperature difference between the two lumps, but it cancels from the overall balance \(P_u u=H(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\) . This is the quantitative reason the one-lump model can predict the final measured temperature and P-control droop even when it fails to predict the high-gain transient.
docs.title: Stability Of Two-Lump PI Control

docs.text: The measured temperature is \(T\) for the one-lump model and \(T_m\) for the two-lump model. Define \[ e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{meas}}. \] The three controller choices are \[ u=u_{\mathrm{user}}\quad\text{(open loop)}, \] \[ u=K_pe\quad\text{(P control)}, \] \[ u=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dt=u_P+u_I\quad\text{(PI control)}. \] The signed command is clamped to the PWM limit. If the anti-windup option is enabled, the program prevents the integral state from continuing to grow when the actuator is saturated in the same direction as the error.
docs.title: Controller Choices

docs.text: The simulation described in How To Run The Python GUI performs the numerical work, but you should understand its sequence: Read the model's measured temperature, \(T_n\) or \(T_{m,n}\) . Calculate the error \(e_n\) . For PI control, propose the integral update \(q_{n+1}=q_n+e_n\Delta t\) . Accept it unless anti-windup prevents the update; otherwise use \(q_{n+1}=q_n\) . Calculate the requested command for the selected controller: \(u_n=u_{\mathrm{user}}\) for open-loop control, \(u_n=K_pe_n\) for P control, or \(u_n=K_pe_n+K_iq_{n+1}\) for PI control. Clamp \(u_n\) to the signed PWM limit. Select \(P_{u,h}\) or \(P_{u,c}\) from the sign of the applied command. Evaluate the heat-balance derivatives and advance \(T\) and, for the two-lump model, \(T_m\) by one Euler step. For example, the first two-lump Euler updates are \[ T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{\Delta t}{C_T} \left[P_u(u_n)u_n-G(T_n-T_{m,n})\right], \] \[ T_{m,n+1}=T_{m,n}+\frac{\Delta t}{C_m} \left[G(T_n-T_{m,n})-H(T_{m,n}-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\right]. \] You are not required to write this code. Use it to develop physical intuition: vary one model, parameter, or initial condition at a time; predict the result; observe the response; and interpret it using the heat balances and controller equations.

docs.text: This part of the course uses lumped thermal models . A lumped model assumes that one object, such as the TEC/block assembly, can be described by one temperature. This is an approximation. It is useful before we move to the long rod, where temperature depends on position.
docs.title: Thermal Transport Theory Assignments

docs.text: In Module 6, Part I , you derived the one-lump energy balance, expressed it using the measured \(\chi\) and \(\tau\) , and found its steady-state temperature. Use those results here; do not repeat that assignment.
docs.title: One-Lump Results Carried Forward From Part I

docs.text: Use the two-lump equations and their definitions above to answer these required pre-class questions: Identify which term transfers heat from the TEC side to the measured thermistor/block side. Identify which term describes heat loss from the measured block to room air. Explain why Tm can lag behind T . Explain why a controller that uses Tm may react too late. Divide the measured-lump equation by \(C_m\) and compare it term by term with the rate-constant form \(dT_m/dt=k_{21}(T-T_m)-k_m(T_m-T_{\mathrm{amb}})\) . Identify \(k_{21}=G/C_m\) and \(k_m=H/C_m\) , give their units, and explain how increasing each one changes the equilibration between the lumps or the relaxation toward room temperature. Looking Ahead: From Lumps To A Temperature Field The two-lump model is a crude spatial approximation. It replaces an extended apparatus with two internally uniform regions connected by a thermal conductance. It distinguishes a region near the TEC from a region near the thermistor, but it contains no continuous distance, temperature gradient, or spatial coordinate. The long-rod experiment cannot be described by a single temperature. It needs a temperature field that depends on longitudinal position and time: \[ T = T(x,t) \] For the rod we will move toward equations of the form \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} \] with an additional term that represents heat loss from the sides to the room: \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} - \beta\left(T - T_{\mathrm{room}}\right) \] In these equations, alpha is the thermal diffusivity in m²/s and beta is a side-loss rate constant in 1/s. You do not need to solve these equations or submit written answers about them in Module 6. They are included to show where the lumped-model sequence leads.

The corresponding damping ratios are approximately \(1.19\) , \(1.00\) , \(0.96\) , and \(1.21\) . docs.text: Before running this study, review the two-lump PI stability criterion , including the Routh-Hurwitz inequality, \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , and \(\rho_I\) . Continue with the common parameter set above, but set \(G=2\ \mathrm{W/K}\) , \(K_p=18\ \mathrm{PWM}/^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , and select PI control. Keep the \(1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) setpoint step and anti-windup on so actuator saturation does not obscure the linear prediction. For these values, \[ K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\approx 2.34\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s}). \] Calculate \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and then reset and run each case: \(K_i\) (PWM/( \(^\circ\) C s)) \(\rho_I\) Prediction \(0.25\) \(0.11\) Stable, relatively well damped \(1.00\) \(0.43\) Stable, more oscillatory \(2.10\) \(0.90\) Stable but weakly damped; long settling time \(2.50\) \(1.07\) Unstable in the linear model For every run, record rise time, overshoot, settling time, and whether the oscillation decays or grows. Verify that increasing \(K_i\) can shorten the initial correction while simultaneously making the final settling slower. Optional extension after the required plots: hold \(K_i=1.00\) and compare \(G=0.5\) , \(1\) , \(2\) , and \(5\ \mathrm{W/K}\) . Recalculate \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I\) each time. Predict the stable or unstable result before pressing Resume , then check the prediction. Finally, restore the common values and move \(C_T/C\) toward either extreme. Observe that concentrating the capacitance in one lump suppresses the two-state oscillatory behavior. These are short parameter studies, not additional A3 plots. docs.text: This exercise tests whether the model can reproduce the eight experimental Goldilocks conditions without asking you to search the entire parameter space. The apparatus did not change between runs, so all eight simulations must use one shared set of physical parameters . Only the controller gains \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) change. The simulated gains need not equal the experimental gains: the comparison asks whether tuning the controller alone can reproduce the same qualitative sequence while the physical model remains fixed. Use the two-lump PI stability criterion to predict and interpret the PI runs in terms of \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) . Step 1: Enter the measured quantities. Select two_lump and enter your measured \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}\) , \(\chi_c\) , \(\chi_h\) , and \(\tau\) . Use the same setpoints, initial temperatures, PWM limit, TEC voltage, and TEC resistance as the eight experiments. Begin with \(G=2\ \mathrm{W/K}\) and \(C_T/C=0.35\) . These are starting estimates for the unresolved internal structure, not additional measurements. Step 2: Calibrate the shared internal parameters once, then lock them. This is a one-time model-calibration step, not part of the controller-gain sweep. Select P control, set \(K_i=0\) , and enter the \(K_p\) from the experimental underdamped P run (Run 3) , whose oscillations decay. Do not use the sustained-oscillation Run 4, because the linear two-lump P model cannot reproduce that behavior. Compare the simulated and measured overshoot and oscillation decay. Read the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . A value above 1 predicts a monotonic response; a value below 1 predicts overshoot or ringing. Change only \(G\) and watch the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Move \(G\) in the direction that makes the simulated damping more like the underdamped experimental trace. If changing \(G\) is insufficient, restore the best \(G\) and vary \(C_T/C\) . Again, use the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) to choose the direction rather than guessing. Stop when the underdamped P simulation reproduces the qualitative behavior: monotonic, one overshoot, or repeated decaying oscillations. Exact fitting is not required. Record this one choice of \(G\) and \(C_T/C\) , then do not change either value again during any of the eight Goldilocks simulations. Step 3: Sweep \(K_p\) , then make the four P plots. Lock every physical parameter, keep \(K_i=0\) , and move only the \(K_p\) slider. Begin at low \(K_p\) and increase it until the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) passes from above 1 to below 1. Observe the corresponding transition from monotonic response to overshoot or ringing. This sweep is for understanding; it need not be saved. Now choose four increasing simulation values of \(K_p\) corresponding to the experimental labels small , critical , underdamped , and oscillatory . These gain values need not equal the experimental values. Use \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\approx1\) to locate the critical case and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}<1\) to locate an underdamped case. For the fourth case, continue increasing \(K_p\) and test whether the ideal two-lump P model ever produces sustained oscillations. It should not: its ringing must decay for every positive set of physical parameters. Preserve the highest-gain decaying response as the model's attempted oscillatory case. This failure to reproduce the sustained experimental trace is evidence against the model, not a reason to change the physical parameters. Plot only \(T_m\) if the TEC-side temperature obscures the measured response. Each retained plot caption must give \(K_p\) and the displayed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) . Also run the one-lump P model at four increasing \(K_p\) values. Its four responses should remain monotonic, showing that it cannot reproduce either underdamped or sustained oscillation. Step 4: Sweep \(K_i\) , then make the four PI plots. First use a parameter set chosen to make the stability transition easy to see. Select direct constants , two_lump , and PI control, then enter: \(T_{\mathrm{amb}}=T_0=29\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{set}}=30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , preserving a small \(1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) step that avoids saturation; \(C=100\ \mathrm{J/K}\) and \(C_T/C=0.50\) , so the two thermal stores are equal and neither state disappears into a one-lump approximation; \(G=2.0\ \mathrm{W/K}\) , which is small enough to create visible internal lag without nearly disconnecting the measured mass; \(H=1.14\ \mathrm{W/K}\) , \(P_{u,c}=0.26\ \mathrm{W/PWM}\) , and \(r=2.0\) ; \(K_p=10\ \mathrm{PWM}/^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , which is large enough to respond but not so large that P action dominates the stability demonstration; PWM limit \(255\) and \(\Delta t=0.05\ \mathrm{s}\) . The equal capacitance split makes both dynamical states important. The appreciable total capacitance stores enough thermal energy to create a visible transient, the modest \(G\) creates phase lag, and the \(1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) step avoids saturation. With these values, the display should give approximately \[ K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\approx 1.25\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s}). \] Fix every setting except \(K_i\) . Try \(K_i=0.10\) , \(0.60\) , \(1.10\) , \(1.25\) , and \(1.40\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s})\) . The corresponding \(\rho_I\) values are approximately \(0.08\) , \(0.48\) , \(0.88\) , \(1.00\) , and \(1.12\) . Move the slider between these checkpoints and observe the continuous transition. The displayed \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) remains fixed because the plant and \(K_p\) are fixed, while \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) increases. For two-lump PI control, the simulation automatically extends the \(K_i\) slider beyond the calculated \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , even when a large \(K_p\) makes that boundary greater than 5. Observe the response in four regions: \(\rho_I\ll1\) : the system is stable and oscillations decay; \(\rho_I\) just below 1: the system is stable and underdamped, but oscillations decay slowly and settling takes a long time; \(\rho_I=1\) : the ideal model is marginally stable and oscillations persist forever at constant amplitude; and \(\rho_I>1\) : oscillations grow and the linear model is unstable. This is a simulation, so you may briefly cross the instability boundary. Pause and reset once the growing oscillation is clear. Keep anti-windup on and use a small enough setpoint step that the PWM does not saturate; otherwise you are testing windup and saturation rather than the linear stability criterion. Optional extension: observe growth followed by actuator saturation. After the required plots are complete, deliberately leave the linear regime. Keep the Step 4 physical parameters, \(K_p=10\) , the \(30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) setpoint, the \(\pm255\) PWM limit, and anti-windup on. Set \(K_i=3.0\ \mathrm{PWM}/(^\circ\mathrm{C\,s})\) , select mass temperature only , use a rolling window of at least \(600\) s, and reset the simulation. Run for about \(700\) simulated seconds. You should see several growing temperature oscillations before the requested command reaches the PWM limit. The applied PWM then clips at \(+255\) or \(-255\) , and the temperature oscillation approaches a bounded amplitude rather than continuing to grow exponentially. Compare the command and temperature plots. Identify (1) the early interval in which the oscillation envelope grows, (2) the first time the applied PWM reaches a limit, and (3) the later bounded oscillation. Explain why the first interval is evidence of linear instability, while the later behavior is controlled by the nonlinear actuator limit. This is an exploration; do not add another plot to A3. After locating the transition, restore the one shared physical parameter set from Steps 1-3. Choose one PI value of \(K_p\) , hold it fixed, and vary only \(K_i\) to make small , critical , underdamped , and oscillatory PI responses. The simulated \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) values need not equal the experimental values. For each one: read the displayed \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) and \(\rho_I=K_i/K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) ; predict whether the oscillation should decay rapidly, decay slowly, or grow; reset the integral, keep anti-windup on, and run the simulation; and put \(K_p\) , \(K_i\) , \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) , and \(\rho_I\) in the plot caption. The retained PI runs should progress from lower to higher \(\rho_I\) while all physical parameters and the chosen PI value of \(K_p\) remain fixed. Use the simulation response to locate the operational transition from monotonic to overshooting behavior for the critical case, a decaying oscillation for the underdamped case, and \(\rho_I\approx1\) for the sustained, marginally stable oscillatory case. Do not confuse the critical Goldilocks response with \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) . The Goldilocks label marks the damping transition from monotonic response to overshoot. In contrast, \(K_{i,\mathrm{crit}}\) is the stability boundary: at that larger value, the ideal two-lump PI model is marginally stable and sustains oscillation. Step 5: Preserve the eight plots. Use the same time range, temperature range, and labeling scheme as the eight experimental plots. Every plot must show the setpoint, measured mass temperature, and signed applied PWM. Before the plots, state the one shared physical parameter set in a sentence. Do not make a parameter table. After the plots, answer these four comparison prompts: Which P and PI simulation best reproduce the corresponding experimental rise time, overshoot, and settling behavior? How do decreasing \(\zeta_{\mathrm{2L,P}}\) and the location of each gain relative to \(K_{p,\mathrm{crit}}\) organize the four P responses? How does increasing \(\rho_I\) organize the four PI responses? State one important agreement and one important disagreement between the eight simulations and eight experiments, then justify the P and PI gains that give the best compromise between speed and settling. In doing so, classify each response as stable non-oscillatory, stable underdamped, marginally stable, or unstable, and identify any observed behavior that falsifies the selected model. Optional windup demonstration: after preserving the eight plots, turn anti-windup off, reduce \(G\) , choose PI control, and apply a setpoint step large enough to saturate the PWM command. The measured temperature responds slowly, so the persistent error continues increasing the integral contribution even while the applied command is clamped. This extra overshoot is caused by stored controller error, not solely by the two-lump damping ratio. Turn anti-windup back on and press Zero integral before continuing. Use the sixteen Goldilocks plots, their captions, and the four comparison answers directly in A3 Questions 3 and 5. Explain why one-lump P control cannot oscillate and identify the heat flow that makes \(T_m\) lag behind \(T\) . Do not write a separate Part II report.
docs.title: Make The Eight Two-Lump Goldilocks Plots

docs.text: Before leaving S15, save the shared model settings, every completed simulation run, captions in progress, the exact run command, and links to the experimental data. After class, finish any remaining retained plots and the four comparison answers, then preserve the prepared simulation and completed A3 working materials in your repository. This is preparation for A3, not a separate submission.

docs.text: Use this modeling question bank to check your understanding and prepare A3: Which physical lag in the apparatus can produce overshoot or oscillation as gain increases? Identify one model parameter, give its units, and explain its physical effect on the simulated response. Also prepare the Module 5 P-control questions and Module 6 PI-control question .

docs.text: This module is a consolidation point after manual control and P/PI control. Keep the emphasis on physical interpretation, not formal control theory. Students should leave understanding why delay plus gain causes trouble. The long-rod model should be introduced as a preview, not fully derived here unless the class is ready.
