Module 7, Part III: Rod Instrument And Stationary Fin ¶ This is the experimental part of Module 7. It builds on Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations and Part II: Finite And Infinite Rod Theory . Purpose ¶ Part III has three priorities, in this order: Build the six-thermistor instrument. This is the primary objective. Establish one TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors as a checked measurement system. Extend the Arduino and Python software so that all six temperatures are acquired, displayed, and recorded together. Use the raw readings by default when the six sensors agree within \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) in a common bath; apply calibration corrections only if that check fails. Understand heat transport along a long, thin cylinder. Develop and understand the one-dimensional heat-transport equation, its boundary conditions, and the finite-length and radial-validity approximations. Measure and test the stationary temperature profile. Measure the steady-state temperature as a function of position along the rod, then fit and compare the finite insulated-tip model and the semi-infinite exponential model using the measured sensor positions and residuals. Part III is where the instrument is completed and used for the principal Module 7 physics measurement. The theory from Parts I and II predicts the stationary profile and provides the two models to test. Class-time priority. Spend no more than one hour of class time beginning the Part I and Part II theory. Finish that work at home and bring questions to class. Use the rest of the laboratory time for Part III: build the six-channel thermistor setup, check all six measurement chains in a common bath, develop and test the Arduino and Python software that displays and records all six temperatures, retain TEC temperature control, and measure the stationary temperature profile for comparison with the finite and semi-infinite models. Fit calibration corrections only if the common-bath check fails. In Modules 1-6, one or two temperatures were enough to describe the TEC process. The aluminum rod cannot be treated as one thermal lump. Its temperature depends on position and time: \[ T=T(x,t). \] In this module you will build and validate the multichannel rod instrument and measure the stationary temperature profile along the rod. Record the complete approach to steady state so that you can verify when the profile has settled and observe qualitatively how a temperature disturbance spreads. The primary physics measurement, however, is the stationary profile and its comparison with the finite-rod and semi-infinite models. The sinusoidal Angstrom experiment begins in Module 8. Thermistor Channels And Common-Bath Check ¶ The Arduino Uno R3 has six analog input channels, A0 through A5 , feeding one multiplexed 10-bit analog-to-digital converter. Use one channel for the thermistor in the TEC base and the other five channels for five thermistors along the rod. The converter samples the six channels in rapid sequence rather than at exactly the same instant. This delay is negligible on the thermal timescales measured here. The purpose here is to assign each thermistor a permanent channel, check all six measurement chains under a common temperature condition, and establish the sensor map used for the non-oscillatory step response and stationary-fin profile. Module 8 reuses the same validated sensor map for the oscillatory Angstrom experiment. Calibration corrections are optional rather than the default. The rod has more thermistor holes than the five available rod channels, so the five rod thermistors can be distributed among selected holes to obtain a useful range of positions and temperatures. Holes in the first group are nominally spaced at \(1/2\) -inch intervals; holes in the second group are nominally spaced at \(1\) -inch intervals. Treat these as orientation values only; measure and record the actual positions you use. The course rod is 6061-T6 aluminum with a nominal diameter of \(1/2\) inch, or \(12.7\ \mathrm{mm}\) . The analysis base at \(x=0\) is the first thermistor hole in the rod, occupied by rod thermistor 1. It is not the physical end of the rod and it is not the thermistor embedded in the TEC. Measure the positions of the other four rod thermistors relative to this origin. Define the analyzed length \(L\) as the distance from the first thermistor hole to the rod tip. Also record the rod's overall physical length, diameter \(d\) , and their uncertainties. The TEC thermistor monitors the actuator, while the measured temperature of rod thermistor 1 supplies the boundary condition \(T(0,t)\) for the rod model. Use one model-testing cycle throughout Part III: Predict: use the Part I and Part II theory to predict the qualitative transient, the stationary profile, and the importance of the end and radius. Measure: acquire synchronized, checked temperature data with the geometry and settings needed to interpret them. Compare: fit the finite and semi-infinite models and inspect residuals, parameter values, and uncertainties. Judge: state which assumptions the evidence supports and where the model is inadequate. Schedule And Due Work ¶ Session In class Due S16, Mon. Oct. 26 Use no more than the first hour to begin Parts I and II and identify questions to finish at home. Then map and common-bath-check all six sensors, calibrating only if needed; develop and test the six-channel Arduino/Python display and recording system with TEC control; begin the stationary-profile run if the instrument is ready. Module 7 home preparation S17, Wed. Oct. 28 Complete the stationary-profile measurement, retaining the full approach to steady state; fit and compare the finite-length and semi-infinite stationary profiles A4: finite-rod model and validity checks ; C5: Rod instrument and data-acquisition chain In-Class Route ¶ Complete the experimental work in this order: Phase 1: wire and permanently label TEC and T1 - T5 . Phase 2: display and record all six channels while retaining TEC control. Phase 3: perform the common-bath check and complete the sensor map. Phase 4: choose useful rod positions and acquire the stationary profile. Phase 5: analyze the profile and test the finite and semi-infinite models. Outside-Class Workload Budget ¶ Session Work Planned time S16 Complete the required Part I and Part II reading route, including the selected Lienhard sections and derivation guide 150 minutes S16 Begin A4: identify boundary conditions and organize the finite-length derivation 75 minutes S16 Total associated with S16 3 hours 45 minutes S17 Complete and check the individual A4 calculations 180 minutes S17 Prepare the sensor-map and common-bath check record 45 minutes S17 Total associated with S17 3 hours 45 minutes The reading allocation includes time to follow the derivation, not merely read the prose. Save all rod measurements during class; the outside-class budget is for theory, analysis, documentation, and submission. Learning Objectives ¶ The objectives below are listed in priority order. By the end of Module 7, Part III, you should be able to: Build and demonstrate the six-thermistor instrument: assign permanent channels to the TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors, check all six measurement chains in a common bath, apply calibration corrections only if required, and extend the Arduino and Python software to display and record synchronized temperatures with units, timestamps, sensor positions, and experimental metadata. Explain and apply the one-dimensional heat-transport equation for a long, thin cylinder, then use the finite-length solution and transverse Biot number to make separate quantitative decisions about whether the far end and radial temperature variation may be neglected. Measure the stationary temperature profile along the rod, fit finite-length and semi-infinite stationary-fin models, examine their residuals, and interpret the fitted decay coefficient and decay length. Explain what the steady experiment can determine and why it cannot determine the thermal conductivity and side heat-transfer coefficient separately. Use the recorded approach to steady state to justify the selected stationary interval and explain qualitatively why more distant sensors respond later and with smaller temperature changes. Part III Vocabulary And Notation ¶ Review the foundational vocabulary in Part I and the fin-model vocabulary in Part II . The terms below connect that theory to the experiment and its analysis. Term Meaning Temperature field, \(T(x,t)\) Temperature as a function of both position along the rod and time. Environmental temperature, \(T_\infty\) The temperature of the environment far from the rod. In this experiment, it is the room temperature measured away from the heated apparatus. Excess temperature, \(	heta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty\) Rod temperature measured relative to the environment. Thermal diffusivity, \(\alpha=k/(ho c)\) The coefficient controlling axial spreading in the Part III model; units m \(^2\) /s. This is Lienhard's notation. Side-loss rate, \(
u=hP/(ho cA)\) The fractional rate, in s \(^{-1}\) , at which side convection removes excess thermal energy in the one-dimensional model. Decay coefficient, \(m=\sqrt{hP/(kA)}=\sqrt{
u/\alpha}\) The spatial decay rate of the stationary profile; \(1/m\) is the decay length. Sensor map A record of each channel name, thermistor position, coordinate origin and direction, and position uncertainty. Common-bath check A comparison under a common temperature condition used to identify sensor offsets or other channel differences. If the full spread of the six readings remains below \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , use the raw readings without calibration corrections. Baseline Measurements made before the imposed temperature change, used to establish room temperature and initial sensor readings. Step response The measured evolution of \(T(x,t)\) after the base-temperature command changes. Boundary condition The measured or prescribed behavior at a boundary. For the rod model, the measured temperature of rod thermistor 1 at the first hole is the boundary condition \(T(0,t)\) ; the TEC setpoint and TEC-thermistor temperature describe the actuator that creates it. Stationary profile The position-dependent temperature after changes with time have become negligible according to a stated criterion. Model fit Estimation of model parameters by comparing a predicted curve with measured data. Residual Measured value minus model prediction at the same position or time. Residual structure can reveal model inadequacy. Uncertainty A quantitative estimate of the plausible range of a measured or fitted result. Metadata Information needed to interpret and reproduce a run, including units, timestamps, channel labels, geometry, settings, and experimental notes. Reading And Preparation ¶ Read selectively in Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook , Section 1.3, pp. 11-26, following the reading guide in Part I. Review Module 7, Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations . For the S16 lecture and S17 guided study, read Lienhard Section 4.5, textbook pp. 163-173. Work through the derivation rather than reading only the final formulas. Use Fin Design: From A Finite Rod To An Infinite Rod as the equation-by-equation guide to Lienhard Eqs. (4.27)-(4.51). Complete A4 , including Lienhard Problems 1.3, 4.12, and 4.20. Problem 1.3 is assigned in Module 7, Part I . Model ¶ Part II set the energy-storage term to zero to obtain the stationary fin equation. We now restore that term while retaining distributed side cooling, so the model describes both the transient response and the stationary profile that it approaches. Let \[ 	heta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty, \] where \(T_\infty\) is the temperature of the environment far from the rod. For the course experiment, \(T_\infty\) is the room temperature measured away from the heated apparatus. For a uniform rod with cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , density \(ho\) , specific heat \(c\) , thermal conductivity \(k\) , and side heat-transfer coefficient \(h\) , conservation of energy gives \[ ho c A rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =kA rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-hP	heta. \] Every term has units of power per unit length, watts per meter. Dividing by \(ho cA\) gives \[  rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =\alpha rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-
u	heta, \qquad \alpha= rac{k}{ho c}, \qquad 
u= rac{hP}{ho c A}. \] Here \(\alpha\) has units of square meters per second and \(
u\) has units of inverse seconds. At steady state, \[  rac{d^2	heta}{dx^2}-m^2	heta=0, \qquad m^2= rac{hP}{kA}= rac{
u}{\alpha}. \] This second-order equation requires two boundary conditions. For the analyzed section, rod thermistor 1 supplies the measured temperature at the analysis base \(x=0\) , and the tip is treated as insulated. Part II then gives the complete finite-rod profile \[  rac{	heta(x)}{	heta(0)} = rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)}. \] Explore The Finite-Rod Model ¶ Open the interactive TEC and finite-rod simulator , developed by Tim Hebert, and use a constant setpoint. The simulator numerically evolves the one-dimensional transient conduction equation with side heat loss, a finite rod, and a dynamic TEC boundary. Move the probe along the rod and observe both the approach to steady state and the final spatial profile. Use it to predict which parts of the measured rod should be sensitive to the far-end boundary condition before fitting the experimental data. Suggested high-gain exploration. Place the probe at \(x=0\) , use proportional control only, and compare successively larger values of \(K_p\) , for example 8, 80, and 800. At modest gain, an overshoot can decay. At large gain, the simulator can instead settle into a sustained oscillation while the PWM repeatedly saturates or reverses. This oscillation is produced by the dynamic TEC actuator included in the simulator; it is absent from the ideal one-lump P-control model. Identify approximately where the qualitative change occurs, and compare the oscillation period with the thermal response times visible in the TEC and rod. Then hold \(K_p=800\) fixed and move the probe from \(x=0\) to a few positions farther along the rod, resetting between trials. Observe qualitatively that the oscillation frequency generally increases as the probe is moved closer to the TEC. What physical model is inside this simulator? The rod is divided into finite-difference elements that obey the one-dimensional transient heat equation \[ ho cA rac{\partial T}{\partial t} =kA rac{\partial^2T}{\partial x^2}-hP(T-T_\infty). \] The simulator does not substitute the analytical cosh or exponential solution. It replaces the axial second derivative with centered finite differences on 24-100 rod elements and advances the resulting coupled ordinary differential equations with a 0.01 s numerical substep. The TEC balances and thermistor equation are advanced with the same substep, while the controller updates every 0.1 s. The analytical stationary profiles derived in Part II are therefore predictions that can be compared with the numerical long-time limit, not formulas built into the simulation. The far tip has zero axial heat flux. The driven end is coupled to a dynamic TEC model. It is not an ideal heat source. The model has a cold-side temperature \(T_c\) and hot-side temperature \(T_h\) , with separate heat capacities \(C_c\) and \(C_h\) . A signed duty command \(u\) applies the averaged voltage \(V=uV_s\) to the TEC. The code calculates the signed current from this voltage, the TEC electrical resistance, and the Seebeck back-emf, then limits the current to the allowed range. Using the conventional current \(I_c\) that is positive in the cooling direction, the heat absorbed at the cold side and rejected at the hot side are \[ \dot Q_c =S I_c T_{c,K}- rac{1}{2}I_c^2R-K_{\mathrm{TEC}}(T_h-T_c), \] \[ \dot Q_h =S I_c T_{h,K}+ rac{1}{2}I_c^2R-K_{\mathrm{TEC}}(T_h-T_c). \] Here \(S\) is the effective Seebeck coefficient, \(R\) is the electrical resistance, \(K_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) is the passive thermal conductance through the TEC, and the temperatures marked \(K\) are absolute temperatures. The terms proportional to \(SI_cT\) describe Peltier transport, the \(I_c^2R/2\) terms split Joule heating between the two faces, and the final terms describe ordinary conduction from the hot face toward the cold face. The two TEC temperatures obey separate energy balances: \[ C_c rac{dT_c}{dt} =-\dot Q_c+G_c[T(0,t)-T_c]+G_{\mathrm{leak}}(T_\infty-T_c), \] \[ C_h rac{dT_h}{dt} =\dot Q_h- rac{T_h-T_\infty}{R_{\mathrm{hs}}}. \] The contact conductance \(G_c=h_{\mathrm{contact}}A\) couples the cold-side plate to the first finite-difference element of the rod. The hot side loses heat to the room through the heat-sink resistance \(R_{\mathrm{hs}}\) , while \(G_{\mathrm{leak}}\) represents an additional cold-side leak to the room. The default parameters approximate a TEC1-12706-type device: \(S=0.0513\) V/K, \(R=1.861\ \Omega\) , \(K_{\mathrm{TEC}}=0.560\) W/K, \(C_c=12\) J/K, \(C_h=180\) J/K, \(R_{\mathrm{hs}}=0.55\) K/W, and a 12 V supply. These values are model parameters, not measurements of the particular classroom TEC. The rod is the distributed thermal load on this two-state actuator. Its first element exchanges heat with \(T_c\) through \(G_c\) ; the remaining elements conduct heat axially and lose heat from their sides. The movable thermistor measures the local rod temperature through a first-order sensor response with a 2 s time constant. The controller samples that measured temperature every 0.1 s and limits the signed PWM command to the range from \(-100\%\) to \(+100\%\) . High-gain P-control exploration. Put the probe at \(x=0\) , turn off I and D, and keep all settings except \(K_p\) fixed. Reset the simulation for each trial. Begin with \(K_p=8\) , then try \(K_p=80\) and \(K_p=800\) , adding intermediate values to locate the transition. For each run, decide whether the response is monotonic, shows damped oscillations, or reaches a sustained oscillation. Record whether the PWM remains proportional or spends most of each cycle at \(+100\%\) and \(-100\%\) , and compare the oscillation period with the visible TEC and rod response times. Next set \(K_p=800\) and move the probe between \(x=0\) and a few downstream positions. Reset at each position and compare only the qualitative oscillation rate. The oscillations are generally faster near the TEC and slower when feedback is based on a more distant temperature. For P control, \[ u_{\mathrm{unsat}}=K_p[T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_s], \qquad u=\operatorname{sat}(u_{\mathrm{unsat}}). \] As \(K_pightarrow\infty\) , almost any nonzero error drives the command to one limit or the other. This is the bang-bang limit : full heating for one sign of the error and full cooling for the other. Reversing the command at the setpoint does not reverse the temperature immediately. Energy already stored in the TEC faces and rod keeps the temperature moving, so the system overshoots, reverses, and may form a bounded limit cycle. The phase lag is cumulative. The separate \(C_c\) and \(C_h\) states give the TEC its own two-lump actuator lag. Finite contact conductance, the distributed diffusion modes of the rod, the thermistor response, and digital sampling add further lag. Placing the probe at \(x=0\) removes the additional propagation delay associated with measuring farther down the rod, but it does not remove the TEC dynamics or the rod's distributed thermal load. At sufficiently high loop gain, enough phase lag can make nominally negative feedback reinforce an oscillation at some frequency; PWM saturation then bounds its amplitude. This behavior is absent from the elementary one-lump P-control model, whose single closed-loop mode remains stable for positive parameters. Moving the probe downstream adds thermal-diffusion delay and attenuates the measured oscillation. The controller therefore reacts to an older, weaker indication of what the actuator has done; in this simulator the sustained oscillations generally become slower as the probe moves away from the TEC. The exact distance scaling is not the point here because the TEC, rod, sensor, and saturation dynamics all contribute. The practical control-design lesson is more general: place the feedback sensor close to the actuator when the goal is fast, stable regulation, unless the temperature at a remote location is itself the quantity that must be controlled. The model is intentionally idealized. It does not include every contact, temperature dependence, electronic delay, or three-dimensional heat-flow path in the physical apparatus. When the far end has negligible influence over the measured region, this finite profile approaches the semi-infinite approximation \[ 	heta(x)=	heta_0 e^{-mx}. \] The fitted \(m\) quantifies the competition between axial conduction and side loss. It does not determine \(k\) and \(h\) separately. The periodic Angstrom experiment in Module 8, Part I, supplies the second independent measurement. Before The Experiment: Model-Validity Checks ¶ Length: Solve It First ¶ For the section of rod extending a distance \(L\) from the first thermistor hole to the insulated tip, the exact normalized stationary solution is \[ \Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x) = rac{	heta(x)}{	heta(0)} = rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)}. \] The semi-infinite model is the limiting expression \[ \Theta_\infty(x)=e^{-mx}. \] Calculate the relative error at every sensor position: \[ \epsilon_T(x)=  rac{\left|\Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x)-\Theta_\infty(x)ight|} {\left|\Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x)ight|}. \] State an acceptable error before deciding whether the far end may be ignored. A reasonable starting criterion is \(\epsilon_T<5\%\) at every sensor used in the analysis, but record and justify a different threshold if the intended measurement requires one. The product \(mL\) is useful, but the answer also depends on which sensor and which observable you use. Radius: Check The Transverse Biot Number ¶ For a circular rod, \[ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}= rac{h(A/P)}{k}= rac{hR}{2k}. \] This validity check is performed in two stages. Before the experiment , make a provisional estimate using a literature value or range for the conductivity of 6061-T6 aluminum and the measured rod geometry. For natural convection from the half-inch rod in still room air, use the planning value \[ h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}. \] Treat this as a provisional convection value, not as a measurement of \(h\) . The small-Biot condition \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) means radial conduction is fast enough that a cross section can be represented by one temperature. Before the experiment, estimate \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) using the rod radius and \(h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}\) , together with a justified literature value or range for \(k\) . At this stage, proceed with the one-dimensional model under the provisional assumption that \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) . You cannot yet test that assumption using the measured profile because \(m\) has not yet been measured. After the experiment , return to this question using the fitted stationary profile. This is a measurement-based self-consistency check rather than another estimate of \(h\) . The fitted spatial decay coefficient obeys \[ m^2= rac{hP}{kA}, \] so \[  rac{h}{k}=m^2 rac{A}{P}, \qquad  oxed{\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} =m^2\left( rac{A}{P}ight)^2}. \] For a circular rod, \(A/P=R/2=d/4\) , and therefore \[  oxed{\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}=\left( rac{mR}{2}ight)^2 =\left( rac{md}{4}ight)^2}. \] Use the following measurement procedure: Calculate \(	heta_i=T_i-T_\infty\) from the stationary temperatures. Fit the finite-length profile first to obtain \(m\) and its uncertainty. This avoids assuming the semi-infinite limit before testing it. Use the measured diameter and the fitted \(m\) to calculate \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) . Propagate the uncertainties in \(m\) and \(d\) . Decide whether \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) adequately supports the assumption of a uniform temperature across each cross section. This final calculation is a self-consistency check , not a logically independent proof: the one-dimensional profile used to fit \(m\) already assumes negligible radial temperature variation. If the fitted value gives \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) , the assumption used at the beginning is self-consistent. If it does not, reject the one-dimensional interpretation of the fitted \(m\) ; a model with radial temperature variation would be required. The same fitted \(m\) also completes the length check above. Calculate \(mL\) and evaluate \(\epsilon_T(x_i)\) at every sensor position. If the finite and semi-infinite profiles differ by less than your stated criterion throughout the measured region, the semi-infinite approximation is adequate there. If not, retain the finite-length solution. Thus \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) tests the radial approximation, while \(mL\) and \(\epsilon_T(x_i)\) test whether the far end can be ignored; they are separate conclusions obtained from the same fit. A4: Finite-Rod Model And Validity Checks ¶ A4 is a 10-point individual written assignment based on Module 7, Parts I and II. It does not require temperature-profile data from Part III. Use the measured rod geometry and your planned sensor positions, together with a literature range for \(k\) and the provisional value \(h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}\) given above. These calculations are predictions to record before heating the rod; they are not the final measurement-based validity checks. Submit one PDF organized under the following four headings. Show units and dimensional checks throughout. Part 1. Apply Fourier's law. Complete Lienhard Problem 1.3 as assigned in Part I . Show how Fourier's law produces each result, include units, and identify any physically unreasonable result. Part 2. Build the stationary finite-rod model. Starting from conservation of energy, Fourier's law, and Newton's law of cooling, derive the stationary fin equation with side heat loss. Follow the finite-fin solution in Lienhard Section 4.5, showing the principal steps from the differential equation to the solution. State the two boundary conditions and explain what each means physically. Part 3. Make a provisional finite-length prediction. Complete Lienhard Problem 4.12 to obtain the semi-infinite limit. Use Example 4.8 and Problem 4.20 to quantify the effect of approximating the tip boundary condition. From the provisional value of \(h\) and literature range for \(k\) , calculate a range for \(m\) , then calculate \(mL\) and \(\epsilon_T(x)\) at every planned course-rod sensor position. State whether you expect the course rod to be adequately semi-infinite over the measured region, and state the positions, parameter ranges, and error criterion on which this prediction depends. Part 4. Make a provisional one-dimensional prediction. Calculate a range for \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) using the same provisional value of \(h\) and literature range for \(k\) . State whether you expect each cross section to be represented adequately by one temperature. Do not combine this radius conclusion with the finite-length conclusion from Part 3. Then answer this brief application question: compare the same electronic heat sink in still air and in forced airflow. Which case should have the larger convective coefficient \(h\) , and how should the larger \(h\) change the decay length \(1/m\) ? The submission details and rubric appear near the end of this page. Prediction Record Before Heating ¶ Before applying heat to the course rod, record the provisional values of \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) , \(mL\) , and \(\epsilon_T(x)\) at every sensor. Predict: the order in which the sensors will respond to a base-temperature step, how the response amplitude will change with distance from the base, the qualitative shape of the stationary temperature profile, and whether the measured region should reveal the finite tip. Use the measured rod geometry and the sensor positions you initially plan to use. If the placement pilot leads you to move a sensor, preserve the original prediction and repeat the calculation using the final measured position. Return to these predictions after fitting the stationary data and state which were supported by the evidence. Phase 1: Wire And Label The Six Thermistors ¶ Build the complete measurement circuit before modifying the software or preparing the common bath. Prepare six thermistors using 26 AWG paired insulated wire for the sensor leads. Separate the pair near the thermistor and insulate the two solder joints individually so they cannot touch. Use the heat-shrink tubing specified and supplied by the instructor. Slide both pieces onto the wires before soldering, keep the joints compact, and stagger the joints so the finished end is not unnecessarily bulky. At the breadboard end, terminate the flexible 26 AWG pair with short 22 AWG solid-wire pigtails so the connections are reliable in the solderless breadboard. Use a meter to measure the actual resistance of each nominal \(100\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) fixed resistor before it is connected in its voltage divider, and record the measured value with its channel assignment. Follow the established thermistor voltage-divider circuit; do not change the TEC power or safety wiring. Label the TEC-base thermistor TEC and the five rod thermistors T1 through T5 . Use durable, water-resistant labels attached securely to the dry portions of the leads. The labels must survive handling, the common-bath check, installation, and the rest of the semester without falling off or moving to another lead. Assign TEC to A0 and T1 through T5 to A1 through A5 , unless your documented apparatus requires a different assignment. Record every sensor, analog input, divider, and wire color in the sensor map. Check every connection for exposed conductors, loose joints, and accidental shorts before powering the Arduino. Keep the TEC power disabled during the first sensor tests. Photograph the labeled, wired measurement chain before proceeding. From this point onward, keep each physical thermistor paired with its assigned divider, Arduino input, software label, and CSV column. Phase 2: Develop The Six-Channel Display And Recording Software ¶ Keep the tested Module 6 files unchanged as a working checkpoint. Make new Module 7 copies of both the Arduino sketch and Python GUI, give the copies clear Module 7 filenames, and extend those copies for the rod experiment. For example, use arduino/module_07_rod_controller/module_07_rod_controller.ino and python/module_07_rod_acquisition_gui.py in your repository. The TEC-base thermistor remains the feedback and safety sensor. The five rod thermistors are additional measurement channels; they do not enter the PI-control law. Develop and test the software in the steps below. Keep each step working before asking Copilot to make the next change. Copilot may write code, but you are responsible for checking the pin assignments, serial interface, units, safety behavior, and saved data. Do not begin the hot-water common-bath check until the Arduino and Python software can display and record all six correctly labeled channels. Step 2A: Extend The Arduino Measurement ¶ Use all six Uno analog inputs. Unless your documented wiring requires a different assignment, use A0 for the TEC-base thermistor and A1 through A5 for rod thermistors 1 through 5. The Uno has one analog-to-digital converter and selects the six inputs sequentially. Read and average each channel, then send all six temperatures together in one measurement record. The resulting time offsets between channels are negligible compared with the rod's thermal response, but the Arduino time must be measured and transmitted with every record. The revised sketch must: retain the existing PI control, zero-PWM startup, H-bridge pin assignments, temperature limit, and hardware-safety instructions, use the TEC-base thermistor alone for feedback and the software temperature limit, calculate all six temperatures with the same thermistor conversion, label every transmitted field unambiguously, emit exactly one complete measurement record per acquisition cycle, and continue accepting the existing commands from the Python GUI. Use a stable serial record such as DATA,time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety DATA,12.50,23.41,23.38,23.36,23.34,23.31,23.29,120,1,45.00,OK The first line is a header printed once at startup; each later DATA line is one measurement. Status and error messages must not begin with DATA . This distinction lets both Python and the serial microSD logger recognize valid records without confusing them with diagnostic text. Suggested Copilot prompt: six-channel Arduino acquisition Inspect the working Module 6 Arduino TEC-controller sketch that is open in VS Code. First copy it to a new Module 7 sketch named arduino/module_07_rod_controller/module_07_rod_controller.ino. Leave the Module 6 file unchanged and edit only the new Module 7 copy. Preserve its PI control, serial-command parser, H-bridge pins, zero-PWM startup, software temperature limit, and all safety behavior. Use A0 for the TEC-base thermistor and A1-A5 for rod thermistors 1-5. The A0 temperature must remain the only temperature used by the PI controller and software safety limit. Read and average all six analog channels and convert each reading with the sketch's existing thermistor-conversion function. Keep the number of averages as a named constant. Record the Arduino elapsed time after the six measurements have been acquired. At startup, print this header once: DATA,time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety For every acquisition cycle, print exactly one comma-separated line beginning with DATA and containing those fields in that order. Diagnostic, command-ack, and error lines must not begin with DATA. Keep accepting the existing Python commands without changing their format. Comment the new pin definitions, six-channel acquisition loop, and serial-output block for an Arduino beginner. After editing, summarize every function and line of control logic that you preserved unchanged. Before connecting TEC power, test this sketch with Serial Monitor. Warm one thermistor at a time with your fingers and verify that only its named column changes. Confirm that the Arduino starts with PWM zero and still responds to a zero-power command. Close Serial Monitor before opening the Python GUI because only one program can own the serial port at a time. Step 2B: Extend The Python Display And Raw-Data Record ¶ Modify the Module 6 GUI so that it parses the new DATA record and displays six simultaneous temperature traces. Retain the existing setpoint, controller, PWM, and safety displays. Give each trace a stable label and color, make the TEC-base trace visually distinct, and provide checkboxes or a legend that makes crowded plots readable. Every accepted record must be written to a new CSV file with at least these columns: time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety These are raw measured temperatures. Do not replace them with calibrated values. Reject incomplete or malformed lines without stopping the program, flush saved data regularly, and never silently overwrite an existing run. Suggested Copilot prompt: six-temperature GUI and CSV logger Inspect both the new Module 7 Arduino sketch and my working Module 6 PySide6 and pyqtgraph TEC-control GUI. First copy the Module 6 GUI to a new file named python/module_07_rod_acquisition_gui.py. Leave the Module 6 file unchanged and edit only the new Module 7 copy. Do not create a different controller or change the Arduino command format. Preserve all PI controls, PWM and direction displays, serial command sending, safety display, and zero-output stop behavior. Parse only complete Arduino lines beginning with DATA. The fields are: time_s, tec_C, rod1_C, rod2_C, rod3_C, rod4_C, rod5_C, pwm, heat_cool, setpoint_C, and safety. Ignore headers, acknowledgments, diagnostics, and malformed lines without crashing. Plot TEC and rod1-rod5 temperatures together against Arduino time. Give every trace a fixed label and color and make the TEC trace thicker than the rod traces. Add live numerical displays for all six temperatures. Preserve the existing rolling-window behavior and controls. Write every accepted raw record to a new CSV file with exactly those column names. Do not apply calibration corrections and do not overwrite an existing file; create a timestamped filename or require a new filename. Flush the file regularly so a long run is not lost if the GUI closes unexpectedly. Add a visible count of accepted and rejected serial lines. Keep the code readable for a Python beginner and comment the parser, data storage, CSV writing, and plot updates. At the end, explain how I can verify that every plotted trace is being written to the correct CSV column. Test with TEC power off. Compare several consecutive Arduino DATA records with the corresponding Python numerical display and CSV rows. The field order, values, and units must agree before the program is used for the common-bath check. Step 2C: Integration Check Before The Common-Bath Test ¶ Demonstrate the complete measurement chain before collecting the cooling-bath record: Show that warming one sensor changes only its assigned Arduino and Python channel. Verify that one Arduino DATA line, one set of displayed values, and one saved CSV row agree. Disconnect one rod thermistor temporarily and verify that the fault is visible without defeating the TEC-base safety shutdown. Restart both programs and confirm that PWM begins at zero and that a new data file is created. Record the Arduino-sketch and Python-GUI filenames and their Git commit hash in the sensor map. Phase 3: Common-Bath Check And Sensor Map ¶ Complete these tasks in order. Do not prepare the hot water until Phases 1 and 2 are complete. Confirm that the six thermistors are securely labeled TEC and T1 through T5 , wired to their permanent channels, and documented in the sensor map. Demonstrate that the Arduino and GUI display all six temperatures and save them in six correctly labeled CSV columns. Open the common-bath popup below and perform the check. Display all six temperatures simultaneously and observe them after the mixed bath has settled at several temperatures. At each observation, calculate the full spread \(T_{\max}-T_{\min}\) across the six thermistors. If the spread remains less than \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , record that the sensors passed and apply no calibration corrections or calibration-specific GUI changes. This is the default outcome. If the spread reaches or exceeds \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , continue to the subsequent Record/Pause and fitting steps in the popup. After the common-bath check, record the rod material as 6061-T6 aluminum. Measure its diameter \(d\) , overall physical length, and analysis length \(L\) from the first thermistor hole to the tip. Calculate its cross-sectional area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\) in SI units. Install rod thermistor 1 in the first rod hole and define that hole as the analysis base \(x=0\) . Measure the other four rod-sensor positions and the tip relative to this origin, so that the tip is at (x=L). Estimate the uncertainty of every position and of \(L\) . Save a diagram or photograph showing the permanent sensor labels, Arduino channel assignments, coordinate direction, and measured rod positions. Common-bath procedure and optional relative calibration Common-Bath Check ¶ The rod experiment measures temperature differences and spatial temperature gradients. It does not require an absolute temperature calibration. It does require a common-bath check so that a large channel-to-channel difference is not mistaken for a temperature gradient along the rod. The default is not to fit or apply calibration corrections. If the full spread of all six readings remains below \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) at every retained bath temperature, document that result and use the raw readings. Use the TEC thermistor as the reference and continue to the optional correction steps only if this criterion fails. Step 1. Confirm the Phase 1 prerequisites. Perform the check before installing the thermistors in the apparatus. Confirm that TEC and T1 - T5 retain their secure, water-resistant labels and that only their waterproof sensing ends will be immersed. Step 2. Confirm the Phase 2 prerequisites. Use the permanent voltage dividers, Arduino inputs, acquisition code, and sample rate. Confirm that the GUI displays and records six correctly labeled channels, then warm one sensor at a time to verify its display and CSV column. Step 3. Heat the water. Put water in a glass beaker and warm the beaker in the microwave. Only the beaker and water go into the microwave; never microwave the thermistors, wires, or any electrical hardware. Swirl the beaker carefully after heating so that the water temperature is reasonably uniform. Handle the hot glass and water cautiously. The calibration range should remain below approximately \(60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . Step 4. Prepare the common bath. Pour the warm water from the glass beaker into a stable Styrofoam cup. Place all six waterproof sensing ends close together in the water. Keep labels, electrical joints, connectors, and exposed conductors dry, and do not allow the sensing ends to touch the cup walls or bottom. Place the meter's thermocouple probe near the six sensing ends without allowing it to touch them or the cup. Step 5. Mix and observe. Run the basic six-temperature GUI. Gently swirl the cup or stir the water so that every sensor experiences the same bath temperature. Watch the six live traces and numerical readings. After mixing, allow any motion-induced fluctuations to settle. If one trace remains much noisier than the others, check its connection before using the readings. Step 6. Decide whether calibration is needed. At several bath temperatures spanning the range expected in the rod experiment, mix the water, allow the display to settle, and note the six simultaneous readings and the thermocouple temperature. Calculate \(T_{\max}-T_{\min}\) . If the spread remains less than \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , save a screenshot or short check record, state that no correction is required, and stop here. Do not add Record/Pause code merely for this check. If the spread reaches or exceeds \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , continue with the remaining steps. Step 7. Only if needed, add Record/Pause. Extend the GUI with a clearly labeled Record/Pause control. Live numerical values and plots must continue updating in both states. In Record , append each accepted DATA record to the calibration CSV. In Pause , append no temperature rows, allowing the bath to be mixed and the readings to settle without adding those transients to the fitting data. Start in Pause, display the current state prominently, flush the file whenever recording is paused, and preserve the continuous Arduino timestamp so that gaps in the saved record are unambiguous. Suggested Copilot prompt: add Record/Pause only after the check fails The six-temperature Arduino acquisition and Python GUI already work. The common-bath check found a spread of at least 1 degree C, so modify the existing Module 7 GUI to support calibration data collection. Do not change the Arduino code, serial format, controller, safety behavior, live numerical displays, or live plots. Add a prominent Record/Pause button that controls only CSV writing. Start in Pause. While paused, continue parsing and plotting all six temperatures but do not append DATA rows. While recording, append every accepted DATA row to the calibration CSV. When recording resumes, continue using Arduino time without resetting it. Show the current state clearly and flush the file whenever the state changes to Pause. Comment the new state variable, button callback, and conditional CSV-writing logic for a Python beginner. Explain how to verify that the display continues in Pause, the CSV row count remains fixed in Pause, and recording resumes without resetting Arduino time. Step 8. Collect quiet fitting intervals. Use the TEC channel as the reference. At several temperatures, keep the GUI paused while mixing the bath and waiting for the displayed readings to settle. Press Record and retain at least 60 seconds of simultaneous data. Record the thermocouple temperature for that interval, then press Pause before stirring again. Repeat the pause-mix-settle-record-pause sequence as the water cools. Step 9. Verify the saved calibration record. Open the calibration CSV and confirm that it contains timestamps and six populated temperature columns with the expected labels. Compare several rows with the GUI and confirm that each recorded interval has a corresponding thermocouple measurement. Step 10. Fit each channel to the reference. Plot each rod-sensor reading, \(T_i\) , against the simultaneous TEC-thermistor reading, \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) . Do the data fall on a straight line? If so, fit \[ T_{\mathrm{TEC}}=a_i+b_iT_i. \] Apply this fitted relation as the correction: \[ T_{i,\mathrm{corrected}}=a_i+b_iT_i. \] Step 11. Check the corrected differences. Plot \[ \Delta T_i =T_{i,\mathrm{corrected}}-T_{\mathrm{TEC}} \] against \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) . Report the mean difference, scatter, and any remaining trend with temperature. Choose and record an acceptance criterion before evaluating the correction. A useful starting criterion is a corrected mean difference smaller than \(0.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) for every channel, with no residual trend larger than \(0.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) across the calibration range. Revise this criterion if the measured noise and resolution justify a different value. Step 12. Preserve the raw readings. Store the correction coefficients separately and apply them during analysis; never overwrite the original data. The thermocouple measurement provides an independent check on the approximate bath temperature and common-bath range. The channel corrections are still obtained by treating the TEC thermistor as the common reference. The corrected channels may therefore share a common absolute bias, but that bias does not affect temperature differences or the measured spatial profile. If Needed, Analyze And Preserve The Correction ¶ Only if the \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) agreement criterion fails, write a separate Python analysis program for the optional correction. It must read the raw CSV rather than modify the acquisition program. For each rod channel, fit \[ T_{\mathrm{TEC}}=a_i+b_iT_i, \] make the comparison and residual plots required above, and save the fitted coefficients and fit-quality measures in a separate calibration file. Keep the raw CSV unchanged. Later analyses may read both files and calculate additional columns named rod1_corrected_C through rod5_corrected_C . Record the calibration-script filename and Git commit hash in the sensor map. Suggested Copilot prompt: relative-calibration analysis Write a separate Python calibration-analysis script for my six-thermistor CSV file. Do not modify or overwrite the raw data. The raw columns are time_s, tec_C, rod1_C, rod2_C, rod3_C, rod4_C, rod5_C, pwm, heat_cool, setpoint_C, and safety. Treat tec_C as the reference. For each rod channel i, perform a linear least-squares fit tec_C = a_i + b_i * rod_i_C over a user-selected calibration time or temperature range. Plot each rod temperature against tec_C with the identity line and fitted line. Then plot the corrected residual (a_i + b_i * rod_i_C) - tec_C against tec_C. Print and save a table containing channel, a_i, b_i, number of fitted points, calibration temperature range, residual mean, residual standard deviation, and maximum absolute residual. Save this table to a separate CSV file. Also write a separate corrected-data CSV that retains every original raw column and adds rod1_corrected_C through rod5_corrected_C. Never replace a raw column. Include clear axis labels with units and comment the file input, range selection, fitting, residual calculation, and output sections for a Python beginner. Phase 4: Configure And Acquire The Stationary Profile ¶ For the initial Part III prediction, use \[ h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}} \] as a reasonable guess for natural convection from the rod in still room air. This is a planning value, not a measurement. The stationary profile will be used to test the model and determine the fitted decay coefficient \(m\) . Install rod thermistor 1 in the first rod hole and use that hole as the analysis base \(x=0\) . It is neither the physical rod end nor the separate thermistor embedded in the TEC. Its measured signal \(T(0,t)\) is the boundary condition for the rod model. For a steady placement pilot, begin with the TEC set to \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . A lower temperature generally reaches steady state faster but may produce temperature differences that are too small to resolve. A higher temperature improves the spatial signal but increases equilibration time and heat loss. If you change the pilot temperature, use the lowest setpoint that gives a clear profile and never exceed \(55^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . Move the other four thermistors among the available fixed holes and measure the resulting steady temperatures. No advance calculation of the positions is required. Choose locations for which the steady excess temperature drops by at least a factor of \(e\) from rod thermistor 1 to the farthest retained sensor: \[ 0<	heta_5(x_5,\infty) \leq rac{	heta_1(0,\infty)}{e}. \] Plot the pilot values as \(\ln	heta\) versus \(x\) while selecting the holes. The retained points should be spread across the semilog plot rather than clustered near one end. Do not retain a position whose excess temperature is indistinguishable from noise or room drift. Once you have identified useful locations, leave the thermistors in those holes. Measure and record every selected position and its uncertainty. Set the TEC to \(20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and allow the entire rod to equilibrate. Record room temperature and all six thermistor channels. Verify that the rod channels agree within the common-bath acceptance criterion. Before heating, review the prediction record and select a numerical steady-state criterion. A useful starting criterion is \( |dT_i/dt|<0.02^{\circ}\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min} \) at every sensor for a couple of minutes; justify any different criterion. Apply a non-oscillatory TEC step from \(20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) using PI control. Record continuously until the selected steady-state criterion is satisfied. The purpose of retaining this complete time history is to document equilibration and select the stationary interval; a quantitative transient-model fit is not required. Plot all temperatures against the same time axis. Use this plot to justify when the profile became stationary and explain qualitatively why farther sensors respond later and with smaller changes. Save the commanded TEC temperature, measured TEC temperature, and measured rod temperature \(T(0,t)\) . The rod thermistor at \(x=0\) , rather than the TEC command or TEC thermistor, supplies the model boundary condition. C5 Checkoff ¶ At S17, demonstrate: a documented common-bath check and any necessary corrections, documented sensor coordinates and wiring, synchronized multichannel logging, a live six-channel record showing the approach toward a stationary profile, files containing timestamps, units, channel labels, and experimental notes, individual understanding of the measurement chain and one dominant uncertainty. Phase 5: Analyze And Test The Stationary-Fin Models ¶ At the constant \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) TEC setpoint, the final stationary \(T(x)\) profile is the principal physics measurement in Module 7. Analyze the record acquired in Phase 4 and compare it quantitatively with both the finite insulated-tip solution and the semi-infinite exponential approximation. You must perform both fits. Do not assume in advance that the rod is long enough for the semi-infinite approximation; use the fitted curves, residuals, and parameter uncertainties to decide whether ignoring the finite end is adequate over the measured sensor positions. Select the final interval of the Phase 4 record and confirm that it satisfies the stated steady-state criterion. No separate heating run is required. Average each sensor over a justified final interval. Five minutes is a reasonable starting interval after the steady-state criterion has been met. Plot \(	heta\) versus \(x\) with error bars. Fit both the exact finite-length model and the semi-infinite exponential. Plot both sets of residuals and report \(m\) in inverse meters with uncertainty. Calculate the characteristic decay length \(1/m\) in meters. Report how much the fitted \(m\) changes when the finite end is ignored and compare that shift with the fit uncertainty. Discuss sensor-position error, room-temperature drift, imperfect contact, and the measured evidence for the tip boundary condition. Compare the measured profile and residuals with the prediction record. State which assumptions are supported, which model is more adequate, and what discrepancy remains unexplained. Stationary-Fin Analysis Record ¶ Evidence To Save During S16-S17 ¶ Keep the sensor map, common-bath check record, any optional calibration coefficients, geometry, raw baseline, complete synchronized temperature history, commanded and measured TEC temperature, measured rod-base temperature, steady profile, run metadata, and exact acquisition code as each item is produced. Use docs/module_notes/module_07_rod_instrument.md , data/module_07/ , and docs/figures/module_07/ . Never overwrite raw rod data with corrected data. A4 Submission And Rubric ¶ Type: individual, 10 points Due: Wednesday, October 28, at 9:05 AM Moodle file: A4_Lastname.pdf Repository file: docs/assessments/a4_finite_length_biot.md The four required parts are listed in A4: Finite-Rod Model And Validity Checks . Submit all four parts in the single PDF and repository file named above. Put your name, assignment code, date, repository URL, and the exact Git commit hash on the first page. C5: Rod Instrument And Data-Acquisition Chain ¶ Demonstrate C5 during S17 on Wednesday, October 28. The C5 Team Checkoff Moodle receipt is due by 11:55 AM and must cite the pushed acquisition-code and evidence commit. Prepare the C5 oral questions . Formative Stationary-Fin Analysis ¶ There is no separate Moodle paper for this step. Keep the team note at docs/module_notes/module_07_stationary_fin.md and authoritative analysis code under python/analysis/ . The result becomes evidence for C6 and the final presentation. Submit one reproducible analysis containing: the dimensional governing equation and assumptions, the sensor map, common-bath result, and any optional correction, a time-history plot documenting the approach to the selected stationary interval, steady \(	heta(x)\) data, finite and semi-infinite fits, and both residual sets, fitted \(m\) and \(1/m\) with units and uncertainty, the sensor-by-sensor finite-length error and transverse Biot-number check, a short explanation of why this result alone cannot separate k from h . A4 Rubric ¶ Criterion Points Part 1 correctly applies Fourier's law, units, and physical judgment to Problem 1.3 1 Part 2 derives the stationary rod equation and finite insulated-tip solution from the stated laws and boundary conditions 3 Part 3 obtains the semi-infinite limit and correctly evaluates the tip approximation and sensor-by-sensor finite-length errors 3 Part 4 correctly calculates the transverse Biot number, gives a separate radius conclusion, and explains how airflow changes \(h\) and the decay length 2 The individual submission is complete, dimensionally checked, clearly organized, and cites the exact Git checkpoint 1 The instructor will give feedback on the stationary-fin record during the rod work. It is judged by whether the data, both fits, residuals, dimensional parameters, uncertainty, and interpretation are ready to reuse in C6. Instructor Notes ¶ Instructor preparation for the hot-water common-bath check Provide a microwave and microwave-safe glass beakers or flasks for heating water. Thermistors, wires, and electrical hardware must never be placed in the microwave. Prepare eight functioning digital meters with thermocouple probes. Students will use resistance mode to measure the nominal \(100\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) divider resistors and the thermocouple probes to measure the common-bath temperature. Provide 26 AWG paired insulated wire, short 22 AWG solid-wire breadboard pigtails, and suitable heat-shrink tubing for the individual joints. Heat-shrink purchasing note: Koowin \(3/32\) -inch-diameter tubing with a 3:1 shrink ratio has been ordered. Test it on the actual 26 AWG paired wire and solder joints, and update the student specification only after confirming the fit. Fill the 4-liter water dispenser in the laboratory and bring it to the classroom, 401 Abelson, before class. Provide Styrofoam cups for the six-thermistor common bath. The drinking fountain outside the classroom can be used as the drain when the bath water is discarded.
docs.title: Module 7, Part III: Rod Instrument And Stationary Fin

docs.text: This is the experimental part of Module 7. It builds on Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations and Part II: Finite And Infinite Rod Theory .
docs.title: Module 7, Part III: Rod Instrument And Stationary Fin

docs.text: Part III has three priorities, in this order: Build the six-thermistor instrument. This is the primary objective. Establish one TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors as a checked measurement system. Extend the Arduino and Python software so that all six temperatures are acquired, displayed, and recorded together. Use the raw readings by default when the six sensors agree within \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) in a common bath; apply calibration corrections only if that check fails. Understand heat transport along a long, thin cylinder. Develop and understand the one-dimensional heat-transport equation, its boundary conditions, and the finite-length and radial-validity approximations. Measure and test the stationary temperature profile. Measure the steady-state temperature as a function of position along the rod, then fit and compare the finite insulated-tip model and the semi-infinite exponential model using the measured sensor positions and residuals. Part III is where the instrument is completed and used for the principal Module 7 physics measurement. The theory from Parts I and II predicts the stationary profile and provides the two models to test. Class-time priority. Spend no more than one hour of class time beginning the Part I and Part II theory. Finish that work at home and bring questions to class. Use the rest of the laboratory time for Part III: build the six-channel thermistor setup, check all six measurement chains in a common bath, develop and test the Arduino and Python software that displays and records all six temperatures, retain TEC temperature control, and measure the stationary temperature profile for comparison with the finite and semi-infinite models. Fit calibration corrections only if the common-bath check fails. In Modules 1-6, one or two temperatures were enough to describe the TEC process. The aluminum rod cannot be treated as one thermal lump. Its temperature depends on position and time: \[ T=T(x,t). \] In this module you will build and validate the multichannel rod instrument and measure the stationary temperature profile along the rod. Record the complete approach to steady state so that you can verify when the profile has settled and observe qualitatively how a temperature disturbance spreads. The primary physics measurement, however, is the stationary profile and its comparison with the finite-rod and semi-infinite models. The sinusoidal Angstrom experiment begins in Module 8.
docs.title: Purpose

docs.text: The Arduino Uno R3 has six analog input channels, A0 through A5 , feeding one multiplexed 10-bit analog-to-digital converter. Use one channel for the thermistor in the TEC base and the other five channels for five thermistors along the rod. The converter samples the six channels in rapid sequence rather than at exactly the same instant. This delay is negligible on the thermal timescales measured here. The purpose here is to assign each thermistor a permanent channel, check all six measurement chains under a common temperature condition, and establish the sensor map used for the non-oscillatory step response and stationary-fin profile. Module 8 reuses the same validated sensor map for the oscillatory Angstrom experiment. Calibration corrections are optional rather than the default. The rod has more thermistor holes than the five available rod channels, so the five rod thermistors can be distributed among selected holes to obtain a useful range of positions and temperatures. Holes in the first group are nominally spaced at \(1/2\) -inch intervals; holes in the second group are nominally spaced at \(1\) -inch intervals. Treat these as orientation values only; measure and record the actual positions you use. The course rod is 6061-T6 aluminum with a nominal diameter of \(1/2\) inch, or \(12.7\ \mathrm{mm}\) . The analysis base at \(x=0\) is the first thermistor hole in the rod, occupied by rod thermistor 1. It is not the physical end of the rod and it is not the thermistor embedded in the TEC. Measure the positions of the other four rod thermistors relative to this origin. Define the analyzed length \(L\) as the distance from the first thermistor hole to the rod tip. Also record the rod's overall physical length, diameter \(d\) , and their uncertainties. The TEC thermistor monitors the actuator, while the measured temperature of rod thermistor 1 supplies the boundary condition \(T(0,t)\) for the rod model. Use one model-testing cycle throughout Part III: Predict: use the Part I and Part II theory to predict the qualitative transient, the stationary profile, and the importance of the end and radius. Measure: acquire synchronized, checked temperature data with the geometry and settings needed to interpret them. Compare: fit the finite and semi-infinite models and inspect residuals, parameter values, and uncertainties. Judge: state which assumptions the evidence supports and where the model is inadequate.

docs.text: The objectives below are listed in priority order. By the end of Module 7, Part III, you should be able to: Build and demonstrate the six-thermistor instrument: assign permanent channels to the TEC-base thermistor and five rod thermistors, check all six measurement chains in a common bath, apply calibration corrections only if required, and extend the Arduino and Python software to display and record synchronized temperatures with units, timestamps, sensor positions, and experimental metadata. Explain and apply the one-dimensional heat-transport equation for a long, thin cylinder, then use the finite-length solution and transverse Biot number to make separate quantitative decisions about whether the far end and radial temperature variation may be neglected. Measure the stationary temperature profile along the rod, fit finite-length and semi-infinite stationary-fin models, examine their residuals, and interpret the fitted decay coefficient and decay length. Explain what the steady experiment can determine and why it cannot determine the thermal conductivity and side heat-transfer coefficient separately. Use the recorded approach to steady state to justify the selected stationary interval and explain qualitatively why more distant sensors respond later and with smaller temperature changes.
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: Review the foundational vocabulary in Part I and the fin-model vocabulary in Part II . The terms below connect that theory to the experiment and its analysis. Term Meaning Temperature field, \(T(x,t)\) Temperature as a function of both position along the rod and time. Environmental temperature, \(T_\infty\) The temperature of the environment far from the rod. In this experiment, it is the room temperature measured away from the heated apparatus. Excess temperature, \(\theta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty\) Rod temperature measured relative to the environment. Thermal diffusivity, \(\alpha=k/(\rho c)\) The coefficient controlling axial spreading in the Part III model; units m \(^2\) /s. This is Lienhard's notation. Side-loss rate, \(\nu=hP/(\rho cA)\) The fractional rate, in s \(^{-1}\) , at which side convection removes excess thermal energy in the one-dimensional model. Decay coefficient, \(m=\sqrt{hP/(kA)}=\sqrt{\nu/\alpha}\) The spatial decay rate of the stationary profile; \(1/m\) is the decay length. Sensor map A record of each channel name, thermistor position, coordinate origin and direction, and position uncertainty. Common-bath check A comparison under a common temperature condition used to identify sensor offsets or other channel differences. If the full spread of the six readings remains below \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , use the raw readings without calibration corrections. Baseline Measurements made before the imposed temperature change, used to establish room temperature and initial sensor readings. Step response The measured evolution of \(T(x,t)\) after the base-temperature command changes. Boundary condition The measured or prescribed behavior at a boundary. For the rod model, the measured temperature of rod thermistor 1 at the first hole is the boundary condition \(T(0,t)\) ; the TEC setpoint and TEC-thermistor temperature describe the actuator that creates it. Stationary profile The position-dependent temperature after changes with time have become negligible according to a stated criterion. Model fit Estimation of model parameters by comparing a predicted curve with measured data. Residual Measured value minus model prediction at the same position or time. Residual structure can reveal model inadequacy. Uncertainty A quantitative estimate of the plausible range of a measured or fitted result. Metadata Information needed to interpret and reproduce a run, including units, timestamps, channel labels, geometry, settings, and experimental notes.

docs.text: Read selectively in Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook , Section 1.3, pp. 11-26, following the reading guide in Part I. Review Module 7, Part I: Thermal Transport Foundations . For the S16 lecture and S17 guided study, read Lienhard Section 4.5, textbook pp. 163-173. Work through the derivation rather than reading only the final formulas. Use Fin Design: From A Finite Rod To An Infinite Rod as the equation-by-equation guide to Lienhard Eqs. (4.27)-(4.51). Complete A4 , including Lienhard Problems 1.3, 4.12, and 4.20. Problem 1.3 is assigned in Module 7, Part I .

Part II set the energy-storage term to zero to obtain the stationary fin equation. We now restore that term while retaining distributed side cooling, so the model describes both the transient response and the stationary profile that it approaches. Let \[ 	heta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty, \] where \(T_\infty\) is the temperature of the environment far from the rod. For the course experiment, \(T_\infty\) is the room temperature measured away from the heated apparatus. For a uniform rod with cross-sectional area \(A\) , perimeter \(P\) , density \(ho\) , specific heat \(c\) , thermal conductivity \(k\) , and side heat-transfer coefficient \(h\) , conservation of energy gives \[ ho c A rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =kA rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-hP	heta. \] Every term has units of power per unit length, watts per meter. Dividing by \(ho cA\) gives \[  rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =\alpha rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-
u	heta, \qquad \alpha= rac{k}{ho c}, \qquad

For the analyzed section, rod thermistor 1 supplies the measured temperature at the analysis base \(x=0\) , and the tip is treated as insulated.
