docs.title: Model

docs.text: Open the interactive TEC and finite-rod simulator , developed by Tim Hebert, and use a constant setpoint. The simulator numerically evolves the one-dimensional transient conduction equation with side heat loss, a finite rod, and a dynamic TEC boundary. Move the probe along the rod and observe both the approach to steady state and the final spatial profile. Use it to predict which parts of the measured rod should be sensitive to the far-end boundary condition before fitting the experimental data. Suggested high-gain exploration. Place the probe at \(x=0\) , use proportional control only, and compare successively larger values of \(K_p\) , for example 8, 80, and 800. At modest gain, an overshoot can decay. At large gain, the simulator can instead settle into a sustained oscillation while the PWM repeatedly saturates or reverses. This oscillation is produced by the dynamic TEC actuator included in the simulator; it is absent from the ideal one-lump P-control model. Identify approximately where the qualitative change occurs, and compare the oscillation period with the thermal response times visible in the TEC and rod. Then hold \(K_p=800\) fixed and move the probe from \(x=0\) to a few positions farther along the rod, resetting between trials. Observe qualitatively that the oscillation frequency generally increases as the probe is moved closer to the TEC. What physical model is inside this simulator? The rod is divided into finite-difference elements that obey the one-dimensional transient heat equation \[ \rho cA\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} =kA\frac{\partial^2T}{\partial x^2}-hP(T-T_\infty). \] The simulator does not substitute the analytical cosh or exponential solution. It replaces the axial second derivative with centered finite differences on 24-100 rod elements and advances the resulting coupled ordinary differential equations with a 0.01 s numerical substep. The TEC balances and thermistor equation are advanced with the same substep, while the controller updates every 0.1 s. The analytical stationary profiles derived in Part II are therefore predictions that can be compared with the numerical long-time limit, not formulas built into the simulation. The far tip has zero axial heat flux. The driven end is coupled to a dynamic TEC model. It is not an ideal heat source. The model has a cold-side temperature \(T_c\) and hot-side temperature \(T_h\) , with separate heat capacities \(C_c\) and \(C_h\) . A signed duty command \(u\) applies the averaged voltage \(V=uV_s\) to the TEC. The code calculates the signed current from this voltage, the TEC electrical resistance, and the Seebeck back-emf, then limits the current to the allowed range. Using the conventional current \(I_c\) that is positive in the cooling direction, the heat absorbed at the cold side and rejected at the hot side are \[ \dot Q_c =S I_c T_{c,K}-\frac{1}{2}I_c^2R-K_{\mathrm{TEC}}(T_h-T_c), \] \[ \dot Q_h =S I_c T_{h,K}+\frac{1}{2}I_c^2R-K_{\mathrm{TEC}}(T_h-T_c). \] Here \(S\) is the effective Seebeck coefficient, \(R\) is the electrical resistance, \(K_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) is the passive thermal conductance through the TEC, and the temperatures marked \(K\) are absolute temperatures. The terms proportional to \(SI_cT\) describe Peltier transport, the \(I_c^2R/2\) terms split Joule heating between the two faces, and the final terms describe ordinary conduction from the hot face toward the cold face. The two TEC temperatures obey separate energy balances: \[ C_c\frac{dT_c}{dt} =-\dot Q_c+G_c[T(0,t)-T_c]+G_{\mathrm{leak}}(T_\infty-T_c), \] \[ C_h\frac{dT_h}{dt} =\dot Q_h-\frac{T_h-T_\infty}{R_{\mathrm{hs}}}. \] The contact conductance \(G_c=h_{\mathrm{contact}}A\) couples the cold-side plate to the first finite-difference element of the rod. The hot side loses heat to the room through the heat-sink resistance \(R_{\mathrm{hs}}\) , while \(G_{\mathrm{leak}}\) represents an additional cold-side leak to the room. The default parameters approximate a TEC1-12706-type device: \(S=0.0513\) V/K, \(R=1.861\ \Omega\) , \(K_{\mathrm{TEC}}=0.560\) W/K, \(C_c=12\) J/K, \(C_h=180\) J/K, \(R_{\mathrm{hs}}=0.55\) K/W, and a 12 V supply. These values are model parameters, not measurements of the particular classroom TEC. The rod is the distributed thermal load on this two-state actuator. Its first element exchanges heat with \(T_c\) through \(G_c\) ; the remaining elements conduct heat axially and lose heat from their sides. The movable thermistor measures the local rod temperature through a first-order sensor response with a 2 s time constant. The controller samples that measured temperature every 0.1 s and limits the signed PWM command to the range from \(-100\%\) to \(+100\%\) . High-gain P-control exploration. Put the probe at \(x=0\) , turn off I and D, and keep all settings except \(K_p\) fixed. Reset the simulation for each trial. Begin with \(K_p=8\) , then try \(K_p=80\) and \(K_p=800\) , adding intermediate values to locate the transition. For each run, decide whether the response is monotonic, shows damped oscillations, or reaches a sustained oscillation. Record whether the PWM remains proportional or spends most of each cycle at \(+100\%\) and \(-100\%\) , and compare the oscillation period with the visible TEC and rod response times. Next set \(K_p=800\) and move the probe between \(x=0\) and a few downstream positions. Reset at each position and compare only the qualitative oscillation rate. The oscillations are generally faster near the TEC and slower when feedback is based on a more distant temperature. For P control, \[ u_{\mathrm{unsat}}=K_p[T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_s], \qquad u=\operatorname{sat}(u_{\mathrm{unsat}}). \] As \(K_p\rightarrow\infty\) , almost any nonzero error drives the command to one limit or the other. This is the bang-bang limit : full heating for one sign of the error and full cooling for the other. Reversing the command at the setpoint does not reverse the temperature immediately. Energy already stored in the TEC faces and rod keeps the temperature moving, so the system overshoots, reverses, and may form a bounded limit cycle. The phase lag is cumulative. The separate \(C_c\) and \(C_h\) states give the TEC its own two-lump actuator lag. Finite contact conductance, the distributed diffusion modes of the rod, the thermistor response, and digital sampling add further lag. Placing the probe at \(x=0\) removes the additional propagation delay associated with measuring farther down the rod, but it does not remove the TEC dynamics or the rod's distributed thermal load. At sufficiently high loop gain, enough phase lag can make nominally negative feedback reinforce an oscillation at some frequency; PWM saturation then bounds its amplitude. This behavior is absent from the elementary one-lump P-control model, whose single closed-loop mode remains stable for positive parameters. Moving the probe downstream adds thermal-diffusion delay and attenuates the measured oscillation. The controller therefore reacts to an older, weaker indication of what the actuator has done; in this simulator the sustained oscillations generally become slower as the probe moves away from the TEC. The exact distance scaling is not the point here because the TEC, rod, sensor, and saturation dynamics all contribute. The practical control-design lesson is more general: place the feedback sensor close to the actuator when the goal is fast, stable regulation, unless the temperature at a remote location is itself the quantity that must be controlled. The model is intentionally idealized. It does not include every contact, temperature dependence, electronic delay, or three-dimensional heat-flow path in the physical apparatus. When the far end has negligible influence over the measured region, this finite profile approaches the semi-infinite approximation \[ \theta(x)=\theta_0 e^{-mx}. \] The fitted \(m\) quantifies the competition between axial conduction and side loss. It does not determine \(k\) and \(h\) separately. The periodic Angstrom experiment in Module 8, Part I, supplies the second independent measurement.
docs.title: Explore The Finite-Rod Model

docs.text: For the section of rod extending a distance \(L\) from the first thermistor hole to the insulated tip, the exact normalized stationary solution is \[ \Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x) =\frac{\theta(x)}{\theta(0)} =\frac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)}. \] The semi-infinite model is the limiting expression \[ \Theta_\infty(x)=e^{-mx}. \] Calculate the relative error at every sensor position: \[ \epsilon_T(x)= \frac{\left|\Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x)-\Theta_\infty(x)\right|} {\left|\Theta_{\mathrm{finite}}(x)\right|}. \] State an acceptable error before deciding whether the far end may be ignored. A reasonable starting criterion is \(\epsilon_T<5\%\) at every sensor used in the analysis, but record and justify a different threshold if the intended measurement requires one. The product \(mL\) is useful, but the answer also depends on which sensor and which observable you use.
docs.title: Length: Solve It First

docs.text: For a circular rod, \[ \mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}=\frac{h(A/P)}{k}=\frac{hR}{2k}. \] This validity check is performed in two stages. Before the experiment , make a provisional estimate using a literature value or range for the conductivity of 6061-T6 aluminum and the measured rod geometry. For natural convection from the half-inch rod in still room air, use the planning value \[ h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}. \] Treat this as a provisional convection value, not as a measurement of \(h\) . The small-Biot condition \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) means radial conduction is fast enough that a cross section can be represented by one temperature. Before the experiment, estimate \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) using the rod radius and \(h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}\) , together with a justified literature value or range for \(k\) . At this stage, proceed with the one-dimensional model under the provisional assumption that \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) . You cannot yet test that assumption using the measured profile because \(m\) has not yet been measured. After the experiment , return to this question using the fitted stationary profile. This is a measurement-based self-consistency check rather than another estimate of \(h\) . The fitted spatial decay coefficient obeys \[ m^2=\frac{hP}{kA}, \] so \[ \frac{h}{k}=m^2\frac{A}{P}, \qquad \boxed{\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp} =m^2\left(\frac{A}{P}\right)^2}. \] For a circular rod, \(A/P=R/2=d/4\) , and therefore \[ \boxed{\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}=\left(\frac{mR}{2}\right)^2 =\left(\frac{md}{4}\right)^2}. \] Use the following measurement procedure: Calculate \(\theta_i=T_i-T_\infty\) from the stationary temperatures. Fit the finite-length profile first to obtain \(m\) and its uncertainty. This avoids assuming the semi-infinite limit before testing it. Use the measured diameter and the fitted \(m\) to calculate \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) . Propagate the uncertainties in \(m\) and \(d\) . Decide whether \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) adequately supports the assumption of a uniform temperature across each cross section. This final calculation is a self-consistency check , not a logically independent proof: the one-dimensional profile used to fit \(m\) already assumes negligible radial temperature variation. If the fitted value gives \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\ll1\) , the assumption used at the beginning is self-consistent. If it does not, reject the one-dimensional interpretation of the fitted \(m\) ; a model with radial temperature variation would be required. The same fitted \(m\) also completes the length check above. Calculate \(mL\) and evaluate \(\epsilon_T(x_i)\) at every sensor position. If the finite and semi-infinite profiles differ by less than your stated criterion throughout the measured region, the semi-infinite approximation is adequate there. If not, retain the finite-length solution. Thus \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) tests the radial approximation, while \(mL\) and \(\epsilon_T(x_i)\) test whether the far end can be ignored; they are separate conclusions obtained from the same fit.
docs.title: Radius: Check The Transverse Biot Number

docs.text: A4 is a 10-point individual written assignment based on Module 7, Parts I and II. It does not require temperature-profile data from Part III. Use the measured rod geometry and your planned sensor positions, together with a literature range for \(k\) and the provisional value \(h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}}\) given above. These calculations are predictions to record before heating the rod; they are not the final measurement-based validity checks. Submit one PDF organized under the following four headings. Show units and dimensional checks throughout. Part 1. Apply Fourier's law. Complete Lienhard Problem 1.3 as assigned in Part I . Show how Fourier's law produces each result, include units, and identify any physically unreasonable result. Part 2. Build the stationary finite-rod model. Starting from conservation of energy, Fourier's law, and Newton's law of cooling, derive the stationary fin equation with side heat loss. Follow the finite-fin solution in Lienhard Section 4.5, showing the principal steps from the differential equation to the solution. State the two boundary conditions and explain what each means physically. Part 3. Make a provisional finite-length prediction. Complete Lienhard Problem 4.12 to obtain the semi-infinite limit. Use Example 4.8 and Problem 4.20 to quantify the effect of approximating the tip boundary condition. From the provisional value of \(h\) and literature range for \(k\) , calculate a range for \(m\) , then calculate \(mL\) and \(\epsilon_T(x)\) at every planned course-rod sensor position. State whether you expect the course rod to be adequately semi-infinite over the measured region, and state the positions, parameter ranges, and error criterion on which this prediction depends. Part 4. Make a provisional one-dimensional prediction. Calculate a range for \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) using the same provisional value of \(h\) and literature range for \(k\) . State whether you expect each cross section to be represented adequately by one temperature. Do not combine this radius conclusion with the finite-length conclusion from Part 3. Then answer this brief application question: compare the same electronic heat sink in still air and in forced airflow. Which case should have the larger convective coefficient \(h\) , and how should the larger \(h\) change the decay length \(1/m\) ? The submission details and rubric appear near the end of this page.
docs.title: A4: Finite-Rod Model And Validity Checks

docs.text: Before applying heat to the course rod, record the provisional values of \(\mathrm{Bi}_{\perp}\) , \(mL\) , and \(\epsilon_T(x)\) at every sensor. Predict: the order in which the sensors will respond to a base-temperature step, how the response amplitude will change with distance from the base, the qualitative shape of the stationary temperature profile, and whether the measured region should reveal the finite tip. Use the measured rod geometry and the sensor positions you initially plan to use. If the placement pilot leads you to move a sensor, preserve the original prediction and repeat the calculation using the final measured position. Return to these predictions after fitting the stationary data and state which were supported by the evidence.
docs.title: Prediction Record Before Heating

docs.text: Build the complete measurement circuit before modifying the software or preparing the common bath. Prepare six thermistors using 26 AWG paired insulated wire for the sensor leads. Separate the pair near the thermistor and insulate the two solder joints individually so they cannot touch. Use the heat-shrink tubing specified and supplied by the instructor. Slide both pieces onto the wires before soldering, keep the joints compact, and stagger the joints so the finished end is not unnecessarily bulky. At the breadboard end, terminate the flexible 26 AWG pair with short 22 AWG solid-wire pigtails so the connections are reliable in the solderless breadboard. Use a meter to measure the actual resistance of each nominal \(100\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) fixed resistor before it is connected in its voltage divider, and record the measured value with its channel assignment. Follow the established thermistor voltage-divider circuit; do not change the TEC power or safety wiring. Label the TEC-base thermistor TEC and the five rod thermistors T1 through T5 . Use durable, water-resistant labels attached securely to the dry portions of the leads. The labels must survive handling, the common-bath check, installation, and the rest of the semester without falling off or moving to another lead. Assign TEC to A0 and T1 through T5 to A1 through A5 , unless your documented apparatus requires a different assignment. Record every sensor, analog input, divider, and wire color in the sensor map. Check every connection for exposed conductors, loose joints, and accidental shorts before powering the Arduino. Keep the TEC power disabled during the first sensor tests. Photograph the labeled, wired measurement chain before proceeding. From this point onward, keep each physical thermistor paired with its assigned divider, Arduino input, software label, and CSV column.
docs.title: Phase 1: Wire And Label The Six Thermistors

docs.text: Keep the tested Module 6 files unchanged as a working checkpoint. Make new Module 7 copies of both the Arduino sketch and Python GUI, give the copies clear Module 7 filenames, and extend those copies for the rod experiment. For example, use arduino/module_07_rod_controller/module_07_rod_controller.ino and python/module_07_rod_acquisition_gui.py in your repository. The TEC-base thermistor remains the feedback and safety sensor. The five rod thermistors are additional measurement channels; they do not enter the PI-control law. Develop and test the software in the steps below. Keep each step working before asking Copilot to make the next change. Copilot may write code, but you are responsible for checking the pin assignments, serial interface, units, safety behavior, and saved data. Do not begin the hot-water common-bath check until the Arduino and Python software can display and record all six correctly labeled channels.
docs.title: Phase 2: Develop The Six-Channel Display And Recording Software

docs.text: Use all six Uno analog inputs. Unless your documented wiring requires a different assignment, use A0 for the TEC-base thermistor and A1 through A5 for rod thermistors 1 through 5. The Uno has one analog-to-digital converter and selects the six inputs sequentially. Read and average each channel, then send all six temperatures together in one measurement record. The resulting time offsets between channels are negligible compared with the rod's thermal response, but the Arduino time must be measured and transmitted with every record. The revised sketch must: retain the existing PI control, zero-PWM startup, H-bridge pin assignments, temperature limit, and hardware-safety instructions, use the TEC-base thermistor alone for feedback and the software temperature limit, calculate all six temperatures with the same thermistor conversion, label every transmitted field unambiguously, emit exactly one complete measurement record per acquisition cycle, and continue accepting the existing commands from the Python GUI. Use a stable serial record such as DATA,time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety DATA,12.50,23.41,23.38,23.36,23.34,23.31,23.29,120,1,45.00,OK The first line is a header printed once at startup; each later DATA line is one measurement. Status and error messages must not begin with DATA . This distinction lets both Python and the serial microSD logger recognize valid records without confusing them with diagnostic text. Suggested Copilot prompt: six-channel Arduino acquisition Inspect the working Module 6 Arduino TEC-controller sketch that is open in VS Code. First copy it to a new Module 7 sketch named arduino/module_07_rod_controller/module_07_rod_controller.ino. Leave the Module 6 file unchanged and edit only the new Module 7 copy. Preserve its PI control, serial-command parser, H-bridge pins, zero-PWM startup, software temperature limit, and all safety behavior. Use A0 for the TEC-base thermistor and A1-A5 for rod thermistors 1-5. The A0 temperature must remain the only temperature used by the PI controller and software safety limit. Read and average all six analog channels and convert each reading with the sketch's existing thermistor-conversion function. Keep the number of averages as a named constant. Record the Arduino elapsed time after the six measurements have been acquired. At startup, print this header once: DATA,time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety For every acquisition cycle, print exactly one comma-separated line beginning with DATA and containing those fields in that order. Diagnostic, command-ack, and error lines must not begin with DATA. Keep accepting the existing Python commands without changing their format. Comment the new pin definitions, six-channel acquisition loop, and serial-output block for an Arduino beginner. After editing, summarize every function and line of control logic that you preserved unchanged. Before connecting TEC power, test this sketch with Serial Monitor. Warm one thermistor at a time with your fingers and verify that only its named column changes. Confirm that the Arduino starts with PWM zero and still responds to a zero-power command. Close Serial Monitor before opening the Python GUI because only one program can own the serial port at a time.
docs.title: Step 2A: Extend The Arduino Measurement

docs.text: Modify the Module 6 GUI so that it parses the new DATA record and displays six simultaneous temperature traces. Retain the existing setpoint, controller, PWM, and safety displays. Give each trace a stable label and color, make the TEC-base trace visually distinct, and provide checkboxes or a legend that makes crowded plots readable. Every accepted record must be written to a new CSV file with at least these columns: time_s,tec_C,rod1_C,rod2_C,rod3_C,rod4_C,rod5_C,pwm,heat_cool,setpoint_C,safety These are raw measured temperatures. Do not replace them with calibrated values. Reject incomplete or malformed lines without stopping the program, flush saved data regularly, and never silently overwrite an existing run. Suggested Copilot prompt: six-temperature GUI and CSV logger Inspect both the new Module 7 Arduino sketch and my working Module 6 PySide6 and pyqtgraph TEC-control GUI. First copy the Module 6 GUI to a new file named python/module_07_rod_acquisition_gui.py. Leave the Module 6 file unchanged and edit only the new Module 7 copy. Do not create a different controller or change the Arduino command format. Preserve all PI controls, PWM and direction displays, serial command sending, safety display, and zero-output stop behavior. Parse only complete Arduino lines beginning with DATA. The fields are: time_s, tec_C, rod1_C, rod2_C, rod3_C, rod4_C, rod5_C, pwm, heat_cool, setpoint_C, and safety. Ignore headers, acknowledgments, diagnostics, and malformed lines without crashing. Plot TEC and rod1-rod5 temperatures together against Arduino time. Give every trace a fixed label and color and make the TEC trace thicker than the rod traces. Add live numerical displays for all six temperatures. Preserve the existing rolling-window behavior and controls. Write every accepted raw record to a new CSV file with exactly those column names. Do not apply calibration corrections and do not overwrite an existing file; create a timestamped filename or require a new filename. Flush the file regularly so a long run is not lost if the GUI closes unexpectedly. Add a visible count of accepted and rejected serial lines. Keep the code readable for a Python beginner and comment the parser, data storage, CSV writing, and plot updates. At the end, explain how I can verify that every plotted trace is being written to the correct CSV column. Test with TEC power off. Compare several consecutive Arduino DATA records with the corresponding Python numerical display and CSV rows. The field order, values, and units must agree before the program is used for the common-bath check.
docs.title: Step 2B: Extend The Python Display And Raw-Data Record

docs.text: Demonstrate the complete measurement chain before collecting the cooling-bath record: Show that warming one sensor changes only its assigned Arduino and Python channel. Verify that one Arduino DATA line, one set of displayed values, and one saved CSV row agree. Disconnect one rod thermistor temporarily and verify that the fault is visible without defeating the TEC-base safety shutdown. Restart both programs and confirm that PWM begins at zero and that a new data file is created. Record the Arduino-sketch and Python-GUI filenames and their Git commit hash in the sensor map.
docs.title: Step 2C: Integration Check Before The Common-Bath Test

docs.text: Complete these tasks in order. Do not prepare the hot water until Phases 1 and 2 are complete. Confirm that the six thermistors are securely labeled TEC and T1 through T5 , wired to their permanent channels, and documented in the sensor map. Demonstrate that the Arduino and GUI display all six temperatures and save them in six correctly labeled CSV columns. Open the common-bath popup below and perform the check. Display all six temperatures simultaneously and observe them after the mixed bath has settled at several temperatures. At each observation, calculate the full spread \(T_{\max}-T_{\min}\) across the six thermistors. If the spread remains less than \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , record that the sensors passed and apply no calibration corrections or calibration-specific GUI changes. This is the default outcome. If the spread reaches or exceeds \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , continue to the subsequent Record/Pause and fitting steps in the popup. After the common-bath check, record the rod material as 6061-T6 aluminum. Measure its diameter \(d\) , overall physical length, and analysis length \(L\) from the first thermistor hole to the tip. Calculate its cross-sectional area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\) in SI units. Install rod thermistor 1 in the first rod hole and define that hole as the analysis base \(x=0\) . Measure the other four rod-sensor positions and the tip relative to this origin, so that the tip is at (x=L). Estimate the uncertainty of every position and of \(L\) . Save a diagram or photograph showing the permanent sensor labels, Arduino channel assignments, coordinate direction, and measured rod positions. Common-bath procedure and optional relative calibration
docs.title: Phase 3: Common-Bath Check And Sensor Map

docs.text: The rod experiment measures temperature differences and spatial temperature gradients. It does not require an absolute temperature calibration. It does require a common-bath check so that a large channel-to-channel difference is not mistaken for a temperature gradient along the rod. The default is not to fit or apply calibration corrections. If the full spread of all six readings remains below \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) at every retained bath temperature, document that result and use the raw readings. Use the TEC thermistor as the reference and continue to the optional correction steps only if this criterion fails. Step 1. Confirm the Phase 1 prerequisites. Perform the check before installing the thermistors in the apparatus. Confirm that TEC and T1 - T5 retain their secure, water-resistant labels and that only their waterproof sensing ends will be immersed. Step 2. Confirm the Phase 2 prerequisites. Use the permanent voltage dividers, Arduino inputs, acquisition code, and sample rate. Confirm that the GUI displays and records six correctly labeled channels, then warm one sensor at a time to verify its display and CSV column. Step 3. Heat the water. Put water in a glass beaker and warm the beaker in the microwave. Only the beaker and water go into the microwave; never microwave the thermistors, wires, or any electrical hardware. Swirl the beaker carefully after heating so that the water temperature is reasonably uniform. Handle the hot glass and water cautiously. The calibration range should remain below approximately \(60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . Step 4. Prepare the common bath. Pour the warm water from the glass beaker into a stable Styrofoam cup. Place all six waterproof sensing ends close together in the water. Keep labels, electrical joints, connectors, and exposed conductors dry, and do not allow the sensing ends to touch the cup walls or bottom. Place the meter's thermocouple probe near the six sensing ends without allowing it to touch them or the cup. Step 5. Mix and observe. Run the basic six-temperature GUI. Gently swirl the cup or stir the water so that every sensor experiences the same bath temperature. Watch the six live traces and numerical readings. After mixing, allow any motion-induced fluctuations to settle. If one trace remains much noisier than the others, check its connection before using the readings. Step 6. Decide whether calibration is needed. At several bath temperatures spanning the range expected in the rod experiment, mix the water, allow the display to settle, and note the six simultaneous readings and the thermocouple temperature. Calculate \(T_{\max}-T_{\min}\) . If the spread remains less than \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , save a screenshot or short check record, state that no correction is required, and stop here. Do not add Record/Pause code merely for this check. If the spread reaches or exceeds \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) , continue with the remaining steps. Step 7. Only if needed, add Record/Pause. Extend the GUI with a clearly labeled Record/Pause control. Live numerical values and plots must continue updating in both states. In Record , append each accepted DATA record to the calibration CSV. In Pause , append no temperature rows, allowing the bath to be mixed and the readings to settle without adding those transients to the fitting data. Start in Pause, display the current state prominently, flush the file whenever recording is paused, and preserve the continuous Arduino timestamp so that gaps in the saved record are unambiguous. Suggested Copilot prompt: add Record/Pause only after the check fails The six-temperature Arduino acquisition and Python GUI already work. The common-bath check found a spread of at least 1 degree C, so modify the existing Module 7 GUI to support calibration data collection. Do not change the Arduino code, serial format, controller, safety behavior, live numerical displays, or live plots. Add a prominent Record/Pause button that controls only CSV writing. Start in Pause. While paused, continue parsing and plotting all six temperatures but do not append DATA rows. While recording, append every accepted DATA row to the calibration CSV. When recording resumes, continue using Arduino time without resetting it. Show the current state clearly and flush the file whenever the state changes to Pause. Comment the new state variable, button callback, and conditional CSV-writing logic for a Python beginner. Explain how to verify that the display continues in Pause, the CSV row count remains fixed in Pause, and recording resumes without resetting Arduino time. Step 8. Collect quiet fitting intervals. Use the TEC channel as the reference. At several temperatures, keep the GUI paused while mixing the bath and waiting for the displayed readings to settle. Press Record and retain at least 60 seconds of simultaneous data. Record the thermocouple temperature for that interval, then press Pause before stirring again. Repeat the pause-mix-settle-record-pause sequence as the water cools. Step 9. Verify the saved calibration record. Open the calibration CSV and confirm that it contains timestamps and six populated temperature columns with the expected labels. Compare several rows with the GUI and confirm that each recorded interval has a corresponding thermocouple measurement. Step 10. Fit each channel to the reference. Plot each rod-sensor reading, \(T_i\) , against the simultaneous TEC-thermistor reading, \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) . Do the data fall on a straight line? If so, fit \[ T_{\mathrm{TEC}}=a_i+b_iT_i. \] Apply this fitted relation as the correction: \[ T_{i,\mathrm{corrected}}=a_i+b_iT_i. \] Step 11. Check the corrected differences. Plot \[ \Delta T_i =T_{i,\mathrm{corrected}}-T_{\mathrm{TEC}} \] against \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) . Report the mean difference, scatter, and any remaining trend with temperature. Choose and record an acceptance criterion before evaluating the correction. A useful starting criterion is a corrected mean difference smaller than \(0.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) for every channel, with no residual trend larger than \(0.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) across the calibration range. Revise this criterion if the measured noise and resolution justify a different value. Step 12. Preserve the raw readings. Store the correction coefficients separately and apply them during analysis; never overwrite the original data. The thermocouple measurement provides an independent check on the approximate bath temperature and common-bath range. The channel corrections are still obtained by treating the TEC thermistor as the common reference. The corrected channels may therefore share a common absolute bias, but that bias does not affect temperature differences or the measured spatial profile.
docs.title: Common-Bath Check

docs.text: Only if the \(1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) agreement criterion fails, write a separate Python analysis program for the optional correction. It must read the raw CSV rather than modify the acquisition program. For each rod channel, fit \[ T_{\mathrm{TEC}}=a_i+b_iT_i, \] make the comparison and residual plots required above, and save the fitted coefficients and fit-quality measures in a separate calibration file. Keep the raw CSV unchanged. Later analyses may read both files and calculate additional columns named rod1_corrected_C through rod5_corrected_C . Record the calibration-script filename and Git commit hash in the sensor map. Suggested Copilot prompt: relative-calibration analysis Write a separate Python calibration-analysis script for my six-thermistor CSV file. Do not modify or overwrite the raw data. The raw columns are time_s, tec_C, rod1_C, rod2_C, rod3_C, rod4_C, rod5_C, pwm, heat_cool, setpoint_C, and safety. Treat tec_C as the reference. For each rod channel i, perform a linear least-squares fit tec_C = a_i + b_i * rod_i_C over a user-selected calibration time or temperature range. Plot each rod temperature against tec_C with the identity line and fitted line. Then plot the corrected residual (a_i + b_i * rod_i_C) - tec_C against tec_C. Print and save a table containing channel, a_i, b_i, number of fitted points, calibration temperature range, residual mean, residual standard deviation, and maximum absolute residual. Save this table to a separate CSV file. Also write a separate corrected-data CSV that retains every original raw column and adds rod1_corrected_C through rod5_corrected_C. Never replace a raw column. Include clear axis labels with units and comment the file input, range selection, fitting, residual calculation, and output sections for a Python beginner.
docs.title: If Needed, Analyze And Preserve The Correction

docs.text: For the initial Part III prediction, use \[ h=10\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}K^{-1}} \] as a reasonable guess for natural convection from the rod in still room air. This is a planning value, not a measurement. The stationary profile will be used to test the model and determine the fitted decay coefficient \(m\) . Install rod thermistor 1 in the first rod hole and use that hole as the analysis base \(x=0\) . It is neither the physical rod end nor the separate thermistor embedded in the TEC. Its measured signal \(T(0,t)\) is the boundary condition for the rod model. For a steady placement pilot, begin with the TEC set to \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . A lower temperature generally reaches steady state faster but may produce temperature differences that are too small to resolve. A higher temperature improves the spatial signal but increases equilibration time and heat loss. If you change the pilot temperature, use the lowest setpoint that gives a clear profile and never exceed \(55^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . Move the other four thermistors among the available fixed holes and measure the resulting steady temperatures. No advance calculation of the positions is required. Choose locations for which the steady excess temperature drops by at least a factor of \(e\) from rod thermistor 1 to the farthest retained sensor: \[ 0<\theta_5(x_5,\infty) \leq\frac{\theta_1(0,\infty)}{e}. \] Plot the pilot values as \(\ln\theta\) versus \(x\) while selecting the holes. The retained points should be spread across the semilog plot rather than clustered near one end. Do not retain a position whose excess temperature is indistinguishable from noise or room drift. Once you have identified useful locations, leave the thermistors in those holes. Measure and record every selected position and its uncertainty. Set the TEC to \(20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and allow the entire rod to equilibrate. Record room temperature and all six thermistor channels. Verify that the rod channels agree within the common-bath acceptance criterion. Before heating, review the prediction record and select a numerical steady-state criterion. A useful starting criterion is \( |dT_i/dt|<0.02^{\circ}\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{min} \) at every sensor for a couple of minutes; justify any different criterion. Apply a non-oscillatory TEC step from \(20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) using PI control. Record continuously until the selected steady-state criterion is satisfied. The purpose of retaining this complete time history is to document equilibration and select the stationary interval; a quantitative transient-model fit is not required. Plot all temperatures against the same time axis. Use this plot to justify when the profile became stationary and explain qualitatively why farther sensors respond later and with smaller changes. Save the commanded TEC temperature, measured TEC temperature, and measured rod temperature \(T(0,t)\) . The rod thermistor at \(x=0\) , rather than the TEC command or TEC thermistor, supplies the model boundary condition.
docs.title: Phase 4: Configure And Acquire The Stationary Profile

docs.text: At S17, demonstrate: a documented common-bath check and any necessary corrections, documented sensor coordinates and wiring, synchronized multichannel logging, a live six-channel record showing the approach toward a stationary profile, files containing timestamps, units, channel labels, and experimental notes, individual understanding of the measurement chain and one dominant uncertainty.
docs.title: C5 Checkoff

docs.text: At the constant \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) TEC setpoint, the final stationary \(T(x)\) profile is the principal physics measurement in Module 7. Analyze the record acquired in Phase 4 and compare it quantitatively with both the finite insulated-tip solution and the semi-infinite exponential approximation. You must perform both fits. Do not assume in advance that the rod is long enough for the semi-infinite approximation; use the fitted curves, residuals, and parameter uncertainties to decide whether ignoring the finite end is adequate over the measured sensor positions. Select the final interval of the Phase 4 record and confirm that it satisfies the stated steady-state criterion. No separate heating run is required. Average each sensor over a justified final interval. Five minutes is a reasonable starting interval after the steady-state criterion has been met. Plot \(\theta\) versus \(x\) with error bars. Fit both the exact finite-length model and the semi-infinite exponential. Plot both sets of residuals and report \(m\) in inverse meters with uncertainty. Calculate the characteristic decay length \(1/m\) in meters. Report how much the fitted \(m\) changes when the finite end is ignored and compare that shift with the fit uncertainty. Discuss sensor-position error, room-temperature drift, imperfect contact, and the measured evidence for the tip boundary condition. Compare the measured profile and residuals with the prediction record. State which assumptions are supported, which model is more adequate, and what discrepancy remains unexplained.

docs.text:
Module 8, Part I: The Angstrom Method ¶ Module 8 has two linked parts. This page develops and applies the Angstrom method. Continue with Part II: Conductivity, Heat Loss, And Final Synthesis . Purpose ¶ The TEC controller creates a sinusoidal temperature boundary at the base of the aluminum rod. Thermal diffusion causes the oscillation amplitude to decrease and its phase to lag with distance. Measuring both effects allows you to separate axial thermal diffusion from heat loss to the air. The module follows three priorities: obtain a trustworthy six-temperature record, understand the Angstrom method, and compare experiment with theory. The learning objectives state what you must be able to do. The S18 experimental overview previews the measurements and control comparisons so that you can see what the theory must explain. The detailed experimental instructions follow the theory in Stages 1-6 . Schedule And Due Work ¶ Session In class Due S18, Mon. Nov. 2 Three-hour live Angstrom lab: display and record all six thermistors with the Python GUI at two or more frequencies Module 8 home preparation; P3 prediction and pilot-plan check S19, Wed. Nov. 4 Fit the live-run amplitudes and phases; select and test additional frequencies Pilot-analysis and production-run plan check S20, Mon. Nov. 9 Acquire the multi-frequency production record with the Arduino, Python GUI, and laptop connected Data-readiness and production-run check S21, Wed. Nov. 11 Fit spatial decay and phase slopes; infer kappa and nu A5 analysis checkpoint S22, Mon. Nov. 16 Repeat or extend the measurement; test frequency consistency, residuals, and model validity P4 ; formative modeling-app check Outside-Class Workload Budget ¶ Session Work Planned time S18 Read this assignment and review the periodic solution 60 minutes S18 Prepare the pilot-run settings and metadata plan 30 minutes S18 Total associated with S18 1 hour 30 minutes S19 Organize the individual A5 S18 evidence, control analysis, and derivation 120 minutes S19 Inspect pilot fits and prepare the production-run plan 45 minutes S19 Total associated with S19 2 hours 45 minutes S20 Complete the individual A5 control comparison, derivation, and validity plan 120 minutes S20 Prepare production filenames, metadata, and data-readiness checklist 45 minutes S20 Total associated with S20 2 hours 45 minutes S21 Complete the spatial fits, uncertainty, and residual displays 150 minutes S21 Document, commit, and push the formative modeling-app checkpoint 30 minutes S21 Total associated with S21 3 hours S22 Prepare a repeat run or frequency-consistency and model-validity check 60 minutes S22 Total associated with S22 1 hour All required measurements are made while the Arduino is connected to the laptop and the Python GUI is displaying and saving the data. Do not leave the apparatus running outside the scheduled protocol or without completing the safety and data-readiness checks below. Learning Objectives ¶ By the end of this module, you should be able to: Generate and measure the sinusoidally driven TEC temperature: Sinusoidally heat the TEC using raw open-loop PWM, susceptibility-based feedforward, closed-loop P control, and closed-loop PI control; verify the stored file; and preserve sensor positions, units, timestamps, controller settings, and run metadata. Explain how the measured base temperature differs among raw PWM, feedforward, P, and PI control in mean error, amplitude, phase lag, waveform distortion, heating-cooling symmetry, and how those differences change with forcing frequency. Measure all six temperature histories: display and record the TEC and T1 - T5 with the live GUI; Derive and understand the settled-periodic temperature profile: derive the complete Angstrom solution for a finite rod with an insulated tip by separating the stationary mean and oscillatory parts, applying the boundary conditions, and taking the real part of the complex solution. Explain how the finite-rod solution approaches the semi-infinite result. Interpret the solution physically in terms of three spatial length scales: the mean-temperature decay length \(\ell_{\mathrm{mean}}=1/m\) , the oscillation-amplitude decay length \(\ell_{\mathrm{amp}}=1/q\) , and the one-radian phase-shift length \(\ell_{\mathrm{phase}}=1/q'\) . Relate these scales to one another and to the dimensional parameters \(\kappa\) , \(
u\) , and \(\omega\) through \(m^2=
u/\kappa\) , \(m^2=q^2-q'^2\) , and \(2qq'=\omega/\kappa\) ; express their ratios using the dimensionless frequency \(\Omega=\omega/
u\) ; and fit the measurements to obtain \(q\) , \(q'\) , \(\kappa\) , and \(
u\) with units and uncertainty. Generate and interpret a theoretical characteristic-length plot using parameters inferred from your own measurements. Explain which part of \(T(x,t)\) each length controls, distinguish a one-radian phase length from a full spatial wavelength, and use the plot to explain the temperature histories and sensor placement. Compare experiment and theory: use per-sensor fits, spatial trends, residuals, frequency consistency, and the finite-length and transverse-Biot checks from Module 7 to judge the one-dimensional model. Roadmap And Student Work ¶ The module follows one experimental argument. First establish and verify the six-channel measurement so that the primary result is a trustworthy set of temperature histories. Then use the Angstrom method to predict and extract amplitude decay and phase lag. Finally, compare those measurements with the model, infer \(\kappa\) and \(
u\) , and test whether the same theory explains all retained sensors and forcing periods. Before S18: read through the periodic solution, write down your qualitative predictions, and prepare proposed pilot settings and metadata. This is the P3 check. Bring your proposed drive period, starting values of \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) , safety limits, and a prediction for how amplitude and phase will change with distance. This is a planning check, not a separate written submission. In class during S18-S20: use Stages 1-4 for the S18 control comparisons and two-frequency pilot measurement. During S19-S20, use the pilot analysis to improve the settings and acquire the production record in Stage 5. Decide from the live data when each response has settled before changing frequency. After the production run during S21-S22: complete the spatial fits, uncertainty and residual analysis, and model-validity checks. The P4 check is a minimum successful periodic dataset, as defined below, together with sensor positions and units, acquisition metadata, and a rod-base waveform check. This is an in-class data-readiness check, not a separate written submission. State the criterion you used to decide that the response was settled. S18 Experimental Overview ¶ A sinusoidal PWM command does not guarantee a sinusoidal temperature. The raw-PWM, feedforward, P, and PI comparisons reveal what the actuator and controller contribute to the measured boundary waveform. Along the rod, the six-temperature record reveals a second question: why does the oscillation shrink and lag with distance? The Angstrom theory connects these observations to thermal diffusion and heat loss, and gives predictions to test at more than one forcing period. Keep three temperatures distinct: \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) is requested; \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) measures the actuator; and T1 at the first rod hole is the boundary \(T(0,t)\) used in the rod model. The detailed actions begin in Stage 1 . Choose Sensor Positions For The Quantity Being Measured ¶ Module 7 established the geometry and validated six thermistor measurement chains: one thermistor in the TEC base and five thermistors at measured positions along the 6061-T6 aluminum rod. Keep the same coordinate origin at the first rod hole, channel assignments, common-bath result, any optional correction coefficients, measured diameter, and analysis length \(L\) from the first hole to the tip. A sensor may be moved to a different hole, but each measurement configuration must have its own recorded sensor map and position uncertainties. The thermistor embedded in the TEC measures the driven actuator, but it is not the rod boundary at \(x=0\) and is not one of the five rod coordinates. Rod thermistor 1 in the first hole measures \(T(0,t)\) , the boundary condition used in the Angstrom model. You will use the Angstrom measurement to determine thermal conductivity rather than substitute a supplied final value. Literature values of \(k\) may guide planning and model-validity checks. This choice of origin does not change the Angstrom result. Shifting \(x=0\) changes the reference amplitude and phase, but the fitted spatial decay and phase coefficients depend on amplitude ratios, phase differences, and sensor separations. Use the first hole as \(x=0\) consistently in every plot and fit. The mean and oscillatory parts require different sensor-placement strategies. For the course rod, the estimated mean-profile length is relatively long: \(mL\approx1.3\) . The stationary mean excess temperature therefore remains measurable over the full rod. Module 7 already measured this profile using a full-length sensor configuration and compared it with the finite- and infinite-rod models. Do not repeat that measurement in Module 8. Retain the Module 7 sensor map, data, and fitted mean-decay coefficient \(m\) for comparison with the oscillatory results. The oscillatory part decays much faster. Over periods from \(100\) to \(500\) s, the estimate is \(qL\approx6.5\) to \(3.0\) . In the semi-infinite approximation, the oscillation amplitude at the far end would therefore be only \(e^{-qL}\approx0.0015\) to \(0.05\) of its value at the base. A full-length sensor layout would place too many thermistors where the oscillatory signal is very small. For the Module 8 Angstrom measurement, begin with T1 in the first hole and define that position as \(x=0\) . Place T2 - T5 at approximately 1-inch intervals in order of increasing \(x\) . This spacing has produced measurable oscillatory signals in prior trials while still providing enough separation to resolve amplitude decay and phase lag. Measure and record every position, and save this oscillatory-measurement map separately from the full-length mean-profile map retained from Module 7. Treat the 1-inch spacing as a starting point, not a permanent requirement. Collect pilot data at a short and a long usable period before finalizing the layout. If the downstream oscillations are too small to fit, move the sensors closer to the base or closer together. If the amplitudes and phases change too little between neighboring sensors, spread the sensors farther apart. After any repositioning, remeasure every \(x\) coordinate and update the oscillatory sensor map before collecting the production data. In principle, the Angstrom method needs temperatures at only two distinct rod positions. Five simultaneous rod measurements are preferable because they provide multiple amplitude and phase differences in one run, support spatial fits and residual checks, and avoid comparing pairs acquired under different room or boundary conditions. Use the pilot run to confirm that at least three rod sensors retain measurable amplitude and phase at every selected frequency. Before the pilot run, verify that the saved diagram or photograph identifies the TEC-base channel, the five rod channels, the positive \(x\) direction, all five measured rod positions, the analysis length from the first hole to the tip, the overall physical length, and the measured diameter. Periodic Solution ¶ Learning Objective 2 in practice — Derive and understand the settled-periodic temperature profile. As you work through this section, follow the complete finite-rod derivation and connect each equation to the three observable spatial scales: mean-temperature decay, oscillation-amplitude decay, and phase shift. Historical drawing of Angstrom's method for determining thermal conductivity. The course replaces the alternating hot and cold reservoirs with a TEC-controlled sinusoidal boundary temperature. Take a few minutes to look at the 1863 English translation of Angstrom's original work . You are not expected to follow every line. Focus on the apparatus, the recorded observations, and the way the measurements are connected to the theory. Recognize the kinship between Angstrom and ourselves; the scientific process isn't different 165 years later, although the tools have progressed. Start With The Rod Equation ¶ Module 7, Part III introduced this rod model and explained each physical term , including its units and the definitions of the transport coefficients. Use excess temperature \(	heta=T-T_\infty\) and the rod equation \[  rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =\kappa rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-
u	heta. \] Here \(\kappa\) is thermal diffusivity in \(\mathrm{m^2/s}\) and \(
u\) is the lateral heat-loss rate coefficient in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) . Every term has units of K/s. We assume constant material properties, linear heat loss, constant environmental temperature, and a temperature uniform across each cross section. Module 7 denoted thermal diffusivity by \(\alpha\) ; here \(\kappa\equiv\alpha=k/(ho c)\) . The symbol \(T_\infty\) does not mean the temperature at the other end of the universe. It is the temperature of the surrounding room, which we treat as a large thermodynamic reservoir whose temperature is not changed appreciably by the rod. We initially treat the rod as semi-infinite, with \(x\geq0\) . Use the measured temperature T1 at the analysis base as \[ 	heta(0,t)=	heta_b\cos(\omega t), \qquad \omega= rac{2\pi}{	au}, \] where \(	au\) is the period in seconds and \(\omega\) is angular frequency in rad/s. The TEC and its embedded thermistor create and monitor the forcing, but the measured rod temperature at the first hole supplies this boundary condition. We seek the settled periodic response after initial transients decay. If the base oscillates about a mean above room temperature, the full solution also contains a stationary mean profile. By linearity, we can solve for that profile and the oscillating component separately; the derivation below gives the oscillating component. Before continuing, make a qualitative prediction. Sketch temperature versus time at the base and at two increasing distances along the rod. Predict which features remain the same, which change with distance, and what a shorter drive period should do to the attenuation and phase lag. Return to this sketch after the derivation and pilot run. Preview The Six-Sensor Angstrom Experiment ¶ Open the interactive six-sensor Angstrom simulator . This version extends the finite-rod simulator used in Module 7. Select the Angstrom sinusoidal drive and begin with \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)=T_a+T_b\sin(\omega t), \qquad T_a=40^\circ\mathrm{C},\quad T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C},\quad 	au=200\ \mathrm{s}. \] The simulator displays the driven temperature and the live responses at six positions along the finite rod. Compare their amplitudes and phase delays, and then change the forcing period to predict which sensor positions will provide measurable signals in the physical experiment. The simulator labels its six modeled rod positions T0 - T5 ; in the apparatus, the embedded TEC sensor is separate and the five rod sensors are named T1 - T5 . Suggested simulation-only exploration. Use the initial settings above and let the response settle into a repeatable periodic state. This simulated setpoint ranges from \(24^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) ; it is an exploration setting, not permission to exceed the \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) hardware limit. For each modeled position, estimate the time-averaged temperature \(\overline{T}(x)\) , oscillation amplitude \(B(x)\) , and phase lag relative to T0 . Look for four features: The mean excess temperature, \(\overline{T}(x)-T_\infty\) , falls approximately exponentially with position. The oscillation amplitude \(B(x)\) also falls approximately exponentially, but generally with a different decay coefficient. The phase lag increases monotonically downstream: each successive temperature trace reaches corresponding points in its cycle later. Compare the PWM phase with both the requested setpoint and the temperature traces. The PWM should generally lead the measured thermal response because actuator effort precedes the temperature change it produces. Its phase relative to the requested setpoint is not universal: it depends on the controller type and gains, the TEC and rod dynamics, and any saturation. A P-only command is in phase with the instantaneous error; adding the integral term changes the command phase. Measure these phase relationships rather than assuming that PWM always leads the setpoint. Test the two exponential statements by plotting \(\ln[\overline{T}(x)-T_\infty]\) and \(\ln B(x)\) against \(x\) . Compare their slopes, and inspect whether points near the finite tip depart systematically from straight lines. What model is being simulated? This simulator uses the same finite-difference rod and dynamic TEC model as the Module 7 simulator. Its rod elements obey \[  rac{\partial	heta}{\partial t} =\kappa rac{\partial^2	heta}{\partial x^2}-
u	heta, \qquad 	heta=T-T_\infty, \] with a finite, zero-flux far tip. The TEC has separate hot- and cold-side thermal states and includes Peltier transport, Joule heating, internal conduction, rod contact, and heat-sink loss. A PID controller drives bounded heating and cooling PWM so that the T0 sensor follows the requested sinusoidal setpoint. Each of the six displayed thermistors has the same first-order sensor lag. Unlike the semi-infinite analytic solution derived below, the numerical model retains the finite tip and actuator dynamics. It therefore lets you explore where the exponential amplitude and phase relations work well and where the ideal Angstrom assumptions begin to fail. Full Complex-Exponential Derivation ¶ Start From The Space-Time Equation ¶ For excess temperature \(	heta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty\) , the semi-infinite rod obeys \[  oxed{  rac{\partial 	heta(x,t)}{\partial t} =\kappa rac{\partial^2	heta(x,t)}{\partial x^2} -
u	heta(x,t) }, \qquad x\geq 0. \] The periodic boundary conditions are \[ 	heta(0,t)=	heta_b\cos(\omega t), \qquad \lim_{xightarrow\infty}	heta(x,t)=0. \] Guess A Complex Exponential ¶ A complex exponential is useful because differentiation returns a constant times the same function. Guess \[ \widetilde{	heta}(x,t)=	heta_b e^{-sx}e^{i\omega t}. \] The physical temperature is the real part of this expression. Because the equation is linear with real coefficients, the real part of a complex solution also satisfies the equation. Allowing \(s\) to be complex lets us describe both amplitude decay and phase delay along the rod. At \(x=0\) , taking the real part gives the specified cosine boundary condition. The derivatives are \[  rac{\partial\widetilde{	heta}}{\partial t} =i\omega\widetilde{	heta}, \qquad  rac{\partial^2\widetilde{	heta}}{\partial x^2} =s^2\widetilde{	heta}. \] Substitution into the rod equation and cancellation of the common exponential turn the differential equation into algebra: \[ i\omega=\kappa s^2-
u, \qquad  oxed{s^2= rac{
u+i\omega}{\kappa}}. \] The two spatial solutions are \(e^{-sx}\) and \(e^{+sx}\) . Choose the square root with positive real part and discard the growing solution \(e^{+sx}\) , because the temperature oscillation must vanish far from the driven end. Separate Amplitude Decay From Phase Delay ¶ Write \(s=q+iq'\) , with \(q>0\) and \(q'>0\) for positive driving frequency. The prime in \(q'\) is part of its name, not a derivative. Squaring gives \[ s^2=q^2-q'^2+2iqq'. \] Equating real and imaginary parts with \((
u+i\omega)/\kappa\) gives \[  oxed{q^2-q'^2= rac{
u}{\kappa}}, \qquad  oxed{2qq'= rac{\omega}{\kappa}}. \] To find the two coefficients explicitly, use \[ (q^2+q'^2)^2=(q^2-q'^2)^2+(2qq')^2 = rac{
u^2+\omega^2}{\kappa^2}. \] Thus \(q^2+q'^2=\sqrt{
u^2+\omega^2}/\kappa\) . Adding and subtracting the expressions for this sum and for \(q^2-q'^2\) gives the amplitude-decay and phase coefficients, both in inverse meters: \[ q=\sqrt{ rac{
u+\sqrt{
u^2+\omega^2}}{2\kappa}}, \qquad q'=\sqrt{ rac{-
u+\sqrt{
u^2+\omega^2}}{2\kappa}}. \] The frequency of the drive therefore sets two useful spatial scales. The oscillatory decay length \(1/q\) is the distance over which the oscillation amplitude falls by a factor of \(e\) . The spatial wavelength \(2\pi/q'\) is the distance over which the oscillation accumulates a full \(2\pi\) phase lag. For comparison, the stationary temperature profile has decay length \(1/q_1=\sqrt{\kappa/
u}\) . Characteristic lengths calculated for a half-inch-diameter aluminum rod. Longer periods penetrate farther into the rod but produce less phase change per unit length. For the first feedforward trial, use the suggested values \[ T_a=40^\circ\mathrm{C}, \qquad T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C}, \qquad 	au=100\ \mathrm{s}, \qquad \omega= rac{2\pi}{100\ \mathrm{s}} \approx 0.0628\ \mathrm{rad/s}. \] The resulting requested TEC profile is \[  oxed{ T_{\mathrm{set}}(t) =40^\circ\mathrm{C} +16^\circ\mathrm{C}\sin\!\left( rac{2\pi t}{100\ \mathrm{s}}ight) }. \] This has a mean of \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , an amplitude of \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , and a requested range from \(24^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . The \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) measured rod-base safety limit still takes precedence; reduce \(T_a\) or \(T_b\) if necessary to prevent tracking error or overshoot from exceeding that limit. We assume an initial room temperature of approximately \(22^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to simplify the starting protocol, but use the actual room temperature measured in S18.3 for the excess-temperature analysis. The requested TEC temperature is the controller input; the measured temperature T1 at \(x=0\) is the boundary condition used in the Angstrom analysis. Load the measured heating and cooling susceptibility curves. Generating the temperature sinusoid may require PWM of either sign. Your Module 4 measurements showed that equal-magnitude PWM commands do not produce equal temperature responses in the two directions. Let \(\chi_h\) and \(\chi_c\) denote the positive magnitudes of the measured heating and cooling susceptibilities, respectively, and calculate \[  oxed{r= rac{\chi_h}{\chi_c}}. \] A useful starting estimate is \(\chi_c\approx\chi_h/2\) , so \(r\approx2\) : cooling may require approximately twice the PWM magnitude of heating for the same temperature response. Use the ratio measured for your own TEC rather than assuming that it is exactly two. Remember that a sine wave is symmetric about its mean: \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}\!\left(t+ rac{	au}{2}ight)-T_a =-\left[T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)-T_aight]. \] The desired temperature therefore spends equal time above and below \(T_a\) and has equal positive and negative excursions. The required PWM need not have this symmetry because heating and cooling have different gains and dynamics. In an open-loop trial, this difference may appear as unequal heating and cooling slopes, unequal extrema, an offset from the intended mean, or waveform distortion. After completing the two raw-PWM trials, do not mistake a sinusoidal PWM for a feedforward temperature command. Use your measured steady-state susceptibility curve to determine the PWM required at each desired temperature. If the calibration is written as \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}}=f(u), \] construct an interpolation or lookup table for the inverse relation and apply \[ u_{\mathrm{ff}}(t)=f^{-1}\!\left(T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)ight). \] Use the appropriate measured heating or cooling branch when the calibration distinguishes them. This is an open-loop feedforward command: it uses the steady-state \(\chi\) calibration but does not correct the instantaneous temperature error. Predict, at each point in the cycle, which value of \(u\) should produce that temperature. Plot the predicted \(u_{\mathrm{ff}}(t)\) before applying it and explain why the required PWM waveform need not itself be sinusoidal. S18.6: Apply The Feedforward Command ¶ Apply the command from S18.5 with no P or I feedback. Inspect the measured T1 boundary rather than assuming that the requested waveform was produced. Use the pilot decision rules if tracking or safety requires a change, and record the revised settings. S18.7: Repeat With P And PI Control ¶ Repeat the corrected trial with proportional-only control and then with PI control at the same temperature-drive settings. First compare P-only and PI with the same \(K_p\) , changing only \(K_i\) . Then systematically tune \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) to bring the measured TEC amplitude toward \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and the phase shift toward zero while retaining a mean near \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . Test periods of \(100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) with the same requested mean and amplitude. At each new period, first test the previous gains, then record any retuning and its effect. Keep the initial and unsuccessful trials as evidence; do not report only the best run. Record the gains, their units, controller sample interval, measured mean, amplitude ratio, phase shift, RMS tracking error, and saturation for each gain pair tested. Check startup as well as settled behavior against the existing safety limits. A small mean error alone does not demonstrate successful sinusoidal tracking. These three control checks are separate from the two usable periods required for the production rod dataset. The feedback response is slow enough that the controller should not rely on the integral term alone to discover this asymmetry. For proportional-only and PI control, compare \[ u_{\mathrm{P}}=K_p e, \qquad u_{\mathrm{PI}}=K_p e+K_i\int e\,dt, \qquad e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{TEC}}. \] Apply the same measured heating-cooling compensation and safety limits in both feedback modes. For example, the PI command becomes \[ u_{\mathrm{cmd}}=  egin{cases} u_{\mathrm{PI}}, & u_{\mathrm{PI}}\geq0 \quad	ext{(heating)},\[4pt] r\,u_{\mathrm{PI}}, & u_{\mathrm{PI}}<0 \quad	ext{(cooling)}. \end{cases} \] The sign of \(u_{\mathrm{cmd}}\) selects the H-bridge direction, and its magnitude sets the PWM after clamping it to the safe range. This measured, direction-dependent scaling is a static actuator compensation , also called static feedforward compensation. It linearizes the unequal heating and cooling gains by supplying the known extra cooling command immediately; it does not predict the rod's dynamic response. PI feedback corrects the remaining tracking error more completely than P-only feedback. Apply saturation in both feedback modes and anti-windup in PI mode, and never energize both H-bridge direction inputs simultaneously. Stage 4: Pilot Analysis And Experiment Plan ¶ Goal: Use the six histories to choose two usable forcing periods and a sensor layout that resolves amplitude decay and phase lag (Learning Objective 2). Do: Complete S18.9-S18.10 using live observations and time fits. S18.9: Settle, Fit, And Improve The First Pilot Run ¶ Acquire pilot data with the best usable control method from Stage 3. Define numerical tolerances for changes in fitted mean, amplitude, and unwrapped phase between successive complete-cycle windows; use the measured noise and fit uncertainty to justify them. Inspect residuals for drift. Apply this settling test to the rod boundary and retained sensors before selecting a fit interval. Do not declare a response settled merely because five cycles have elapsed. Five cycles are the minimum retained after the team's quantitative settling criterion has been satisfied. The time required to approach a settled periodic response depends on both the amplitude and frequency of the drive. A larger amplitude can lengthen the transient and bring the actuator closer to its limits. At higher frequency the PI controller has less time to follow the changing setpoint, so tracking error, phase lag, attenuation, and waveform distortion generally increase. Use the measured T1 waveform and the settling test above to decide when the response is usable; do not assume that a fixed waiting time works for every choice of \(T_b\) and \(\omega\) . For each sensor, fit \[ T_i(t)=a_i+B_i\cos(\omega t+\phi_i). \] With this convention, a downstream phase lag appears as a smaller unwrapped value of \(\phi_i\) . Therefore a plot of unwrapped phase versus position has slope \(-q'\) . Reversing the sinusoid convention reverses the phase signs but must not change the inferred physics. The experimental example below shows temperatures measured at two rod positions. The traces have the same temporal frequency, while the downstream response has a smaller amplitude and reaches each peak later. Course data acquired with a 100-second forcing period, showing the two observables used by the Angstrom method: amplitude decay and phase lag. Fit each trace independently to obtain \(B_i\) and \(\phi_i\) ; spatial fits of \(\ln B_i\) and unwrapped \(\phi_i\) then determine \(q\) and \(q'\) . Optimize The Waveform From The Pilot Data ¶ The best waveform is the one that produces both measurable attenuation and a resolvable phase lag across several rod sensors while remaining safe and close to sinusoidal. Do not use a forcing period shorter than \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) . A \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) period with \(T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is an intentionally aggressive starting trial and may be difficult for the PI controller to track cleanly. Use the T1 waveform and pilot fits from S18.3-S18.8, not the command alone, to judge whether the boundary is usable. If the specified \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) , \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) temperature waveform is poorly tracked, try a \(200\ \mathrm{s}\) period or reduce \(T_b\) to \(10^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . Retune \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) after changing frequency or amplitude; gains that work for one waveform may not work well for another. Apply these decision rules: For the primary forcing period, aim for the farthest retained sensor to have \(B_{\mathrm{far}}\approx B_1/e\) . A substantially smaller response may be difficult to distinguish from sensor noise; a much larger response means that the sensor array spans less than one amplitude-decay length. Aim for an unwrapped phase lag from the first to the farthest retained sensor of roughly 0.5-2 radians. This is a planning target, not a fit constraint. If distant oscillations are too small, first try a longer period. If all sensors have nearly the same phase, a shorter period may help, but never go below \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) . If the measured waveform clips, flattens, or tracks poorly, reduce \(T_b\) , reduce the mean temperature, or retune the controller before collecting production data. Lower amplitude waveforms are generally easier for the PI controller to generate cleanly, but the temperature oscillation decreases with distance from the TEC. Reducing \(T_b\) can therefore make the response at downstream sensors difficult to distinguish from noise. If the oscillation is clean but too small at every sensor, increase \(T_b\) cautiously. Keep the measured rod-base temperature below \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and retain margin for overshoot. Keep \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) fixed while comparing periods unless the pilot data show that a change is necessary. This makes frequency comparisons easier to interpret. docs.title: Module 8, Part I: The Angstrom Method

docs.text: The TEC controller creates a sinusoidal temperature boundary at the base of the aluminum rod. Thermal diffusion causes the oscillation amplitude to decrease and its phase to lag with distance. Measuring both effects allows you to separate axial thermal diffusion from heat loss to the air. The module follows three priorities: obtain a trustworthy six-temperature record, understand the Angstrom method, and compare experiment with theory. The learning objectives state what you must be able to do. The S18 experimental overview previews the measurements and control comparisons so that you can see what the theory must explain. The detailed experimental instructions follow the theory in Stages 1-6 .
