By the end of this module, you should be able to: Generate and measure the sinusoidally driven TEC temperature: Sinusoidally heat the TEC using raw open-loop PWM, susceptibility-based feedforward, closed-loop P control, and closed-loop PI control; verify the stored file; and preserve sensor positions, units, timestamps, controller settings, and run metadata. Explain how the measured base temperature differs among raw PWM, feedforward, P, and PI control in mean error, amplitude, phase lag, waveform distortion, heating-cooling symmetry, and how those differences change with forcing frequency. Measure all six temperature histories: display and record the TEC and T1 - T5 with the live GUI; Derive and understand the settled-periodic temperature profile: derive the complete Angstrom solution for a finite rod with an insulated tip by separating the stationary mean and oscillatory parts, applying the boundary conditions, and taking the real part of the complex solution. Explain how the finite-rod solution approaches the semi-infinite result. Interpret the solution physically in terms of three spatial length scales: the mean-temperature decay length \(\ell_{\mathrm{mean}}=1/m\) , the oscillation-amplitude decay length \(\ell_{\mathrm{amp}}=1/q\) , and the one-radian phase-shift length \(\ell_{\mathrm{phase}}=1/q'\) . Relate these scales to one another and to the dimensional parameters \(\kappa\) , \(
u\) , and \(\omega\) through \(m^2=
u/\kappa\) , \(m^2=q^2-q'^2\) , and \(2qq'=\omega/\kappa\) ; express their ratios using the dimensionless frequency \(\Omega=\omega/
u\) ; and fit the measurements to obtain \(q\) , \(q'\) , \(\kappa\) , and \(
u\) with units and uncertainty. Generate and interpret a theoretical characteristic-length plot using parameters inferred from your own measurements. Explain which part of \(T(x,t)\) each length controls, distinguish a one-radian phase length from a full spatial wavelength, and use the plot to explain the temperature histories and sensor placement. Compare experiment and theory: use per-sensor fits, spatial trends, residuals, frequency consistency, and the finite-length and transverse-Biot checks from Module 7 to judge the one-dimensional model.
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: The module follows one experimental argument. First establish and verify the six-channel measurement so that the primary result is a trustworthy set of temperature histories. Then use the Angstrom method to predict and extract amplitude decay and phase lag. Finally, compare those measurements with the model, infer \(\kappa\) and \(\nu\) , and test whether the same theory explains all retained sensors and forcing periods. Before S18: read through the periodic solution, write down your qualitative predictions, and prepare proposed pilot settings and metadata. This is the P3 check. Bring your proposed drive period, starting values of \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) , safety limits, and a prediction for how amplitude and phase will change with distance. This is a planning check, not a separate written submission. In class during S18-S20: use Stages 1-4 for the S18 control comparisons and two-frequency pilot measurement. During S19-S20, use the pilot analysis to improve the settings and acquire the production record in Stage 5. Decide from the live data when each response has settled before changing frequency. After the production run during S21-S22: complete the spatial fits, uncertainty and residual analysis, and model-validity checks. The P4 check is a minimum successful periodic dataset, as defined below, together with sensor positions and units, acquisition metadata, and a rod-base waveform check. This is an in-class data-readiness check, not a separate written submission. State the criterion you used to decide that the response was settled.
docs.title: Roadmap And Student Work

docs.text: A sinusoidal PWM command does not guarantee a sinusoidal temperature. The raw-PWM, feedforward, P, and PI comparisons reveal what the actuator and controller contribute to the measured boundary waveform. Along the rod, the six-temperature record reveals a second question: why does the oscillation shrink and lag with distance? The Angstrom theory connects these observations to thermal diffusion and heat loss, and gives predictions to test at more than one forcing period. Keep three temperatures distinct: \(T_{\mathrm{set}}\) is requested; \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) measures the actuator; and T1 at the first rod hole is the boundary \(T(0,t)\) used in the rod model. The detailed actions begin in Stage 1 .
docs.title: S18 Experimental Overview

docs.text: Module 7 established the geometry and validated six thermistor measurement chains: one thermistor in the TEC base and five thermistors at measured positions along the 6061-T6 aluminum rod. Keep the same coordinate origin at the first rod hole, channel assignments, common-bath result, any optional correction coefficients, measured diameter, and analysis length \(L\) from the first hole to the tip. A sensor may be moved to a different hole, but each measurement configuration must have its own recorded sensor map and position uncertainties. The thermistor embedded in the TEC measures the driven actuator, but it is not the rod boundary at \(x=0\) and is not one of the five rod coordinates. Rod thermistor 1 in the first hole measures \(T(0,t)\) , the boundary condition used in the Angstrom model. You will use the Angstrom measurement to determine thermal conductivity rather than substitute a supplied final value. Literature values of \(k\) may guide planning and model-validity checks. This choice of origin does not change the Angstrom result. Shifting \(x=0\) changes the reference amplitude and phase, but the fitted spatial decay and phase coefficients depend on amplitude ratios, phase differences, and sensor separations. Use the first hole as \(x=0\) consistently in every plot and fit. The mean and oscillatory parts require different sensor-placement strategies. For the course rod, the estimated mean-profile length is relatively long: \(mL\approx1.3\) . The stationary mean excess temperature therefore remains measurable over the full rod. Module 7 already measured this profile using a full-length sensor configuration and compared it with the finite- and infinite-rod models. Do not repeat that measurement in Module 8. Retain the Module 7 sensor map, data, and fitted mean-decay coefficient \(m\) for comparison with the oscillatory results. The oscillatory part decays much faster. Over periods from \(100\) to \(500\) s, the estimate is \(qL\approx6.5\) to \(3.0\) . In the semi-infinite approximation, the oscillation amplitude at the far end would therefore be only \(e^{-qL}\approx0.0015\) to \(0.05\) of its value at the base. A full-length sensor layout would place too many thermistors where the oscillatory signal is very small. For the Module 8 Angstrom measurement, begin with T1 in the first hole and define that position as \(x=0\) . Place T2 - T5 at approximately 1-inch intervals in order of increasing \(x\) . This spacing has produced measurable oscillatory signals in prior trials while still providing enough separation to resolve amplitude decay and phase lag. Measure and record every position, and save this oscillatory-measurement map separately from the full-length mean-profile map retained from Module 7. Treat the 1-inch spacing as a starting point, not a permanent requirement. Collect pilot data at a short and a long usable period before finalizing the layout. If the downstream oscillations are too small to fit, move the sensors closer to the base or closer together. If the amplitudes and phases change too little between neighboring sensors, spread the sensors farther apart. After any repositioning, remeasure every \(x\) coordinate and update the oscillatory sensor map before collecting the production data. In principle, the Angstrom method needs temperatures at only two distinct rod positions. Five simultaneous rod measurements are preferable because they provide multiple amplitude and phase differences in one run, support spatial fits and residual checks, and avoid comparing pairs acquired under different room or boundary conditions. Use the pilot run to confirm that at least three rod sensors retain measurable amplitude and phase at every selected frequency. Before the pilot run, verify that the saved diagram or photograph identifies the TEC-base channel, the five rod channels, the positive \(x\) direction, all five measured rod positions, the analysis length from the first hole to the tip, the overall physical length, and the measured diameter.
docs.title: Choose Sensor Positions For The Quantity Being Measured

docs.text: Learning Objective 2 in practice — Derive and understand the settled-periodic temperature profile. As you work through this section, follow the complete finite-rod derivation and connect each equation to the three observable spatial scales: mean-temperature decay, oscillation-amplitude decay, and phase shift. Historical drawing of Angstrom's method for determining thermal conductivity. The course replaces the alternating hot and cold reservoirs with a TEC-controlled sinusoidal boundary temperature. Take a few minutes to look at the 1863 English translation of Angstrom's original work . You are not expected to follow every line. Focus on the apparatus, the recorded observations, and the way the measurements are connected to the theory. Recognize the kinship between Angstrom and ourselves; the scientific process isn't different 165 years later, although the tools have progressed.
docs.title: Periodic Solution

docs.text: Module 7, Part III introduced this rod model and explained each physical term , including its units and the definitions of the transport coefficients. Use excess temperature \(\theta=T-T_\infty\) and the rod equation \[ \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t} =\kappa\frac{\partial^2\theta}{\partial x^2}-\nu\theta. \] Here \(\kappa\) is thermal diffusivity in \(\mathrm{m^2/s}\) and \(\nu\) is the lateral heat-loss rate coefficient in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) . Every term has units of K/s. We assume constant material properties, linear heat loss, constant environmental temperature, and a temperature uniform across each cross section. Module 7 denoted thermal diffusivity by \(\alpha\) ; here \(\kappa\equiv\alpha=k/(\rho c)\) . The symbol \(T_\infty\) does not mean the temperature at the other end of the universe. It is the temperature of the surrounding room, which we treat as a large thermodynamic reservoir whose temperature is not changed appreciably by the rod. We initially treat the rod as semi-infinite, with \(x\geq0\) . Use the measured temperature T1 at the analysis base as \[ \theta(0,t)=\theta_b\cos(\omega t), \qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{\tau}, \] where \(\tau\) is the period in seconds and \(\omega\) is angular frequency in rad/s. The TEC and its embedded thermistor create and monitor the forcing, but the measured rod temperature at the first hole supplies this boundary condition. We seek the settled periodic response after initial transients decay. If the base oscillates about a mean above room temperature, the full solution also contains a stationary mean profile. By linearity, we can solve for that profile and the oscillating component separately; the derivation below gives the oscillating component. Before continuing, make a qualitative prediction. Sketch temperature versus time at the base and at two increasing distances along the rod. Predict which features remain the same, which change with distance, and what a shorter drive period should do to the attenuation and phase lag. Return to this sketch after the derivation and pilot run.
docs.title: Start With The Rod Equation

docs.text: Open the interactive six-sensor Angstrom simulator . This version extends the finite-rod simulator used in Module 7. Select the Angstrom sinusoidal drive and begin with \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)=T_a+T_b\sin(\omega t), \qquad T_a=40^\circ\mathrm{C},\quad T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C},\quad \tau=200\ \mathrm{s}. \] The simulator displays the driven temperature and the live responses at six positions along the finite rod. Compare their amplitudes and phase delays, and then change the forcing period to predict which sensor positions will provide measurable signals in the physical experiment. The simulator labels its six modeled rod positions T0 - T5 ; in the apparatus, the embedded TEC sensor is separate and the five rod sensors are named T1 - T5 . Suggested simulation-only exploration. Use the initial settings above and let the response settle into a repeatable periodic state. This simulated setpoint ranges from \(24^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) ; it is an exploration setting, not permission to exceed the \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) hardware limit. For each modeled position, estimate the time-averaged temperature \(\overline{T}(x)\) , oscillation amplitude \(B(x)\) , and phase lag relative to T0 . Look for four features: The mean excess temperature, \(\overline{T}(x)-T_\infty\) , falls approximately exponentially with position. The oscillation amplitude \(B(x)\) also falls approximately exponentially, but generally with a different decay coefficient. The phase lag increases monotonically downstream: each successive temperature trace reaches corresponding points in its cycle later. Compare the PWM phase with both the requested setpoint and the temperature traces. The PWM should generally lead the measured thermal response because actuator effort precedes the temperature change it produces. Its phase relative to the requested setpoint is not universal: it depends on the controller type and gains, the TEC and rod dynamics, and any saturation. A P-only command is in phase with the instantaneous error; adding the integral term changes the command phase. Measure these phase relationships rather than assuming that PWM always leads the setpoint. Test the two exponential statements by plotting \(\ln[\overline{T}(x)-T_\infty]\) and \(\ln B(x)\) against \(x\) . Compare their slopes, and inspect whether points near the finite tip depart systematically from straight lines. What model is being simulated? This simulator uses the same finite-difference rod and dynamic TEC model as the Module 7 simulator. Its rod elements obey \[ \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t} =\kappa\frac{\partial^2\theta}{\partial x^2}-\nu\theta, \qquad \theta=T-T_\infty, \] with a finite, zero-flux far tip. The TEC has separate hot- and cold-side thermal states and includes Peltier transport, Joule heating, internal conduction, rod contact, and heat-sink loss. A PID controller drives bounded heating and cooling PWM so that the T0 sensor follows the requested sinusoidal setpoint. Each of the six displayed thermistors has the same first-order sensor lag. Unlike the semi-infinite analytic solution derived below, the numerical model retains the finite tip and actuator dynamics. It therefore lets you explore where the exponential amplitude and phase relations work well and where the ideal Angstrom assumptions begin to fail.
docs.title: Preview The Six-Sensor Angstrom Experiment

docs.text: For excess temperature \(\theta(x,t)=T(x,t)-T_\infty\) , the semi-infinite rod obeys \[ \boxed{ \frac{\partial \theta(x,t)}{\partial t} =\kappa\frac{\partial^2\theta(x,t)}{\partial x^2} -\nu\theta(x,t) }, \qquad x\geq 0. \] The periodic boundary conditions are \[ \theta(0,t)=\theta_b\cos(\omega t), \qquad \lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\theta(x,t)=0. \]
docs.title: Start From The Space-Time Equation

docs.text: A complex exponential is useful because differentiation returns a constant times the same function. Guess \[ \widetilde{\theta}(x,t)=\theta_b e^{-sx}e^{i\omega t}. \] The physical temperature is the real part of this expression. Because the equation is linear with real coefficients, the real part of a complex solution also satisfies the equation. Allowing \(s\) to be complex lets us describe both amplitude decay and phase delay along the rod. At \(x=0\) , taking the real part gives the specified cosine boundary condition. The derivatives are \[ \frac{\partial\widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t} =i\omega\widetilde{\theta}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2\widetilde{\theta}}{\partial x^2} =s^2\widetilde{\theta}. \] Substitution into the rod equation and cancellation of the common exponential turn the differential equation into algebra: \[ i\omega=\kappa s^2-\nu, \qquad \boxed{s^2=\frac{\nu+i\omega}{\kappa}}. \] The two spatial solutions are \(e^{-sx}\) and \(e^{+sx}\) . Choose the square root with positive real part and discard the growing solution \(e^{+sx}\) , because the temperature oscillation must vanish far from the driven end.
docs.title: Guess A Complex Exponential
Separate Amplitude Decay From Phase Delay

docs.text: The complex solution can now be written \[ \widetilde{\theta}(x,t)=\theta_b e^{-qx}e^{i(\omega t-q'x)}. \] Taking its real part gives \[ \boxed{\theta(x,t)=\theta_b e^{-qx}\cos(\omega t-q'x)}. \] At every position, temperature oscillates at the imposed frequency. Its amplitude decreases as \(e^{-qx}\) and it lags the base by \(q'x\) radians, corresponding to a time delay \(q'x/\omega\) . This wave-like pattern is a diffusive response, not ordinary wave propagation. Allowing an arbitrary base amplitude \(B_0\) and phase \(\phi_0\) gives the form used to fit the experiment: \[ \theta(x,t)=B_0e^{-qx}\cos(\omega t-q'x+\phi_0). \] For the boundary condition chosen above, \(B_0=\theta_b\) and \(\phi_0=0\) .
docs.title: Take The Real Part
Combine The Mean And Oscillatory Solutions

docs.text:
For a finite rod, let the analysis base be at \(x=0\) and the insulated tip be at \(x=L\) . The boundary conditions are \[ T(0,t)=T_a+T_b\cos(\omega t), \qquad \left. rac{\partial T}{\partial x}ight|_{x=L}=0. \] Step 1: Separate the mean and oscillatory parts. Write \[ T(x,t)=T_\infty+\overline{	heta}(x) +\operatorname{Re}\!\left\{\widetilde{	heta}_{\mathrm{osc}}(x,t)ight\}. \] The stationary part obeys \[  rac{d^2\overline{	heta}}{dx^2}-m^2\overline{	heta}=0, \qquad \overline{	heta}(0)=T_a-T_\infty, \qquad \overline{	heta}'(L)=0. \] Use the finite insulated-tip solution from Module 7 to obtain \[  oxed{ \overline{	heta}(x) =(T_a-T_\infty)  rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)} }. \] Step 2: Solve the oscillatory spatial problem. Use \[ \widetilde{	heta}_{\mathrm{osc}}(x,t)=F(x)e^{i\omega t}. \] Substitution into the rod equation gives \[ F''-s^2F=0, \qquad s^2= rac{
u+i\omega}{\kappa}. \] Apply \[ F(0)=T_b, \qquad F'(L)=0. \] The finite-rod oscillatory solution is \[  oxed{ \widetilde{	heta}_{\mathrm{osc}}(x,t) =T_b  rac{\cosh[s(L-x)]}{\cosh(sL)} e^{i\omega t} }. \] Step 3: Combine the two pieces and take the real part. The complete finite-rod settled-periodic solution is \[  oxed{  egin{aligned} T(x,t)=T_\infty &+(T_a-T_\infty)  rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)} \ &+\operatorname{Re}\!\left\{ T_b rac{\cosh[s(L-x)]}{\cosh(sL)}e^{i\omega t} ight\}. \end{aligned} } \] Define \[  rac{\cosh[s(L-x)]}{\cosh(sL)} =A(x)e^{-i\phi(x)}. \] Here \(A(x)\) is the dimensionless oscillation amplitude relative to the base, so the temperature-oscillation amplitude is \(T_bA(x)\) , and \(\phi(x)\) is the phase lag. With \(s=q+iq'\) , its explicit magnitude is \[ A(x)=\left| rac{\cosh[s(L-x)]}{\cosh(sL)}ight| =\sqrt{ rac{\cosh[2q(L-x)]+\cos[2q'(L-x)]} {\cosh(2qL)+\cos(2q'L)}}. \] In particular, \(A(0)=1\) . Then the same result can be written entirely with real quantities: \[ T(x,t)=T_\infty +(T_a-T_\infty)  rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)} +T_bA(x)\cos[\omega t-\phi(x)]. \] Expanding the complex hyperbolic functions gives an explicit expression for \(T(x,t)\) without the amplitude and phase functions: \[  oxed{  egin{aligned} T(x,t)={}&T_\infty +(T_a-T_\infty) rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)} \[6pt] &+T_b rac{ \cosh[q(2L-x)]\cos(q'x)+\cosh(qx)\cos[q'(2L-x)] }{\cosh(2qL)+\cos(2q'L)}\cos(\omega t) \[6pt] &+T_b rac{ \sinh[q(2L-x)]\sin(q'x)+\sinh(qx)\sin[q'(2L-x)] }{\cosh(2qL)+\cos(2q'L)}\sin(\omega t). \end{aligned} } \] The spatial parameters \(m\) , \(q\) , and \(q'\) are defined above by \(m^2=
u/\kappa\) , \(q^2-q'^2=
u/\kappa\) , and \(2qq'=\omega/\kappa\) , with \(q,q'>0\) . Checks for you to complete: Check 1. Set \(x=0\) and verify that the solution gives \(T(0,t)=T_a+T_b\cos(\omega t)\) . Check 2. Differentiate with respect to \(x\) and verify that both contributions have zero slope at \(x=L\) . Check 3. Show that when \(mL\gg1\) and \(qL\gg1\) , \[  rac{\cosh[m(L-x)]}{\cosh(mL)}ightarrow e^{-mx}, \qquad  rac{\cosh[s(L-x)]}{\cosh(sL)}ightarrow e^{-sx}. \] Thus the finite solution reduces to the semi-infinite solution above. Check 4. Explain why data near the tip are the most sensitive to the difference between the finite and semi-infinite models.
docs.title: Guided Student Solution: The Finite Insulated-Tip Rod

docs.text:
For two sensors separated by \(\Delta x=x_2-x_1>0\) , let their oscillation amplitudes be \(B_1>B_2\) , and let the downstream sensor lag by \(\Delta\phi=\phi_1-\phi_2>0\) radians after phase unwrapping. Then \[ q= rac{\ln(B_1/B_2)}{\Delta x}, \qquad q'= rac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta x}. \] With several sensors, fit the slopes of log amplitude and unwrapped phase versus position. Rearranging the real- and imaginary-part equations gives the useful inverse relations: \[ \kappa= rac{\omega}{2qq'}, \qquad 
u=\kappa(q^2-q'^2). \] This is an important experimental advantage of the Angstrom method. Thermal conductivity follows directly from the product of the measured amplitude-decay and phase slopes: \[  oxed{k=ho c\kappa =ho c rac{\omega}{2qq'}}. \] Determining \(k\) therefore does not require an independent measurement of the convective coefficient \(h\) or the total heat lost from the rod. Such a measurement would be difficult because convection depends on airflow, orientation, surface condition, and temperature. Instead, the amplitude and phase measurements contain enough independent information to separate axial diffusion from convective side loss. Numerical sanity check For example, suppose a 100-second run gives \(\omega=0.0628\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) , \(q=25\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\) , and \(q'=18\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\) . Then \[ \kappa= rac{0.0628}{2(25)(18)} =6.98	imes10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}, \] and \[ 
u=\kappa(25^2-18^2) =2.10	imes10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}. \] Use this only as a unit and order-of-magnitude check; it is not a supplied result for the course rod. The second inverse relation separately gives the side-loss rate \(
u\) , from which the convective coefficient \(h\) can also be inferred. Here \(ho\) is density in \(\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) and \(c\) is specific heat capacity in \(\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\) , so \(k\) has units \(\mathrm{W/(m\,K)}\) . As a check, with no lateral loss, \(
u=0\) , so \[ q=q'=\sqrt{ rac{\omega}{2\kappa}}. \] Positive lateral heat loss makes \(q>q'\) . Therefore a fitted result with \(q\leq q'\) , a negative \(
u\) , or strongly frequency-dependent \(\kappa\) is evidence to investigate the data, uncertainty, settling criterion, or model assumptions rather than a number to repair silently. A shorter driving period produces stronger attenuation and phase change per unit distance. These expressions describe the settled periodic response; they do not include startup transients. A finite rod generally requires both spatial exponentials to satisfy its far-end boundary condition. These equations use a one-dimensional, semi-infinite rod. Before selecting sensors for the fit, carry forward the finite-length error and transverse-Biot checks from Module 7. State which sensors and conditions satisfy your chosen approximation tolerances, and then use the measured residuals and frequency-consistency test to determine whether those approximations were adequate in practice.
docs.title: Recover Diffusivity And Heat Loss From Measurements

docs.text: Symbol or channel Meaning \(T_\infty\) Measured room temperature, treated as the surrounding thermal reservoir \(T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)\) Requested temperature waveform; distinct from both measured temperatures below \(T_a\) Requested mean TEC setpoint temperature \(T_b\) Requested TEC setpoint amplitude \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}\) or TEC Temperature measured by the thermistor embedded in the TEC base \(T(0,t)\) or T1 Temperature at the first rod hole, which defines the analysis boundary \(x=0\) T2 - T5 Temperatures at the four downstream rod sensors \(a_i\) Mean temperature obtained by fitting rod sensor \(i\) \(B_i\) Oscillation amplitude obtained by fitting rod sensor \(i\) \(\phi_i\) Unwrapped phase obtained by fitting rod sensor \(i\) \(\tau\) , \(\omega=2\pi/\tau\) Forcing period and angular frequency \(q\) Spatial amplitude-decay coefficient obtained from \(\ln B_i\) versus \(x_i\) \(q'\) Spatial phase coefficient obtained from unwrapped \(\phi_i\) versus \(x_i\) \(\kappa\) Thermal diffusivity inferred from \(q\) , \(q'\) , and \(\omega\) \(\nu\) Convective side-loss rate inferred from \(q\) , \(q'\) , and \(\omega\) \(r=\chi_{\mathrm{heat}}/\chi_{\mathrm{cool}}\) Measured heating-to-cooling response ratio used in the feedforward compensation In this module, \(\tau\) denotes the forcing period . It is not the thermal relaxation time denoted by \(\tau\) in Module 6.
docs.title: Experimental Notation

docs.text: S18 control objective: Find operating conditions and controller gains that make the measured TEC temperature follow \[ T_{\mathrm{TEC}}(t)\approx T_{\mathrm{set}}(t) =40^\circ\mathrm{C}+16^\circ\mathrm{C}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right) \] using forcing periods of \(100\) , \(200\) , \(300\) , \(400\) , or \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) . Test \(100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) : seek a measured mean of \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , a fixed measured amplitude of \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , and a phase shift relative to the setpoint as close to zero as possible. A sinusoidal command alone does not establish that the measured temperature meets this goal. Use the open-loop and P-only trials to identify why they fall short of this tracking objective under the tested conditions. Then tune PI control: enabling integral action is not enough, and gains that work at one period may need adjustment at another. Demonstrate what worked with measured amplitude, phase, mean error, and waveform quality, and explain why. Distinguish the measured TEC temperature from the rod-boundary temperature T1 ; continue to use T1 for the Angstrom analysis. The existing temperature limits remain in force; if they prevent the full target from being achieved, document the limitation and any reduced-amplitude trial rather than claiming that it meets the target. Work through S18.1-S18.10 in order in Stages 1-4 . Stages 5-6 use the pilot results to acquire the production record and compare it with theory. Maintain an S18 evidence table with one row for each action: cite the saved file, figure, code checkpoint, measurement, or written observation; record the principal result; and describe any departure from the procedure. This table becomes the first part of A5. A checked box by itself is not evidence. Required experimental core: the raw-PWM and feedforward/P/PI comparisons, followed by two usable forcing periods with at least five complete settled cycles at each and measurable amplitude and phase at three or more rod sensors. Extensions: additional frequencies up to roughly five, an automated frequency schedule, and the optional global fit in Stage 6. Secure the required dataset first.
docs.title: Experimental Stages

docs.text: Goal: Verify the measurement and recording system before energizing the TEC. Do: Complete S18.1-S18.2 with the TEC output off.
docs.title: Stage 1: Prepare The Six-Channel Measurement And Live Record

docs.text: Verify the TEC and T1 - T5 channel labels, units, common-bath result, optional correction coefficients, measured sensor positions, and safety limits. Begin with T1 in the first rod hole at \(x=0\) and T2 - T5 at approximately 1-inch intervals in order of increasing distance. Use the sensor-placement reasoning above to document the initial map and later pilot-based changes. For every trial, keep the measured rod-base temperature at or below \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , retain margin for overshoot, and use no forcing period shorter than \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) . Preserve the existing safety limits and physical thermal cutoff. Stop the run if a safety limit or the cutoff is reached.
docs.title: S18.1: Verify The Measurement And Safety Limits

docs.text: Connect the Arduino to the laptop and start the Python GUI. Verify the live display and timestamped local file against the requirements below before proceeding. Revise the Arduino sketch and Python GUI so that one serial record contains, at minimum, time_ms,run_state,control_mode,step,Ta_C,Tb_C,period_s,setpoint_C,feedforward_pwm,TEC_C,T1_C,T2_C,T3_C,T4_C,T5_C,controller_pwm,heating_to_cooling_ratio,signed_pwm The GUI must display the TEC thermistor and all five rod thermistors live, display the requested setpoint, control mode, and PWM output, and save a local copy of every complete record it receives. Fields that do not apply in the selected control mode must have a documented placeholder rather than changing the record structure. The Arduino must use one documented Serial.print() record format throughout the experiment. Preserve every startup transient, control-mode change, frequency transition, and safety event in the same documented record. Do not replace raw data with a cleaned file. The step field identifies the active run segment even when frequency changes are selected manually. Suggested Copilot prompts for the Arduino sketch and Python GUI For the existing tested Arduino sketch: Extend this sketch without removing its working PI control or safety limits. Add two diagnostic raw-PWM modes: u = ub*sin(omega*t) , which alternates between positive and negative PWM about room temperature, and u = ua + ub*sin(omega*t) , constrained by ua > ub > 0 , which remains on the heating branch with a mean TEC temperature near 40 C. Do not apply the heating-cooling compensation in either diagnostic mode. Also add selectable susceptibility-based feedforward, proportional-only, and PI modes for the corrected comparison. Derive feedforward PWM from an interpolation or lookup table of the measured steady-state susceptibility curve rather than assuming that PWM itself should be sinusoidal. Print one documented CSV record containing elapsed milliseconds, operating state, control mode, run segment, requested sinusoid parameters, setpoint, feedforward command, TEC temperature, five rod temperatures, raw controller command, cooling compensation ratio, and applied signed PWM. Compute the selected signed P or PI command, multiply negative commands by the measured ratio \(r=\chi_h/\chi_c\) , and then apply PWM saturation, direction selection, safety limits, and anti-windup. Never energize both H-bridge directions. Use one documented Serial record format for the live GUI. For the existing tested Python GUI: Extend this GUI without removing its current controls. Parse and validate the new CSV record, display the TEC and five rod thermistors live on a common time axis, display control mode, setpoint, and PWM, report malformed or missing records, and save every unmodified valid record to a timestamped local CSV file. Stop when: All six channels update plausibly, the saved file contains the documented complete records, and the controls and safety limits are ready. Save: The sensor map and calibration record, acquisition code checkpoint, sample raw file, and evidence for S18.1-S18.2.
docs.title: S18.2: Verify The Live Display And Saved Record

docs.text: Goal: Observe how the actuator responds before compensating its unequal heating and cooling response. Do: Complete the two raw-PWM trials below while displaying and saving all six temperatures. Begin with a \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) period and retain the safety limits established in Stage 1.
docs.title: Stage 2: Explore Uncompensated Sinusoidal PWM

docs.text: Before asking the TEC to track a temperature setpoint, drive it with the signed PWM command in Arduino counts: \[ \boxed{u(t)=u_a+u_b\sin(\omega t)}, \qquad -255\leq u(t)\leq255. \] The sign selects heating or cooling; \(|u|\) gives the PWM magnitude from 0 to 255. Measure and record room temperature and verify the signed-PWM convention. Use \(u_a=0\) and keep \(u_b=100\) PWM counts fixed for all three forcing periods: \(100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) . Begin with the \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) period. Changing only the period lets you observe its effect on temperature amplitude and phase lag. One could estimate the time varying temperature using the Module 6 one-lump model with its simulation defaults: room temperature \(22^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , heating susceptibility \(\chi_h=0.46\ ^\circ\mathrm{C/PWM}\) , cooling susceptibility \(\chi_c=0.23\ ^\circ\mathrm{C/PWM}\) , and thermal relaxation time \(\tau_{\mathrm{th}}=80\ \mathrm{s}\) . Integrating \(\tau_{\mathrm{th}}\dot T=T_{\mathrm{room}}+\chi(u)u-T\) , with the appropriate heating or cooling branch, gives the model response. But before we solve the case with different heating and cooling susceptibilities we first solve the case with equal heating and cooling susceptibility magnitudes, as derived below. A single sinusoidal particular solution applies to that case; it does not give the full response when the two susceptibility magnitudes differ. Here \(\tau_{\mathrm{th}}\) is the thermal relaxation time, not the forcing period. Use your measured Module 6 parameters to refine this estimate if they differ from the defaults; the attached rod can also change the response. Start near room temperature and apply \(u(t)=100\sin(\omega t)\) , which varies between \(-100\) and \(+100\) PWM counts. Allow the response to settle at each forcing period, keeping \(u_b=100\) fixed, and record the measured temperature peak. Keep the Stage 1 safety limits active throughout the trial. How do you expect the temperature to respond? Does it meet your expectations? Explain what you observe. This is a deliberately uncompensated experiment. A symmetric PWM command does not imply a symmetric temperature response when heating and cooling have different susceptibilities. Plot the measured TEC temperature against \(u(t)\) and identify unequal excursions, slopes, phase lag, and distortion. Collect data for 3 periods; 100 sec, 200 sec and 500 sec.
docs.title: S18.3: Apply Zero-Centered Sinusoidal PWM

docs.text: First assume \(\chi_h=\chi_c=\chi>0\) . Since \(u\) is signed, the same positive \(\chi\) multiplies \(u\) on both branches: positive PWM heats and negative PWM cools. Equivalently, susceptibilities written as \(+\chi\) and \(-\chi\) would multiply the unsigned magnitude \(|u|\) . Set \(\theta(t)=T(t)-T_{\mathrm{room}}\) and \(u_a=0\) . For \(u(t)=u_b\sin(\omega t)\) , the one-lump equation becomes \[ \tau_{\mathrm{th}}\dot\theta+\theta =\chi u_b\sin(\omega t). \tag{S18.3.1} \] Try the particular solution \[ \theta_p(t)=a\sin(\omega t)+b\cos(\omega t). \] Substitution and matching the sine and cosine coefficients gives \[ a-\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}}b=\chi u_b, \qquad b+\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}}a=0. \] Therefore, \[ a=\frac{\chi u_b}{1+(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}})^2}, \qquad b=-\frac{\chi u_b\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}}} {1+(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}})^2}. \] Here \(T(t)\) is the predicted actual temperature of the TEC's controlled face, represented by the single temperature in the one-lump model, when the applied PWM command is \(u(t)=u_b\sin(\omega t)\) . It assumes equal heating and cooling susceptibilities and includes room temperature, the driven temperature oscillation, and a decaying startup transient. Compare this prediction with your measured TEC temperature. It is not a desired temperature setpoint or the temperature along the attached rod. Adding the homogeneous solution gives the complete temperature history: \[ \boxed{ T(t)=T_{\mathrm{room}} +\frac{\chi u_b}{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}})^2}} \sin(\omega t-\delta) +C e^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{th}}} }, \qquad \delta=\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}}). \] The initial temperature determines \(C\) . If \(T(0)=T_{\mathrm{room}}\) , then \[ C=\frac{\chi u_b\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}}} {1+(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}})^2}. \] After the exponential transient decays, the temperature oscillates about room temperature with amplitude \(T_{\mathrm{amp}}\) and phase lag \(\delta\) relative to the PWM: \[ \boxed{T_{\mathrm{amp}}= \frac{\chi u_b}{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau_{\mathrm{th}})^2}}}, \qquad \Delta t_{\mathrm{lag}}=\frac{\delta}{\omega}. \] The thermal response attenuates the oscillation and delays it. Setting \(u_b=1\) gives the solution for \(u(t)=\sin(\omega t)\) . A sinusoidal guess alone describes the settled response; the exponential term is needed to satisfy the initial condition.
docs.title: Derive The Response For Equal Heating And Cooling Susceptibilities

docs.text: Substitute the complete solution, with \(\theta=T-T_{\mathrm{room}}\) , into the differential equation Eq. (S18.3.1) and verify the initial condition \(T(0)=T_{\mathrm{room}}\) . For forcing periods \(\tau=100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) , use \(\omega=2\pi/\tau\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{th}}=80\ \mathrm{s}\) . Calculate the normalized amplitude \(T_{\mathrm{amp}}/(\chi u_b)\) , phase lag \(\delta\) in radians, and time lag \(\delta/\omega\) . Keep the same \(\chi\) and use \(u_b=100\) PWM counts for all three model calculations. Numerically integrate Eq. (S18.3.1) from room temperature and overlay the analytical solution for each period, showing both the startup transient and the settled oscillation. Compare these predictions with your raw-PWM measurements at 100, 200, and 500 s. Report the mean temperature, oscillation amplitude, and phase lag relative to the applied PWM, with \(u_b=100\) PWM counts fixed in all three runs. Explain how amplitude and phase lag change with period, and which departures from the equal-susceptibility prediction could arise from the actual unequal heating and cooling responses. How well does open-loop uncompensated sinusoidal PWM produce a sinusoidally varying TEC temperature with a constant oscillation amplitude independent of driving frequency ? Keep \(u_b=100\) PWM counts fixed and assess the settled temperature waveform at periods of 100, 200, and 500 s. Use your theoretical predictions, measured amplitudes, and sinusoidal-fit residuals to distinguish how nearly sinusoidal each waveform is from how nearly its amplitude remains the same across frequencies. Explain whether a constant PWM amplitude is sufficient to produce a constant temperature amplitude, and why.
docs.title: Check The Derivation At 100, 200, And 500 Seconds

docs.text: Next choose \(u_a>u_b>0\) , so that \[ u_{\min}=u_a-u_b>0. \] Adjust \(u_a\) until the mean TEC temperature is approximately \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) while retaining a safe oscillation amplitude. The PWM now remains on the positive heating branch throughout the cycle. Compare this response with the zero-centered trial. Separating these cases lets you decide which asymmetry comes from reversing the TEC current and which discrepancies remain even when the actuator stays in one direction. These raw-PWM trials are diagnostic open-loop experiments, not yet feedforward temperature control. They establish what the uncorrected actuator does before the measured susceptibility is used to construct a command. Stop when: The two trials show how polarity reversal changes the mean, amplitude, phase, symmetry, and distortion of the TEC response. Save: The raw records, \(u_a\) , \(u_b\) , period, room temperature, PWM-temperature plots, predictions, and observations for S18.3-S18.4.
docs.title: S18.4: Apply Positive-Only Sinusoidal PWM

docs.text: Goal: Make the measured TEC temperature track the requested \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) mean and fixed \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) amplitude with minimal phase shift at periods of \(100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) . Compare open-loop feedforward, P-only, and tuned PI control, and evaluate the resulting measured rod boundary. Do: Complete S18.5-S18.8, keeping the requested temperature-drive settings fixed for the three-method comparison.
docs.title: Stage 3: Establish And Compare Feedforward, P, And PI Control

docs.text: Specify the requested sinusoidal temperature setpoint \[ \boxed{T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)=T_a+T_b\sin(\omega t)}, \qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{\tau}. \] Here \(T_a\) is the mean TEC setpoint, \(T_b\) is its oscillation amplitude, \(\tau\) is the forcing period, and \(\omega\) is the angular frequency. For the first feedforward trial, use the suggested values \[ T_a=40^\circ\mathrm{C}, \qquad T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C}, \qquad \tau=100\ \mathrm{s}, \qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{100\ \mathrm{s}} \approx 0.0628\ \mathrm{rad/s}. \] The resulting requested TEC profile is \[ \boxed{ T_{\mathrm{set}}(t) =40^\circ\mathrm{C} +16^\circ\mathrm{C}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{100\ \mathrm{s}}\right) }. \] This has a mean of \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , an amplitude of \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , and a requested range from \(24^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . The \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) measured rod-base safety limit still takes precedence; reduce \(T_a\) or \(T_b\) if necessary to prevent tracking error or overshoot from exceeding that limit. We assume an initial room temperature of approximately \(22^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to simplify the starting protocol, but use the actual room temperature measured in S18.3 for the excess-temperature analysis. The requested TEC temperature is the controller input; the measured temperature T1 at \(x=0\) is the boundary condition used in the Angstrom analysis. Load the measured heating and cooling susceptibility curves. Generating the temperature sinusoid may require PWM of either sign. Your Module 4 measurements showed that equal-magnitude PWM commands do not produce equal temperature responses in the two directions. Let \(\chi_h\) and \(\chi_c\) denote the positive magnitudes of the measured heating and cooling susceptibilities, respectively, and calculate \[ \boxed{r=\frac{\chi_h}{\chi_c}}. \] A useful starting estimate is \(\chi_c\approx\chi_h/2\) , so \(r\approx2\) : cooling may require approximately twice the PWM magnitude of heating for the same temperature response. Use the ratio measured for your own TEC rather than assuming that it is exactly two. Remember that a sine wave is symmetric about its mean: \[ T_{\mathrm{set}}\!\left(t+\frac{\tau}{2}\right)-T_a =-\left[T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)-T_a\right]. \] The desired temperature therefore spends equal time above and below \(T_a\) and has equal positive and negative excursions. The required PWM need not have this symmetry because heating and cooling have different gains and dynamics. In an open-loop trial, this difference may appear as unequal heating and cooling slopes, unequal extrema, an offset from the intended mean, or waveform distortion. After completing the two raw-PWM trials, do not mistake a sinusoidal PWM for a feedforward temperature command. Use your measured steady-state susceptibility curve to determine the PWM required at each desired temperature. If the calibration is written as \[ T_{\mathrm{ss}}=f(u), \] construct an interpolation or lookup table for the inverse relation and apply \[ u_{\mathrm{ff}}(t)=f^{-1}\!\left(T_{\mathrm{set}}(t)\right). \] Use the appropriate measured heating or cooling branch when the calibration distinguishes them. This is an open-loop feedforward command: it uses the steady-state \(\chi\) calibration but does not correct the instantaneous temperature error. Predict, at each point in the cycle, which value of \(u\) should produce that temperature. Plot the predicted \(u_{\mathrm{ff}}(t)\) before applying it and explain why the required PWM waveform need not itself be sinusoidal.
docs.title: S18.5: Specify The Setpoint And Construct Feedforward

docs.text: Apply the command from S18.5 with no P or I feedback. Inspect the measured T1 boundary rather than assuming that the requested waveform was produced. Use the pilot decision rules if tracking or safety requires a change, and record the revised settings.
docs.title: S18.6: Apply The Feedforward Command

docs.text: Repeat the corrected trial with proportional-only control and then with PI control at the same temperature-drive settings. First compare P-only and PI with the same \(K_p\) , changing only \(K_i\) . Then systematically tune \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) to bring the measured TEC amplitude toward \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and the phase shift toward zero while retaining a mean near \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . Test periods of \(100\) , \(200\) , and \(500\ \mathrm{s}\) with the same requested mean and amplitude. At each new period, first test the previous gains, then record any retuning and its effect. Keep the initial and unsuccessful trials as evidence; do not report only the best run. Record the gains, their units, controller sample interval, measured mean, amplitude ratio, phase shift, RMS tracking error, and saturation for each gain pair tested. Check startup as well as settled behavior against the existing safety limits. A small mean error alone does not demonstrate successful sinusoidal tracking. These three control checks are separate from the two usable periods required for the production rod dataset. The feedback response is slow enough that the controller should not rely on the integral term alone to discover this asymmetry. For proportional-only and PI control, compare \[ u_{\mathrm{P}}=K_p e, \qquad u_{\mathrm{PI}}=K_p e+K_i\int e\,dt, \qquad e=T_{\mathrm{set}}-T_{\mathrm{TEC}}. \] Apply the same measured heating-cooling compensation and safety limits in both feedback modes. For example, the PI command becomes \[ u_{\mathrm{cmd}}= \begin{cases} u_{\mathrm{PI}}, & u_{\mathrm{PI}}\geq0 \quad\text{(heating)},\\[4pt] r\,u_{\mathrm{PI}}, & u_{\mathrm{PI}}<0 \quad\text{(cooling)}. \end{cases} \] The sign of \(u_{\mathrm{cmd}}\) selects the H-bridge direction, and its magnitude sets the PWM after clamping it to the safe range. This measured, direction-dependent scaling is a static actuator compensation , also called static feedforward compensation. It linearizes the unequal heating and cooling gains by supplying the known extra cooling command immediately; it does not predict the rod's dynamic response. PI feedback corrects the remaining tracking error more completely than P-only feedback. Apply saturation in both feedback modes and anti-windup in PI mode, and never energize both H-bridge direction inputs simultaneously.
docs.title: S18.7: Repeat With P And PI Control

docs.text: Compare the two uncompensated PWM trials—zero-centered (S18.3) and positive-only (S18.4)—corrected feedforward (S18.5–S18.6), P-only (S18.7), and PI (S18.7) using mean temperature, amplitude, phase, heating-cooling symmetry, waveform distortion, residuals, and applied PWM. For feedforward/P/PI, compare mean tracking error and measured-to-requested amplitude at common \(T_a\) , \(T_b\) , and period. Use the time fits in Stage 4 and the A5 comparison requirements to quantify the differences. Raw-PWM trials have no requested temperature waveform; compare their measured response to the applied PWM. If settings must change, repeat the feedforward/P/PI comparison at common safe settings. Explain what worked and why: State which cases met the tracking objective and which did not, using explicit numerical criteria for acceptable mean error, amplitude error, and phase shift. Explain the limitations observed in open-loop and P-only control, what integral action improved, and why the PI gains needed tuning. Identify the selected gains at each tested period and support your choice with before-and-after tuning results. If no safe conditions achieved the full target, state that clearly and explain the limiting factor. Stop when: You have the common-setting comparison required by A5, including at least three settled cycles per method. If a trial is unusable, document it and return to this comparison after revising settings with Stage 4. Save: Evidence for S18.5-S18.8: susceptibility curves, measured ratio, feedforward map and predicted PWM, controller gains, raw records, and comparison plots and metrics. Use measured T1 as the boundary in every Angstrom fit.
docs.title: S18.8: Compare The Measured Boundary Responses

docs.text: Goal: Use the six histories to choose two usable forcing periods and a sensor layout that resolves amplitude decay and phase lag (Learning Objective 2). Do: Complete S18.9-S18.10 using live observations and time fits.
docs.title: Stage 4: Pilot Analysis And Experiment Plan

docs.text: Acquire pilot data with the best usable control method from Stage 3. Define numerical tolerances for changes in fitted mean, amplitude, and unwrapped phase between successive complete-cycle windows; use the measured noise and fit uncertainty to justify them. Inspect residuals for drift. Apply this settling test to the rod boundary and retained sensors before selecting a fit interval. Do not declare a response settled merely because five cycles have elapsed. Five cycles are the minimum retained after the team's quantitative settling criterion has been satisfied. The time required to approach a settled periodic response depends on both the amplitude and frequency of the drive. A larger amplitude can lengthen the transient and bring the actuator closer to its limits. At higher frequency the PI controller has less time to follow the changing setpoint, so tracking error, phase lag, attenuation, and waveform distortion generally increase. Use the measured T1 waveform and the settling test above to decide when the response is usable; do not assume that a fixed waiting time works for every choice of \(T_b\) and \(\omega\) . For each sensor, fit \[ T_i(t)=a_i+B_i\cos(\omega t+\phi_i). \] With this convention, a downstream phase lag appears as a smaller unwrapped value of \(\phi_i\) . Therefore a plot of unwrapped phase versus position has slope \(-q'\) . Reversing the sinusoid convention reverses the phase signs but must not change the inferred physics. The experimental example below shows temperatures measured at two rod positions. The traces have the same temporal frequency, while the downstream response has a smaller amplitude and reaches each peak later. Course data acquired with a 100-second forcing period, showing the two observables used by the Angstrom method: amplitude decay and phase lag. Fit each trace independently to obtain \(B_i\) and \(\phi_i\) ; spatial fits of \(\ln B_i\) and unwrapped \(\phi_i\) then determine \(q\) and \(q'\) .
docs.title: S18.9: Settle, Fit, And Improve The First Pilot Run

docs.text: The best waveform is the one that produces both measurable attenuation and a resolvable phase lag across several rod sensors while remaining safe and close to sinusoidal. Do not use a forcing period shorter than \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) . A \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) period with \(T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is an intentionally aggressive starting trial and may be difficult for the PI controller to track cleanly. Use the T1 waveform and pilot fits from S18.3-S18.8, not the command alone, to judge whether the boundary is usable. If the specified \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) , \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) temperature waveform is poorly tracked, try a \(200\ \mathrm{s}\) period or reduce \(T_b\) to \(10^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . Retune \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) after changing frequency or amplitude; gains that work for one waveform may not work well for another. Apply these decision rules: For the primary forcing period, aim for the farthest retained sensor to have \(B_{\mathrm{far}}\approx B_1/e\) . A substantially smaller response may be difficult to distinguish from sensor noise; a much larger response means that the sensor array spans less than one amplitude-decay length. Aim for an unwrapped phase lag from the first to the farthest retained sensor of roughly 0.5-2 radians. This is a planning target, not a fit constraint. If distant oscillations are too small, first try a longer period. If all sensors have nearly the same phase, a shorter period may help, but never go below \(100\ \mathrm{s}\) . If the measured waveform clips, flattens, or tracks poorly, reduce \(T_b\) , reduce the mean temperature, or retune the controller before collecting production data. Lower amplitude waveforms are generally easier for the PI controller to generate cleanly, but the temperature oscillation decreases with distance from the TEC. Reducing \(T_b\) can therefore make the response at downstream sensors difficult to distinguish from noise. If the oscillation is clean but too small at every sensor, increase \(T_b\) cautiously. Keep the measured rod-base temperature below \(56^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and retain margin for overshoot. Keep \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) fixed while comparing periods unless the pilot data show that a change is necessary. This makes frequency comparisons easier to interpret. Exclude the initial transient from the fit, keeping the raw file unchanged, and justify the selected interval. Fit at least five complete settled periods; plot the data and fitted sinusoid for every sensor, amplitude \(B_i\) versus position on a logarithmic vertical scale, and unwrapped phase versus position. Retain at least three rod sensors with measurable amplitude and phase.
docs.title: Optimize The Waveform From The Pilot Data

docs.text: Candidate periods are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 seconds while initially retaining the same \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) . Longer periods penetrate farther along the rod but produce less phase change per unit length. Select a second forcing period from the observed attenuation, phase lag, and base tracking. Keep \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) fixed unless a documented change is needed for safety or tracking. Record the change, watch the new transient decay, apply the same settling test, and retain at least five complete settled cycles with measurable amplitude and phase at three or more rod sensors. Keep the sinusoidal phase continuous when the frequency changes so that the requested temperature does not jump merely because a new frequency segment begins. At every transition, print a metadata/event line and include the active step and forcing parameters in subsequent data records. Preserve the transient after each frequency change; the analysis will later identify the settled interval for that frequency. Make the frequency change from the GUI when the live record is ready. An automatic scheduler is optional. Use the two pilot frequencies to finalize the sensor layout; if sensors move, remeasure the positions and update the map before production. Additional frequencies, up to roughly five spanning periods from 100 to 500 s, are an extension after the required pair is usable. Stop when: Two usable periods satisfy the settling, retained-cycle, and sensor requirements, and the pilot fits support the production settings. Save: Evidence for S18.9-S18.10, including fit intervals and settling comparisons. Your experiment plan must state the periods, mean, amplitude, run durations, sampling interval, safety limits, settling criterion, channels, files, and the tests you will use to decide whether each run is usable. At the end of S18, stop the apparatus safely and verify that the GUI file contains the complete run, including the raw-PWM, feedforward, P-only, and PI trials, startup transients, control-mode changes, and every frequency change. Preserve the raw file unchanged for the S19 analysis.
docs.title: S18.10: Select And Test A Second Usable Frequency

docs.text: Goal: Secure the required two-period dataset with the selected settings. Do: Acquire the required dataset using the settling and retained-cycle criteria established in S18.9-S18.10. Identify the settled interval independently for each frequency. Keep the rod geometry and sensor map unchanged. Record room temperature and check for drift. Preserve raw data. Apply any optional correction coefficients and all exclusions in analysis code, not by overwriting the original file. Record every restart, frequency transition, safety event, and departure from the approved protocol. If time permits after securing the required pair, acquire additional periods manually or with the optional tested schedule below. Stop when: Both required periods have verified complete records that pass the pilot-defined data-quality checks. Save: Raw production files, metadata, event records, sensor map, and the selected settled intervals for the P4 data-readiness check. Optional extension: build and test a frequency schedule For an optional automated schedule, revise the GUI and Arduino code so the GUI can define a sequence of frequency steps. Each step must specify at least its duration, \(T_a\) , \(T_b\) , and either \(\omega\) or the period. The Arduino advances the schedule and calculates the setpoint while the laptop remains connected and the Python GUI displays and records the measurements. Test an accelerated multi-step schedule before using it to collect data. Demonstrate safe completion, correct metadata, continuous recording, and at least two automatic frequency changes before restoring the intended durations. Use the candidate periods in S18.10 , the pilot data, and the stated settling criterion to choose each step duration; do not assume that every frequency settles on the same schedule. Allow the operator to hold or extend a step until the settling test and retained-cycle requirement are satisfied. Automatic elapsed-time transitions alone do not establish that the data are usable. Suggested Copilot prompt for the frequency schedule: Add a multi-frequency schedule to this working Arduino/Python system. Each step contains duration, mean temperature, sinusoidal amplitude, and period. Let the GUI edit, send, and display the schedule. Let the Arduino validate and execute it while the GUI remains connected, maintain continuous sinusoidal phase when the period changes, print step metadata in every CSV record, let the operator hold or extend a step for settling, preserve all existing safety limits, and finish with zero TEC output.
docs.title: Stage 5: Production Data

docs.text: Goal: Compare experiment and theory (Learning Objective 3). Use the spatial fits, residuals, frequency consistency, and finite-rod checks below to decide where the model succeeds and where its assumptions fail. Do: At each retained forcing period, fit \[ B(x)=B_0e^{-qx}, \qquad \phi(x)=\phi_0-q'x. \] Also fit the mean temperatures \(a_i\) to the finite insulated-tip rod model. Define \[ \xi_i=\frac{x_i}{L}, \qquad \mu=mL. \] Then fit the measured pairs \((\xi_i,a_i)\) to \[ \boxed{ a(\xi)-T_\infty =(a_0-T_\infty) \frac{\cosh[\mu(1-\xi)]}{\cosh(\mu)} }, \] where \(T_\infty\) is the measured room temperature and \(a_0\) is the fitted or measured mean temperature at \(x=0\) . Extract the dimensionless parameter \(\mu=mL\) , and then use the measured analysis length \(L\) to obtain \[ \boxed{m=\frac{\mu}{L}}. \] Propagate the uncertainties in both \(\mu\) and \(L\) . Compare this value of \(m\) with the Module 7 full-length mean-profile result and with the independent Angstrom relation \[ m=\sqrt{q^2-q'^2}. \] Because the Module 8 oscillatory sensor map is concentrated near the base, its \(a_i\) values may constrain \(mL\) less strongly than the full-length Module 7 data. Report the fit uncertainty and residuals rather than assuming that the finite-rod fit is precise.
docs.title: Stage 6: Spatial Fits

docs.text: Use your measured positions and temperature histories to infer \(\kappa\) and \(\nu\) from the spatial fits. Report the parameter values, units, uncertainty, and source data. Use one justified pair of material/heat-loss parameters for the theoretical curves across the period range; compare the estimates from different measured periods before combining them. If they disagree beyond uncertainty, show that disagreement and discuss the model limitations. Generate a theoretical plot of length versus forcing period from 100 to 500 s, with ticks at 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 s. Use \(\omega=2\pi/\tau\) and the derived expressions for \(m\) , \(q\) , and \(q'\) to plot \(\ell_{\mathrm{mean}}=\sqrt{\kappa/\nu}\) , \(\ell_{\mathrm{amp}}=1/q\) , and the spatial wavelength \(\lambda=2\pi/q'\) . Also show \(\ell_{\mathrm{phase}}=1/q'\) as a distinctly labeled curve so that a one-radian lag cannot be confused with a full cycle. Label axes and units, include parameter uncertainties as bands or explain their effect, and mark the measured analysis length \(L\) for comparison. At the periods actually measured, overlay the lengths obtained directly from your fits: \(1/m\) from the mean profile, \(1/q\) from amplitude decay, and \(1/q'\) and \(2\pi/q'\) from phase. Include uncertainties. Identify which measurements supplied the theoretical parameters; agreement with those same measurements is a consistency check, not an independent validation. Interpret every curve using the semi-infinite expression \[ T(x,t)=T_\infty+(a_0-T_\infty)e^{-x/\ell_{\mathrm{mean}}} +B_0e^{-x/\ell_{\mathrm{amp}}} \cos\!\left(\omega t-\frac{x}{\ell_{\mathrm{phase}}}+\phi_0\right). \] Here \(a_0\) , \(B_0\) , and \(\phi_0\) come from the measured rod-boundary temperature T1 , not the requested TEC setpoint. Explain what happens to the mean excess temperature over \(\ell_{\mathrm{mean}}\) , to the oscillation amplitude over \(\ell_{\mathrm{amp}}\) , and to the phase over \(\ell_{\mathrm{phase}}\) and \(\lambda\) . Relate spatial phase lag to time lag through \(\Delta t=q'x/\omega\) . Explain why the mean-decay length is independent of forcing period while the other lengths change, and why a full spatial wavelength may extend beyond the rod or beyond the region where the oscillation is measurable. Use your inferred parameters and measured boundary waveform to plot theoretical \(T(x,t)\) at the retained sensor positions for each measured period. Connect the mean offsets, shrinking amplitudes, and delayed peaks explicitly to the length plot. Use the finite insulated-tip solution where the semi-infinite approximation fails: the lengths remain model scales, but the finite-rod profiles need not be simple exponentials or have phase exactly proportional to \(x\) . Explain how the curves justify your chosen periods and sensor positions.
docs.title: Generate And Interpret Your Characteristic-Length Plot

docs.text: Your Python app, notebook, or script must visibly show: imported raw data and selected fitting interval, TEC tracking and the measured rod-base waveform, sinusoid fit for every retained sensor, mean temperature \(a_i\) versus position and the finite-rod fit yielding \(mL\) and \(m\) , amplitude and unwrapped phase versus position, fitted q and q_prime with units and uncertainty, calculated kappa and nu , the theoretical characteristic-length plot based on measured parameters, fitted length estimates with uncertainty, and the corresponding theoretical temperature histories with a physical interpretation of each length, residuals and any excluded data with justification, the finite-length and transverse-Biot-number checks that justify the one-dimensional semi-infinite analysis for the retained sensors. Use the two-stage analysis above as the primary method: first fit each temperature trace to obtain \(a_i\) , \(B_i\) , and \(\phi_i\) , and then fit their spatial dependence. This makes individual sensor behavior, phase unwrapping, and exclusions visible. As an optional model-validity extension, fit all retained \(T_i(t)\) data globally with one shared set of spatial parameters and compare the resulting \(q\) , \(q'\) , residuals, and uncertainties with the transparent two-stage result. Stop when: You have compared the inferred parameters across both required periods, inspected residuals and uncertainties, and stated where finite-length and transverse-Biot checks support or limit the model. Save: The runnable analysis, per-sensor and spatial fits, residuals, uncertainties, exclusions, the characteristic-length plot and its generating code, the corresponding temperature histories, and experiment-theory comparison.

docs.title: A5: S18 Evidence, Boundary-Control Analysis, And Angstrom Theory

docs.text: Include a ten-row table, one row for each action S18.1-S18.10 in Stages 1-4 . Each row must contain: the S18 action number and a concise statement of what was done, a specific evidence reference such as a filename and interval, figure, sensor map, calibration value, controller setting, GUI screenshot, code checkpoint, or event record, the measured or observed result, and any deviation from the procedure and its consequence. At minimum, the evidence must identify the six channels and sensor positions; show that the GUI displayed and saved complete records; report room temperature; identify the zero-centered and positive-only raw-PWM trials; report the measured heating-to-cooling ratio and feedforward map; identify the corrected feedforward, P-only, and PI intervals; document the settling test and retained cycles; and identify the second forcing frequency and its transition. Do not substitute a checklist of unsupported claims for evidence.
docs.title: Part 1: Evidence That The S18 Procedure Was Followed

docs.text: Begin with a concise comparison of the two uncompensated raw-PWM trials. Show the signed PWM and measured TEC temperature for the zero-centered command and the positive-only command, and explain what changed when polarity reversal was removed. Then, at one common value of \(T_a\) , \(T_b\) , and forcing period, compare corrected feedforward, P-only, and PI control. Include: A three-panel plot with common axes showing the requested setpoint, measured TEC temperature \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}(t)\) , and measured rod boundary \(T_1(t)\) for each control method over at least three settled cycles. A table reporting, for every method, the mean tracking error, measured-to- requested TEC amplitude ratio, TEC phase lag relative to the setpoint, RMS tracking error, and a quantitative measure of waveform distortion or fit residual. A plot of tracking error and signed PWM over representative settled cycles. Mark saturation and distinguish heating from cooling. A second comparison showing PI tuning at forcing periods of 100, 200, and 500 s. Include the initial and selected gain pairs and the before-and-after tracking metrics at each period. Hold \(T_a\) and \(T_b\) fixed unless safety or tracking requires a documented change. Plot the setpoint and measured TEC temperature and report how amplitude ratio, phase lag, RMS error, and distortion change with frequency. Answer these questions using the measurements: At the common frequency, how do feedforward, P-only, and PI control differ in mean error, amplitude, phase, heating-cooling symmetry, distortion, and required PWM? Which discrepancy does the susceptibility-based feedforward command reduce, and which dynamic errors can it not correct? Why can P-only control retain tracking error, and what does integral action improve? What new lag, overshoot, saturation, or windup behavior appears? As forcing frequency increases, why does the measured TEC temperature generally depart more strongly from the requested sinusoid? Relate the result to thermal inertia, controller bandwidth, actuator limits, and the gains used. How do \(T_{\mathrm{TEC}}(t)\) and \(T_1(t)\) differ in amplitude and phase? Explain why \(T_1(t)\) , rather than the requested setpoint or embedded TEC thermistor, is the boundary condition for the rod model. Conclude Part 2 with what worked and why . State whether the measured TEC achieved the requested \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) mean and \(16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) amplitude with a sufficiently small phase shift at each tested period. Give your numerical acceptance criteria and cite the measurements that support each verdict. Explain why the open-loop and P-only cases fell short under your test conditions, how PI changed the result, and why tuning \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) was necessary. If a case performed better than expected, explain that evidence rather than forcing the expected conclusion. Report any remaining tracking error, safety limitation, or failure to reach the full target.
docs.title: Part 2: Measured Boundary-Control Comparison

docs.text: First use the six-sensor numerical model as a controlled experiment. Reproduce the two diagnostic commands in order: a zero-centered sinusoidal PWM that reverses sign, followed by a positive-only sinusoidal PWM whose mean produces approximately \(40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) . Do not compensate heating and cooling in these two simulations. Explain the resulting symmetry, mean, amplitude, phase, and distortion of the simulated TEC temperature. Next use the course geometry, \(T_a=40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , \(T_b=16^\circ\mathrm{C}\) , and one common period for all three corrected control methods. Construct open-loop feedforward from the model's steady PWM-temperature susceptibility curve; then run P-only and PI control with the same \(K_p\) , changing only \(K_i\) between those two runs. Retain at least five settled cycles. For each method, fit the simulated TEC temperature to a sinusoid and report its mean, amplitude, phase lag, mean error, RMS error, waveform-fit residual, and the fraction of time for which the PWM saturates. Include setpoint-temperature and error-PWM plots with common axes. Repeat the PI simulation at periods of 100 s, 200 s, and 500 s. If a run is not usable, keep the result and explain the failure rather than silently retuning it. After preserving this fixed-gain comparison, tune \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) at each period to approach the requested amplitude and minimize the phase shift. Report the initial and selected gains, their units, and the resulting changes in tracking error, amplitude, phase, distortion, and saturation. Explain which settings worked and why; do not treat PI control as automatically successful. Answer the following questions from the simulations: Why can susceptibility-based feedforward reproduce the correct mean yet show substantial attenuation and phase lag at finite frequency? Why does P-only control have a nonzero mean tracking error? Relate the sign and size of that error to the mean PWM required to hold the rod above room temperature. Which error does integral action remove in the settled-periodic state, and why does zero mean error not imply zero instantaneous sinusoidal error? As the period decreases, how do amplitude ratio, phase lag, RMS error, and controller effort change? Identify the TEC, rod, sensor, and controller time scales responsible for the trend. Which method gives the smallest tracking error under these model conditions? Does that make it unconditionally best for the physical apparatus? Discuss saturation, windup, noise, robustness to model error, and the need to retune gains. Then run the simulator with the measured geometry and the closest available experimental values of \(T_a\) , \(T_b\) , period, controller type, and gains. Include at least one plot that compares measured and simulated TEC and rod temperatures over matched settled cycles. A side-by-side plot is acceptable when the simulated and measured time origins differ; normalize the phase reference explicitly. Explain which measured features the simulation reproduces and which it misses. Discuss TEC tracking, attenuation and phase lag along the rod, waveform distortion, finite-length effects, and plausible differences between the modeled and physical actuator, sensors, heat loss, and controller. Complete the amplitude/phase derivation, inverse relations for kappa and nu , and dimensional checks. Use the settled-periodic solution to explain why the mean excess temperature, oscillation amplitude, and phase are governed by three spatial scales. Connect the observed frequency dependence to \(q\) , \(q'\) , \(\kappa\) , and \(\nu\) , rather than describing the plots only. Include the justified acquisition plan and the finite-length and transverse-Biot checks carried forward from Module 7. State explicitly whether the retained sensors support the proposed one-dimensional analysis. Required characteristic-length evidence: Include your own Stage 6 characteristic-length plot , the measured parameters and data used to generate it, uncertainty estimates, and the corresponding theoretical \(T(x,t)\) histories. Explain in your own words what each length means in the temperature expression and in the plotted histories. Distinguish \(1/q'\) from \(2\pi/q'\) , explain the period dependence, and use the lengths to justify the measured sensor spacing and usable periods. Identify where finite-rod effects limit the exponential interpretation. The supplied illustration or a plot made only with handbook/default parameters does not satisfy this requirement.
